entry.guide_markdown:
# Locality Guide: Pulaski County, Kentucky (1840–1880)

## Jurisdiction overview
- **Formed:** December 10, 1798, from Lincoln and Green counties
- **County seat:** Somerset, Kentucky
- **Parent jurisdiction:** Kentucky, United States
- **Population during period:** Population data was not returned by place_population in this survey session; consult the Kentucky State Data Center or decennial census totals directly.
- **Economy:** Predominantly agricultural (subsistence farming, tobacco); timber; some river trade along the Cumberland River. The county was not heavily industrialized during this period.
- **Ethnic composition:** Predominantly Anglo-American settlers of Scots-Irish and English descent from Virginia and the Carolinas; small enslaved Black population.
- **Religious denominations:** Baptist (predominant), Methodist, and Presbyterian churches were the largest denominations in Kentucky before 1900, per the Kentucky Church Records wiki page (https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Kentucky_Church_Records).
- **Key historical events:** Civil War (1861–1865) — Kentucky was a border state; significant guerrilla activity and divided loyalties in south-central Kentucky.

## Boundary changes
- Pulaski County's boundaries have been stable since formation in 1798. No boundary changes during the 1840–1880 target period are documented in the place_search_all result.
- Records before 1798: search Lincoln County, Kentucky, and Green County, Kentucky (parent jurisdictions).

## Known record losses
- A disaster destroyed some Pulaski County records in 1838 and again in 1871, per the Pulaski County Genealogy wiki page (https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Pulaski_County,_Kentucky_Genealogy). The nature of each disaster (fire, flood) is not specified in that source.
- Expect gaps in court, deed, and other county records around those years. Substitute sources: Kentucky tax lists, church records, newspaper notices, and family bibles.

## Available record types

### Vital records (civil registration)
- **Start dates (county level):** Births and deaths — 1853–1862 and 1874–1878 only within this research window; marriages — from county formation (1799), per the Kentucky Vital Records wiki page (https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Kentucky_Vital_Records).
- **Statewide registration:** Did not begin until 1911 (general compliance by 1917) — entirely outside the 1840–1880 window.
- **What exists:** Marriage bonds and licenses from 1799 are the most consistent civil vital record. Birth and death registrations for 1853–1862 and 1874–1878 were recorded by county tax assessors and are fragmentary due to poor compliance.
- **Where held:** Pulaski County Courthouse (100 N. Main Street, #208, Somerset, KY 42502) — originals. Kentucky Department for Libraries and Archives (KDLA), Frankfort — microfilmed copies. FamilySearch — marriage bonds and consent forms 1799–1871 are digitized, per the county wiki page.
- **Gaps:** No civil birth or death registration outside 1853–1862 and 1874–1878 for this period. Civil War years (1862–1874) have no registration at all.
- **Pre-registration alternatives:** Church baptism and burial records; family bibles; cemetery inscriptions; newspaper death notices; mortality schedules in 1850, 1860, 1870, and 1880 censuses.

### Church records
- **Denominations present:** Baptist, Methodist, and Presbyterian were the largest groups in Kentucky before 1900, per the Kentucky Church Records wiki page (https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Kentucky_Church_Records). Individual congregations in Pulaski County are not enumerated in the tool results returned for this session.
- **Record types:** Baptisms/christenings, marriages, funerals/burials, membership lists, and congregation minutes.
- **Where held:** FamilySearch Library (microfilmed church records from many Kentucky congregations); Kentucky Historical Society, Frankfort (manuscript church records); Pulaski County Historical Society (described as holding the most comprehensive collection of church records for the county, per the county wiki page); individual active congregations. FamilySearch online: "Kentucky Church Records, 1818–1995" (index and images, incomplete); "Kentucky Births and Christenings, 1839–1960" (index only); "Kentucky Deaths and Burials, 1843–1970" (index only).
- **Language:** English.
- **Note:** Pulaski County falls within the Diocese of Lexington for Roman Catholic records; contact that diocese for any Catholic sacramental registers.

### Census records
- **Federal census:** 1840, 1850, 1860, 1870, 1880 — all available for Pulaski County. The 1890 federal census was largely destroyed (national loss).
- **Mortality schedules:** Available for 1850, 1860, 1870, and 1880 — record deaths in the year preceding the census enumeration. These are valuable substitutes for missing death registrations.
- **State/territorial census:** Kentucky did not conduct its own state census; no state enumeration supplements the federal series here.
- **Access:** Federal census years 1840–1880 are indexed and available with images on FamilySearch and Ancestry. Mortality schedules are also available on FamilySearch and Ancestry.

### Probate and court records
- **Types:** Wills, administrations, guardianships, inventories, estate distributions, court orders, equity suits.
- **Date range:** Probate from 1801; court records from 1799 — both from near county formation.
- **Where held:** Pulaski County Courthouse (Somerset) — originals. FamilySearch — early will books 1801–1929 are digitized, per the county wiki page (https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Pulaski_County,_Kentucky_Genealogy).
- **Note on 1838 and 1871 losses:** Some court records were destroyed in those disasters — gaps should be anticipated for records created before those dates.

### Land records
- **Survey system:** Kentucky is a state-land (metes and bounds) state, not a federal rectangular-survey state, per the Kentucky Land and Property wiki page (https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Kentucky_Land_and_Property).
- **Land-distribution jurisdiction:** Kentucky Land Office, Frankfort — holds land grants, original warrants, surveys, and patents. Grants relevant to the 1840–1880 window include Old Kentucky Grants (1793–1856) and Kentucky Land Warrants (1816–1873).
- **Types:** Deeds (county level from 1799); land grants and warrants (Kentucky Land Office); tax records (annual, county level).
- **Where held:** Pulaski County Courthouse — deed books from county formation. Kentucky Land Office, Frankfort — grants and patents. Kentucky Historical Society — additional land records and manuscripts. Online: FamilySearch holds Kentucky Land Office warrants, surveys, grants, and related records (1700–1955); Ancestry also holds Kentucky land grants.
- **Access:** Deed books in the county courthouse are primarily physical/in-person or via KDLA microfilm. Land grants are available online via FamilySearch and Ancestry.

### Military records
- **Relevant conflicts:** Mexican-American War (1846–1848); Civil War (1861–1865) — both Union and Confederate service for Kentucky men.
- **Record types:** Service records and pension files (NARA); bounty land warrants (War of 1812 and Mexican War claims); Civil War draft records; regimental histories.
- **Where held:** National Archives and Records Administration (NARA), Washington D.C. and regional facilities — service records and pension files. Fold3.com — military records including Civil War service records. Kentucky State Archives — state adjutant general records and state militia records.
- **Note:** Kentucky fielded both Union and Confederate regiments. Search both Union (NARA Record Group 94) and Confederate (NARA Record Group 109) records for men of military age during 1861–1865.

### Cemetery records
- **Major cemeteries:** Specific cemetery names in Pulaski County were not returned in this survey's tool results. The Pulaski County Historical Society holds cemetery survey data.
- **Online coverage:** Find A Grave (findagrave.com) — free, user-contributed; covers many Pulaski County cemeteries. BillionGraves — additional coverage.
- **Physical records:** Sexton records and burial registers, where they survive, are held by individual churches and cemeteries. The Pulaski County Historical Society holds compiled cemetery records.

### Newspaper records
- **Local papers:** Specific newspaper titles and date ranges for Somerset / Pulaski County were not returned in this survey's tool results. Consult the Kentucky Press Association archives or the Kentucky Digital Library.
- **Where held:** Newspapers.com (subscription) — historical newspapers including Kentucky titles. Kentucky Digital Library (kdl.kyvl.org) — digitized Kentucky newspapers, some free.
- **Content value:** Obituaries, marriage notices, legal notices (estate settlements, land sales), Civil War correspondence, and court reports.

### Immigration and emigration records
- **Context:** Pulaski County is an inland jurisdiction far from any port of entry. The population in this period was predominantly native-born. Immigration records are less central than for coastal or Great Lakes regions, but are not irrelevant.
- **Relevant ports:** Louisville, Cincinnati (Ohio River), and New Orleans were the nearest points of entry for immigrants settling in south-central Kentucky.
- **Record types:** Declarations of intention and naturalizations filed in Pulaski County Circuit Court (pre-1906, any court of record could naturalize); passenger lists at NARA for named ports.
- **Note:** Passenger lists record every person aboard, including infants and children traveling with parents. Examine the full manifest when researching a family.

### Tax records
- **Types:** Annual county tax lists (property and poll tax) from near county formation.
- **Date range:** From 1799 (county formation); coverage during 1840–1880 expected to be consistent.
- **Where held:** KDLA (microfilmed); some available on Ancestry (Kentucky tax lists). County originals at Pulaski County Courthouse.
- **Substitute value:** Tax lists appear annually and can place a person in the county in years between federal censuses, making them especially valuable for the 1841–1849, 1851–1859, 1861–1869, and 1871–1879 intercensal years.

### Other record types
- **County histories:** Published county and regional histories (typically late 19th to early 20th century) sometimes reprint early records and contain biographical sketches of prominent families. Check WorldCat and the Kentucky Historical Society for Pulaski County histories.
- **School records:** District school records, where they survive, are held at the county level. Enrollment records for this period are fragmentary.
- **Institutional and occupational records:** No major institutions (asylums, prisons, factories) are identified for Pulaski County in this period from tool results.

## Repository guide

### Online repositories
| Repository | Collections for this place | Access |
|---|---|---|
| FamilySearch | Will books (1801–1929); marriage bonds and consent forms (1799–1871); Kentucky Church Records (partial); Kentucky Births/Christenings, Deaths/Burials, Marriages indexes; Kentucky land grants and warrants; federal census 1840–1880; mortality schedules | Free |
| Ancestry | Federal census 1840–1880; Kentucky land grants; county tax lists; vital record indexes; military records | Subscription |
| Fold3 | Civil War service records (Union and Confederate); pension files; draft records | Subscription |
| Find A Grave | Cemetery inscriptions for Pulaski County | Free |
| Newspapers.com | Historical Kentucky newspapers including local titles | Subscription |
| Kentucky Digital Library (kdl.kyvl.org) | Digitized Kentucky newspapers | Free |
| BLM General Land Office (glorecords.blm.gov) | Federal land patents (limited applicability for KY state-land grants) | Free |

**Coverage of this survey:** The FamilySearch collections_search and volume_search tools returned zero results for both the county and state levels in this session — this represents a tool place-resolution gap, not confirmed absence of FamilySearch holdings. The Pulaski County Genealogy wiki page confirms specific digitized holdings on FamilySearch (will books, marriage bonds). The number of digitized FamilySearch volumes for Pulaski County could not be verified in this session.

### Physical repositories
| Repository | Holdings | Access method |
|---|---|---|
| Pulaski County Courthouse, 100 N. Main St. #208, Somerset, KY 42502 | Marriage bonds, deeds, court orders, wills from county formation (1799) | In-person or mail request |
| Pulaski County Historical Society, Somerset, KY | Church records, obituary files, surname vertical files, cemetery surveys | In-person; contact for hours |
| Kentucky Department for Libraries and Archives (KDLA), Frankfort, KY | Microfilmed county records statewide including Pulaski; pre-1911 vital records | In-person; some microfilm available via interlibrary loan |
| Kentucky Historical Society, Frankfort, KY | Land records, manuscripts, published county histories | In-person; some online finding aids |
| Kentucky Land Office, Frankfort, KY | Land grants, warrants, surveys, patents | In-person; online via FamilySearch and Ancestry |
| NARA (National Archives), Washington D.C. | Federal census originals; military service records and pension files; naturalization records | In-person; many records online via Ancestry and Fold3 |

## Records NOT online
- Original deed books from the Pulaski County Courthouse (1799 onward) are largely physical or available only on KDLA microfilm, not comprehensively digitized with images online.
- Most church congregation records for individual Pulaski County churches are held by local churches or the Pulaski County Historical Society and are not online.
- County court order books and minute books (beyond the will books on FamilySearch) are not comprehensively online.
- Original annual county tax lists are primarily on KDLA microfilm; partial coverage on Ancestry.
- School records from this period are not online.

## Research tips
- **Record losses in 1838 and 1871:** When records appear missing for certain years, these disasters are the likely cause. Pivot to church records, Kentucky tax lists, and newspaper notices as substitutes. (Source: Pulaski County Genealogy wiki, https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Pulaski_County,_Kentucky_Genealogy)
- **Civil War border-state complexity:** Kentucky officially remained in the Union, but many men served in Confederate units. Search both Union and Confederate record series at NARA and on Fold3.
- **Marriage records are the most reliable vital record for this window:** County-level marriage bonds run from 1799 and FamilySearch has digitized them through 1871. For 1872–1880 marriages, check the courthouse directly.
- **Kentucky is a state-land state:** Do not expect to find Pulaski County land grants in the BLM GLO federal records system. Go to the Kentucky Land Office (online via FamilySearch) for grants. Deed books at the courthouse handle person-to-person transfers. (Source: Kentucky Land and Property wiki, https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Kentucky_Land_and_Property)
- **Tax lists as census substitutes:** Annual county tax lists place individuals in the county every year between federal censuses. KDLA microfilm and partial Ancestry coverage are the access points.

added.guide_markdown:
# Locality Guide: Pulaski County, Kentucky (1840–1880)

## Jurisdiction overview
- **Formed:** December 10, 1798, from Lincoln and Green counties
- **County seat:** Somerset, Kentucky
- **Parent jurisdiction:** Kentucky, United States
- **Population during period:** Population data was not returned by place_population in this survey session; consult the Kentucky State Data Center or decennial census totals directly.
- **Economy:** Predominantly agricultural (subsistence farming, tobacco); timber; some river trade along the Cumberland River. The county was not heavily industrialized during this period.
- **Ethnic composition:** Predominantly Anglo-American settlers of Scots-Irish and English descent from Virginia and the Carolinas; small enslaved Black population.
- **Religious denominations:** Baptist (predominant), Methodist, and Presbyterian churches were the largest denominations in Kentucky before 1900, per the Kentucky Church Records wiki page (https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Kentucky_Church_Records).
- **Key historical events:** Civil War (1861–1865) — Kentucky was a border state; significant guerrilla activity and divided loyalties in south-central Kentucky.

## Boundary changes
- Pulaski County's boundaries have been stable since formation in 1798. No boundary changes during the 1840–1880 target period are documented in the place_search_all result.
- Records before 1798: search Lincoln County, Kentucky, and Green County, Kentucky (parent jurisdictions).

## Known record losses
- A disaster destroyed some Pulaski County records in 1838 and again in 1871, per the Pulaski County Genealogy wiki page (https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Pulaski_County,_Kentucky_Genealogy). The nature of each disaster (fire, flood) is not specified in that source.
- Expect gaps in court, deed, and other county records around those years. Substitute sources: Kentucky tax lists, church records, newspaper notices, and family bibles.

## Available record types

### Vital records (civil registration)
- **Start dates (county level):** Births and deaths — 1853–1862 and 1874–1878 only within this research window; marriages — from county formation (1799), per the Kentucky Vital Records wiki page (https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Kentucky_Vital_Records).
- **Statewide registration:** Did not begin until 1911 (general compliance by 1917) — entirely outside the 1840–1880 window.
- **What exists:** Marriage bonds and licenses from 1799 are the most consistent civil vital record. Birth and death registrations for 1853–1862 and 1874–1878 were recorded by county tax assessors and are fragmentary due to poor compliance.
- **Where held:** Pulaski County Courthouse (100 N. Main Street, #208, Somerset, KY 42502) — originals. Kentucky Department for Libraries and Archives (KDLA), Frankfort — microfilmed copies. FamilySearch — marriage bonds and consent forms 1799–1871 are digitized, per the county wiki page.
- **Gaps:** No civil birth or death registration outside 1853–1862 and 1874–1878 for this period. Civil War years (1862–1874) have no registration at all.
- **Pre-registration alternatives:** Church baptism and burial records; family bibles; cemetery inscriptions; newspaper death notices; mortality schedules in 1850, 1860, 1870, and 1880 censuses.

### Church records
- **Denominations present:** Baptist, Methodist, and Presbyterian were the largest groups in Kentucky before 1900, per the Kentucky Church Records wiki page (https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Kentucky_Church_Records). Individual congregations in Pulaski County are not enumerated in the tool results returned for this session.
- **Record types:** Baptisms/christenings, marriages, funerals/burials, membership lists, and congregation minutes.
- **Where held:** FamilySearch Library (microfilmed church records from many Kentucky congregations); Kentucky Historical Society, Frankfort (manuscript church records); Pulaski County Historical Society (described as holding the most comprehensive collection of church records for the county, per the county wiki page); individual active congregations. FamilySearch online: "Kentucky Church Records, 1818–1995" (index and images, incomplete); "Kentucky Births and Christenings, 1839–1960" (index only); "Kentucky Deaths and Burials, 1843–1970" (index only).
- **Language:** English.
- **Note:** Pulaski County falls within the Diocese of Lexington for Roman Catholic records; contact that diocese for any Catholic sacramental registers.

### Census records
- **Federal census:** 1840, 1850, 1860, 1870, 1880 — all available for Pulaski County. The 1890 federal census was largely destroyed (national loss).
- **Mortality schedules:** Available for 1850, 1860, 1870, and 1880 — record deaths in the year preceding the census enumeration. These are valuable substitutes for missing death registrations.
- **State/territorial census:** Kentucky did not conduct its own state census; no state enumeration supplements the federal series here.
- **Access:** Federal census years 1840–1880 are indexed and available with images on FamilySearch and Ancestry. Mortality schedules are also available on FamilySearch and Ancestry.

### Probate and court records
- **Types:** Wills, administrations, guardianships, inventories, estate distributions, court orders, equity suits.
- **Date range:** Probate from 1801; court records from 1799 — both from near county formation.
- **Where held:** Pulaski County Courthouse (Somerset) — originals. FamilySearch — early will books 1801–1929 are digitized, per the county wiki page (https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Pulaski_County,_Kentucky_Genealogy).
- **Note on 1838 and 1871 losses:** Some court records were destroyed in those disasters — gaps should be anticipated for records created before those dates.

### Land records
- **Survey system:** Kentucky is a state-land (metes and bounds) state, not a federal rectangular-survey state, per the Kentucky Land and Property wiki page (https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Kentucky_Land_and_Property).
- **Land-distribution jurisdiction:** Kentucky Land Office, Frankfort — holds land grants, original warrants, surveys, and patents. Grants relevant to the 1840–1880 window include Old Kentucky Grants (1793–1856) and Kentucky Land Warrants (1816–1873).
- **Types:** Deeds (county level from 1799); land grants and warrants (Kentucky Land Office); tax records (annual, county level).
- **Where held:** Pulaski County Courthouse — deed books from county formation. Kentucky Land Office, Frankfort — grants and patents. Kentucky Historical Society — additional land records and manuscripts. Online: FamilySearch holds Kentucky Land Office warrants, surveys, grants, and related records (1700–1955); Ancestry also holds Kentucky land grants.
- **Access:** Deed books in the county courthouse are primarily physical/in-person or via KDLA microfilm. Land grants are available online via FamilySearch and Ancestry.

### Military records
- **Relevant conflicts:** Mexican-American War (1846–1848); Civil War (1861–1865) — both Union and Confederate service for Kentucky men.
- **Record types:** Service records and pension files (NARA); bounty land warrants (War of 1812 and Mexican War claims); Civil War draft records; regimental histories.
- **Where held:** National Archives and Records Administration (NARA), Washington D.C. and regional facilities — service records and pension files. Fold3.com — military records including Civil War service records. Kentucky State Archives — state adjutant general records and state militia records.
- **Note:** Kentucky fielded both Union and Confederate regiments. Search both Union (NARA Record Group 94) and Confederate (NARA Record Group 109) records for men of military age during 1861–1865.

### Cemetery records
- **Major cemeteries:** Specific cemetery names in Pulaski County were not returned in this survey's tool results. The Pulaski County Historical Society holds cemetery survey data.
- **Online coverage:** Find A Grave (findagrave.com) — free, user-contributed; covers many Pulaski County cemeteries. BillionGraves — additional coverage.
- **Physical records:** Sexton records and burial registers, where they survive, are held by individual churches and cemeteries. The Pulaski County Historical Society holds compiled cemetery records.

### Newspaper records
- **Local papers:** Specific newspaper titles and date ranges for Somerset / Pulaski County were not returned in this survey's tool results. Consult the Kentucky Press Association archives or the Kentucky Digital Library.
- **Where held:** Newspapers.com (subscription) — historical newspapers including Kentucky titles. Kentucky Digital Library (kdl.kyvl.org) — digitized Kentucky newspapers, some free.
- **Content value:** Obituaries, marriage notices, legal notices (estate settlements, land sales), Civil War correspondence, and court reports.

### Immigration and emigration records
- **Context:** Pulaski County is an inland jurisdiction far from any port of entry. The population in this period was predominantly native-born. Immigration records are less central than for coastal or Great Lakes regions, but are not irrelevant.
- **Relevant ports:** Louisville, Cincinnati (Ohio River), and New Orleans were the nearest points of entry for immigrants settling in south-central Kentucky.
- **Record types:** Declarations of intention and naturalizations filed in Pulaski County Circuit Court (pre-1906, any court of record could naturalize); passenger lists at NARA for named ports.
- **Note:** Passenger lists record every person aboard, including infants and children traveling with parents. Examine the full manifest when researching a family.

### Tax records
- **Types:** Annual county tax lists (property and poll tax) from near county formation.
- **Date range:** From 1799 (county formation); coverage during 1840–1880 expected to be consistent.
- **Where held:** KDLA (microfilmed); some available on Ancestry (Kentucky tax lists). County originals at Pulaski County Courthouse.
- **Substitute value:** Tax lists appear annually and can place a person in the county in years between federal censuses, making them especially valuable for the 1841–1849, 1851–1859, 1861–1869, and 1871–1879 intercensal years.

### Other record types
- **County histories:** Published county and regional histories (typically late 19th to early 20th century) sometimes reprint early records and contain biographical sketches of prominent families. Check WorldCat and the Kentucky Historical Society for Pulaski County histories.
- **School records:** District school records, where they survive, are held at the county level. Enrollment records for this period are fragmentary.
- **Institutional and occupational records:** No major institutions (asylums, prisons, factories) are identified for Pulaski County in this period from tool results.

## Repository guide

### Online repositories
| Repository | Collections for this place | Access |
|---|---|---|
| FamilySearch | Will books (1801–1929); marriage bonds and consent forms (1799–1871); Kentucky Church Records (partial); Kentucky Births/Christenings, Deaths/Burials, Marriages indexes; Kentucky land grants and warrants; federal census 1840–1880; mortality schedules | Free |
| Ancestry | Federal census 1840–1880; Kentucky land grants; county tax lists; vital record indexes; military records | Subscription |
| Fold3 | Civil War service records (Union and Confederate); pension files; draft records | Subscription |
| Find A Grave | Cemetery inscriptions for Pulaski County | Free |
| Newspapers.com | Historical Kentucky newspapers including local titles | Subscription |
| Kentucky Digital Library (kdl.kyvl.org) | Digitized Kentucky newspapers | Free |
| BLM General Land Office (glorecords.blm.gov) | Federal land patents (limited applicability for KY state-land grants) | Free |

**Coverage of this survey:** The FamilySearch collections_search and volume_search tools returned zero results for both the county and state levels in this session — this represents a tool place-resolution gap, not confirmed absence of FamilySearch holdings. The Pulaski County Genealogy wiki page confirms specific digitized holdings on FamilySearch (will books, marriage bonds). The number of digitized FamilySearch volumes for Pulaski County could not be verified in this session.

### Physical repositories
| Repository | Holdings | Access method |
|---|---|---|
| Pulaski County Courthouse, 100 N. Main St. #208, Somerset, KY 42502 | Marriage bonds, deeds, court orders, wills from county formation (1799) | In-person or mail request |
| Pulaski County Historical Society, Somerset, KY | Church records, obituary files, surname vertical files, cemetery surveys | In-person; contact for hours |
| Kentucky Department for Libraries and Archives (KDLA), Frankfort, KY | Microfilmed county records statewide including Pulaski; pre-1911 vital records | In-person; some microfilm available via interlibrary loan |
| Kentucky Historical Society, Frankfort, KY | Land records, manuscripts, published county histories | In-person; some online finding aids |
| Kentucky Land Office, Frankfort, KY | Land grants, warrants, surveys, patents | In-person; online via FamilySearch and Ancestry |
| NARA (National Archives), Washington D.C. | Federal census originals; military service records and pension files; naturalization records | In-person; many records online via Ancestry and Fold3 |

## Records NOT online
- Original deed books from the Pulaski County Courthouse (1799 onward) are largely physical or available only on KDLA microfilm, not comprehensively digitized with images online.
- Most church congregation records for individual Pulaski County churches are held by local churches or the Pulaski County Historical Society and are not online.
- County court order books and minute books (beyond the will books on FamilySearch) are not comprehensively online.
- Original annual county tax lists are primarily on KDLA microfilm; partial coverage on Ancestry.
- School records from this period are not online.

## Research tips
- **Record losses in 1838 and 1871:** When records appear missing for certain years, these disasters are the likely cause. Pivot to church records, Kentucky tax lists, and newspaper notices as substitutes. (Source: Pulaski County Genealogy wiki, https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Pulaski_County,_Kentucky_Genealogy)
- **Civil War border-state complexity:** Kentucky officially remained in the Union, but many men served in Confederate units. Search both Union and Confederate record series at NARA and on Fold3.
- **Marriage records are the most reliable vital record for this window:** County-level marriage bonds run from 1799 and FamilySearch has digitized them through 1871. For 1872–1880 marriages, check the courthouse directly.
- **Kentucky is a state-land state:** Do not expect to find Pulaski County land grants in the BLM GLO federal records system. Go to the Kentucky Land Office (online via FamilySearch) for grants. Deed books at the courthouse handle person-to-person transfers. (Source: Kentucky Land and Property wiki, https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Kentucky_Land_and_Property)
- **Tax lists as census substitutes:** Annual county tax lists place individuals in the county every year between federal censuses. KDLA microfilm and partial Ancestry coverage are the access points.
- **Mortality schedules:** The 1850, 1860, 1870, and 1880 mortality schedules record deaths in the year before the census and are essential substitutes for the fragmentary civil death registration. Search these on FamilySearch and Ancestry.
- **Pulaski County Historical Society:** This repository is specifically described as holding the most comprehensive church records and obituary collection for the county — contact them before concluding that church records are unavailable. (Source: Pulaski County Genealogy wiki, https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Pulaski_County,_Kentucky_Genealogy)
- **Neighboring counties:** Families near county lines may have records in adjacent jurisdictions. Lincoln County (north, also a parent jurisdiction), Wayne County (south), Laurel County (east), Casey County (northwest), Russell County (southwest), and Rockcastle County (northeast) are the likely neighbors — verify via the county wiki page, as the neighboring-counties table was not returned in this session.
- **FamilySearch catalog:** The catalog search returned zero results in this session due to a place-resolution issue. Search the FamilySearch Catalog manually at familysearch.org/catalog using "Pulaski County, Kentucky" to find microfilmed volumes of court records, deed books, and other record sets not captured in this survey.

- **FamilySearch** — several indexed collections covering marriages from 1809, probate from 1809, and church records from 1803; also browse-only (not name-searchable) image volumes for territorial court, land, deed, and probate records from roughly 1803–1820.
- **Bureau of Land Management – General Land Office Records** (glorecords.blm.gov) — federal land patents, often the earliest documentary evidence placing a settler in the territory; searchable free online.

**Colonial-era records** (pre-1798): if your ancestor was in the Mobile area under Spanish or British rule, records are held in archives in Seville, Aix-en-Provence, and the Library of Congress.

The next step would be to narrow the survey to the specific county where your ancestor lived, since county formation dates (the earliest formed in 1799–1810) determine exactly where records were filed and whether those county records survive or were lost to later courthouse fires.

entry.guide_markdown:
# Locality Guide: Alabama Region (Pre-Statehood) (ca. 1780-1820)

## Jurisdiction overview
- **Formed:** Alabama achieved statehood December 14, 1819. Before that, the region passed through multiple jurisdictions: Mississippi Territory (1798-1817), Alabama Territory (1817-1819), and before 1798, French, British, and Spanish colonial authority.
- **County seat / administrative center:** Mobile was the principal town during the colonial and early territorial period. Huntsville (in the Tennessee Valley) and St. Stephens (Washington County) were early American settlements.
- **Parent jurisdiction:** Mississippi Territory (1798-1817), then Alabama Territory (1817-1819), then state of Alabama (1819+).
- **Population during period:** Population data was not returned by place_population for these jurisdictions. According to Wikipedia, the region saw significant migration from the Carolinas, Virginia, and Georgia especially after the Creek War of 1813-1814. The 1810 federal census enumerated the Mississippi Territory.
- **Economy:** Subsistence farming, fur trade, early cotton cultivation (especially in the Tombigbee and Tennessee River valleys). Mobile was a port trading post.
- **Ethnic composition:** Creek and Cherokee nations held most of the interior. European settlers were mainly Anglo-American migrants from the Carolinas, Virginia, and Georgia; a French Creole and Spanish Creole population in and around Mobile; enslaved African Americans.
- **Religious denominations:** Predominantly Protestant (Baptist, Methodist) among American settlers; Roman Catholic in the Mobile area (French and Spanish Catholic tradition).
- **Key historical events:** French founding of Mobile, 1702; British acquisition, 1763; Spanish takeover, 1780; U.S. acquisition of Mississippi Territory, 1798; War of 1812 and Creek War, 1813-1814; Alabama Territory, 1817; statehood, 1819.

## Boundary changes
- **Before 1798:** The territory was not under U.S. authority. The Mobile district was Spanish; interior lands were British (before 1780), then nominally Spanish and/or unceded Native territory.
- **1798:** Mississippi Territory established, covering present-day Mississippi and Alabama south of the Tennessee River.
- **1804:** Mississippi Territory expanded northward to cover all of present-day Alabama.
- **1817:** Mississippi achieved statehood; the Alabama Territory was carved out of the eastern portion of the Mississippi Territory.
- **1819:** Alabama achieved statehood (December 14).
- **Implication:** Any record created before 1817 is a Mississippi Territory record. Any county formed after statehood holds only post-1819 records at the county level — earlier events must be sought in territorial records or the predecessor county.

## Available record types

### Vital records (civil registration)
- **Start date:** There was no statewide civil registration of births or deaths in Alabama during the 1780-1820 period. The FamilySearch wiki pages for Alabama Vital Records, Alabama Naming Customs, and related topics all redirected to generic content and could not confirm a specific statewide start date. Marriage bonds and licenses were recorded at the county level beginning in some counties from 1809 onward (FamilySearch collection "Alabama, County Marriages, 1809-1950", collection id 1598408).
- **What exists:** Marriage records from 1809 in early-formed counties. No indexed birth or death records from this period.
- **Where held:** County probate courts (which in Alabama handled marriages); Alabama Department of Archives and History (ADAH), Montgomery, holds microfilm copies of many county marriage records. FamilySearch collection 1598408 covers 1809-1950.
- **Gaps:** Births and deaths — no civil registration. Marriage records exist only from the date a given county was formed and began keeping records.
- **Pre-registration alternatives:** Church baptism and burial registers; family Bible records; probate records naming heirs; estate inventories.

### Church records
- **Denominations present:** Roman Catholic (Mobile area — French and Spanish tradition); Baptist and Methodist (American settler communities).
- **Record types:** Baptisms, marriages, burials, confirmations.
- **Where held:** Catholic records for Mobile are at the Archdiocese of Mobile archives and at the Mobile Municipal Archives. French Catholic colonial records are at the Archives Nationales d'Outre-Mer, Aix-en-Provence, France, with some microfilm at the Mobile Municipal Archives. Spanish-era church registers for the Mobile District are at the Archivo General de Indias, Seville, with copies at the Library of Congress (per FamilySearch wiki https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Alabama_Genealogy#Colonial_Records). Protestant church records are scattered at local congregations and some denominations' archives. FamilySearch collection "Alabama, Church Records, 1803-1950" (id 1986396) covers some records from 1803.
- **Language:** French-era records in French; Spanish-era records in Spanish; Protestant records in English.

### Census records
- **Federal/national census:** The 1810 federal census covered the Mississippi Territory (including present-day Alabama). The 1820 federal census covered Alabama as a newly admitted state.
- **Territorial censuses:** The Mississippi Territory conducted censuses in 1801, 1805, 1808, and 1810 enumerating settlers in present-day Alabama. These are held at ADAH in Montgomery (per FamilySearch wiki https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Alabama_Genealogy#Territorial_Records).
- **Access:** FamilySearch collection "Alabama, Compiled Census and Census Substitutes Index, 1810-1890" (id 2016756, 287,634 records, no images) and "Mississippi, Compiled Census and Census Substitutes, 1792-1890" (id 1927171, 198,340 records, no images) are indexed but image-free — they are indexes only. Volume_search returned no dedicated census image volumes for this period.

### Probate and court records
- **Types:** Wills, administrations, guardianships, inventories, estate petitions. Also territorial court records (suits, land disputes).
- **Date range:** County-level probate begins from each county's formation date (the earliest Alabama counties formed 1799-1810 under territorial administration). Territorial court records begin 1798.
- **Where held:** Original county records at each county's probate court or courthouse. ADAH holds microfilm of many county records. FamilySearch collection "Alabama, Probate Records, 1809-1985" (id 1537764, 438,210 records, images available). Two browse-only image volumes on FamilySearch: imageGroupNumber 004512889 (territorial court and land records, 1808-1819, 214 images, 0% indexed) and 004512890 (Washington County deed and probate, 1803-1820, 96 images, 0% indexed). Both must be browsed image by image with no name search.
- **Digitization level:** Partially indexed (collection 1537764); browse-only for the territorial-era volumes.

### Land records
- **Survey system:** Federal rectangular survey (Alabama is a public-land state; the federal government, not the state, distributed original land grants).
- **Land-distribution jurisdiction:** The U.S. General Land Office (GLO) issued patents; records are online at the Bureau of Land Management GLO website (glorecords.blm.gov). Spanish land grants in the Mobile district were issued by Spanish colonial authorities; those records are at the Archivo General de Indias, Seville, with copies at ADAH and the Library of Congress.
- **Types:** Federal land patents, Spanish land grants, subsequent deeds, tax records.
- **Date range:** American land sales in what is now Alabama began after 1800; the first federal land office for Alabama opened in 1803 at St. Stephens. Spanish land grants predate 1813.
- **Where held:** Federal patents: BLM GLO website (free, online). Subsequent deeds: county courthouses. Territorial land records: volume 004512889 on FamilySearch (browse-only, 1808-1819). FamilySearch collection "Mississippi, Territorial and State Land Records, 1798-1907" (id 1919694, 312,450 records, images) covers the territorial period and includes Alabama-area lands.
- **Digitization level:** BLM GLO patents — indexed + images online (free). Territorial land records on FamilySearch — browse-only images or partially indexed (collection 1919694).

### Military records
- **Relevant conflicts:** Creek War 1813-1814; War of 1812 (defense of Mobile).
- **Record types:** Service records, pension files, bounty land warrants. Territorial militia rolls.
- **Where held:** NARA (federal service records and pension files). ADAH holds Alabama militia and territorial records. Fold3 (fold3.com) has digitized many NARA military records.

### Cemetery records
- **Major cemeteries:** Few formal cemeteries from this period; family burial plots and church graveyards are the main type.
- **Online coverage:** Find A Grave (findagrave.com) indexes some early Alabama graves; coverage for pre-1820 is sparse.
- **Physical records:** Sexton records for this period are rare or nonexistent. Cemetery survey transcriptions by genealogical societies (especially the Alabama Genealogical Society) exist for some counties.

### Newspaper records
- **Local papers:** The Mobile Centinel (later Gazette) was one of Alabama's earliest papers, founded ca. 1811. Very few newspapers existed in the Alabama region before 1810.
- **Where held:** ADAH holds some early Alabama newspaper microfilm. Newspapers.com and Chronicling America (Library of Congress) have some digitized Alabama newspapers, but coverage for pre-1820 is minimal.
- **Content value:** Legal notices, land sale notices, and some death/marriage notices.

### Immigration and emigration records
- **Relevant ports:** Mobile (Gulf Coast); New Orleans (for migrants arriving by sea or river).
- **Record types:** Passenger lists (NARA); Spanish-era passport and travel records (Archivo General de Indias).
- **Where held:** NARA holds post-1820 passenger lists. For the 1800 period, formal arrival records are sparse. The FamilySearch wiki notes that the region attracted migrants overland from the Carolinas, Virginia, and Georgia — those migrants left few formal arrival records but may appear in land entry files.
- **Content note:** Passenger lists record every person aboard, including infants and young children traveling with parents.

### Tax records
- **Types:** Territorial and county-level property and poll tax lists.
- **Date range:** Territorial tax records begin 1798-1800 in some districts.
- **Where held:** ADAH; county archives.
- **Substitute value:** Tax lists substitute for missing census years and are especially important for 1801-1809 before county marriage records begin.

### Other record types
- **Spanish colonial records:** Census returns, church registers, land grants, and civil records of the Mobile District under Spanish administration (1780-1813) are at the Archivo General de Indias, Seville, with some copies at the Library of Congress and ADAH.
- **French colonial records:** Records of the French colonial period (1702-1763) are at the Archives Nationales d'Outre-Mer, Aix-en-Provence, France, and on microfilm at the Mobile Municipal Archives.
- **Creek and Cherokee records:** Records of Native nations from this period are in specialized collections at NARA and at tribal archives.

## Repository guide

### Online repositories
| Repository | Collections for this place | Access |
|---|---|---|
| FamilySearch | County Marriages 1809-1950 (1598408); Probate Records 1809-1985 (1537764); Compiled Census/Substitutes 1810-1890 (2016756); Church Records 1803-1950 (1986396); Mississippi Territorial and State Land Records 1798-1907 (1919694); Mississippi County Court Records 1799-1920 (1855293); Mississippi Census Substitutes 1792-1890 (1927171); Mississippi Church Records 1800-1950 (2034891); Browse-only volumes 004512889 and 004512890 | Free |
| BLM General Land Office | Federal land patents for Alabama public-land sales | Free (glorecords.blm.gov) |
| Ancestry.com | U.S. Federal Census Collection (includes 1810 and 1820) | Subscription |
| Fold3 | Military service records and pension files | Subscription |
| Find A Grave | Cemetery records | Free |
| NARA (archives.gov) | Military records, pension files | Free finding aids; some records online via Fold3/Ancestry |

**Coverage of this survey:** The FamilySearch volume_search returned 2 digitized but browse-only image volumes matching Alabama for 1780-1820 (total results: 2; this is the complete set for that query). These are the only named volumes in tool results; additional holdings will exist in physical or partially described form at ADAH and county courthouses.

### Physical repositories
| Repository | Holdings | Access method |
|---|---|---|
| Alabama Department of Archives and History (ADAH), Montgomery, AL | Territorial censuses 1801/1805/1808/1810; county records microfilm; militia records; tax lists; newspapers | In-person; some digitized at adah.alabama.gov |
| County courthouses | Deed books, probate records, marriage bonds (from county formation date) | In-person or mail |
| Archdiocese of Mobile Archives | Catholic parish registers (Mobile area) | Contact archive for access |
| Mobile Municipal Archives | French colonial church register microfilm; early city records | In-person |
| Archives Nationales d'Outre-Mer, Aix-en-Provence, France | French colonial records 1702-1763 | In-person or correspondence |
| Archivo General de Indias, Seville, Spain | Spanish colonial records 1780-1813 (church, land, census) | In-person; partial digitization at pares.mcu.es |
| Library of Congress, Washington DC | Copies of Spanish colonial records | In-person; some online |
| NARA (Atlanta regional facility and Washington DC) | Federal land entry files, military records, 1810 and 1820 federal census originals | In-person; many records online |

## Records NOT online
- Territorial tax lists (1798-1819): primarily physical at ADAH.
- Spanish-era church registers and land grants: primarily at Archivo General de Indias with partial digitization; copies at Library of Congress.
- French colonial records: at Archives Nationales d'Outre-Mer; microfilm at Mobile Municipal Archives.
- Most pre-1809 county-level records (where counties existed): physical at county courthouses or ADAH microfilm.
- Creek and Cherokee nation records from this period: specialized collections at NARA and tribal archives.

## Known record losses
- Many early Alabama county courthouses suffered fire and flood damage in the 19th century, destroying deed books, probate files, and court minutes. Specific losses vary by county — check ADAH's county records survey before assuming a record survives.
- The mobile area's records changed hands (France to Britain to Spain to United States) and some records were removed or lost during each transition.
- No single known catastrophic loss is named in tool results for this period, but the multiple-jurisdiction transitions mean scattered survival.

## Research tips
- **Think in three layers:** For any person in Alabama around 1800, you need to search Mississippi Territory records (not Alabama records), then Alabama Territory records, then early Alabama state records — three different filing systems. The FamilySearch wiki notes territorial censuses (1801, 1805, 1808, 1810) and colonial records are at ADAH (https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Alabama_Genealogy#Territorial_Records).
- **Mobile-area ancestors:** Spanish colonial records are the primary source; search the Archivo General de Indias and its copies at the Library of Congress before assuming records don't exist (https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Alabama_Genealogy#Colonial_Records).
- **Land as a finding tool:** Because civil vital registration did not exist, the federal land entry files at BLM GLO and NARA are often the first documentary record placing a settler in Alabama. Land entries name the individual, the date, and the land description.
- **Tax and militia substitutes:** Territorial tax lists and militia muster rolls (at ADAH) name adult white males in years before county marriage or probate records begin — use them as census substitutes.
- **County formation sequencing:** Identify when the specific county was formed. Baldwin, Madison, Washington, and other early counties were formed 1799-1810 under territorial authority. Any event before that county's formation must be sought in the parent county or territorial records.
- **FamilySearch browse-only volumes:** Volumes 004512889 (territorial court and land, 1808-1819) and 004512890 (Washington County deed and probate, 1803-1820) are online but 0% name-indexed and not full-text searchable — browse image by image.
- **Cross-border research:** Settlers who arrived through Tennessee, Georgia, or the Carolinas may have left records in those states en route. Search the origin state's records alongside Alabama territorial records.

Marriage bonds and licenses were recorded at the county level beginning in some counties from 1809 onward (FamilySearch collection "Alabama, County Marriages, 1809-1950", collection id 1598408).
- **What exists:** Marriage records from 1809 in early-formed counties. No indexed birth or death records from this period.
- **Where held:** County probate courts (which in Alabama handled marriages); Alabama Department of Archives and History (ADAH), Montgomery, holds microfilm copies of many county marriage records. FamilySearch collection 1598408 covers 1809-1950.
- **Gaps:** Births and deaths — no civil registration. Marriage records exist only from the date a given county was formed and began keeping records.
- **Pre-registration alternatives:** Church baptism and burial registers; family Bible records; probate records naming heirs; estate inventories.

### Church records
- **Denominations present:** Roman Catholic (Mobile area — French and Spanish tradition); Baptist and Methodist (American settler communities).
- **Record types:** Baptisms, marriages, burials, confirmations.
- **Where held:** Catholic records for Mobile are at the Archdiocese of Mobile archives and at the Mobile Municipal Archives. French Catholic colonial records are at the Archives Nationales d'Outre-Mer, Aix-en-Provence, France, with some microfilm at the Mobile Municipal Archives. Spanish-era church registers for the Mobile District are at the Archivo General de Indias, Seville, with copies at the Library of Congress (per FamilySearch wiki https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Alabama_Genealogy#Colonial_Records). Protestant church records are scattered at local congregations and some denominations' archives. FamilySearch collection "Alabama, Church Records, 1803-1950" (id 1986396) covers some records from 1803.
- **Language:** French-era records in French; Spanish-era records in Spanish; Protestant records in English.

### Census records
- **Federal/national census:** The 1810 federal census covered the Mississippi Territory (including present-day Alabama). The 1820 federal census covered Alabama as a newly admitted state.
- **Territorial censuses:** The Mississippi Territory conducted censuses in 1801, 1805, 1808, and 1810 enumerating settlers in present-day Alabama. These are held at ADAH in Montgomery (per FamilySearch wiki https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Alabama_Genealogy#Territorial_Records).
- **Access:** FamilySearch collection "Alabama, Compiled Census and Census Substitutes Index, 1810-1890" (id 2016756, 287,634 records, no images) and "Mississippi, Compiled Census and Census Substitutes, 1792-1890" (id 1927171, 198,340 records, no images) are indexed but image-free — they are indexes only. Volume_search returned no dedicated census image volumes for this period.

### Probate and court records
- **Types:** Wills, administrations, guardianships, inventories, estate petitions. Also territorial court records (suits, land disputes).
- **Date range:** County-level probate begins from each county's formation date (the earliest Alabama counties formed 1799-1810 under territorial administration). Territorial court records begin 1798.
- **Where held:** Original county records at each county's probate court or courthouse. ADAH holds microfilm of many county records. FamilySearch collection "Alabama, Probate Records, 1809-1985" (id 1537764, 438,210 records, images available). Two browse-only image volumes on FamilySearch: imageGroupNumber 004512889 (territorial court and land records, 1808-1819, 214 images, 0% indexed) and 004512890 (Washington County deed and probate, 1803-1820, 96 images, 0% indexed). Both must be browsed image by image with no name search.
- **Digitization level:** Partially indexed (collection 1537764); browse-only for the territorial-era volumes.

### Land records
- **Survey system:** Federal rectangular survey (Alabama is a public-land state; the federal government, not the state, distributed original land grants).
- **Land-distribution jurisdiction:** The U.S. General Land Office (GLO) issued patents; records are online at the Bureau of Land Management GLO website (glorecords.blm.gov). Spanish land grants in the Mobile district were issued by Spanish colonial authorities; those records are at the Archivo General de Indias, Seville, with copies at ADAH and the Library of Congress.
- **Types:** Federal land patents, Spanish land grants, subsequent deeds, tax records.
- **Date range:** American land sales in what is now Alabama began after 1800; the first federal land office for Alabama opened in 1803 at St. Stephens. Spanish land grants predate 1813.
- **Where held:** Federal patents: BLM GLO website (free, online). Subsequent deeds: county courthouses. Territorial land records: volume 004512889 on FamilySearch (browse-only, 1808-1819). FamilySearch collection "Mississippi, Territorial and State Land Records, 1798-1907" (id 1919694, 312,450 records, images) covers the territorial period and includes Alabama-area lands.
- **Digitization level:** BLM GLO patents — indexed + images online (free). Territorial land records on FamilySearch — browse-only images or partially indexed (collection 1919694).

### Military records
- **Relevant conflicts:** Creek War 1813-1814; War of 1812 (defense of Mobile).
- **Record types:** Service records, pension files, bounty land warrants. Territorial militia rolls.
- **Where held:** NARA (federal service records and pension files). ADAH holds Alabama militia and territorial records. Fold3 (fold3.com) has digitized many NARA military records.

### Cemetery records
- **Major cemeteries:** Few formal cemeteries from this period; family burial plots and church graveyards are the main type.
- **Online coverage:** Find A Grave (findagrave.com) indexes some early Alabama graves; coverage for pre-1820 is sparse.
- **Physical records:** Sexton records for this period are rare or nonexistent. Cemetery survey transcriptions by genealogical societies (especially the Alabama Genealogical Society) exist for some counties.

### Newspaper records
- **Local papers:** The Mobile Centinel (later Gazette) was one of Alabama's earliest papers, founded ca. 1811. Very few newspapers existed in the Alabama region before 1810.
- **Where held:** ADAH holds some early Alabama newspaper microfilm. Newspapers.com and Chronicling America (Library of Congress) have some digitized Alabama newspapers, but coverage for pre-1820 is minimal.
- **Content value:** Legal notices, land sale notices, and some death/marriage notices.

### Immigration and emigration records
- **Relevant ports:** Mobile (Gulf Coast); New Orleans (for migrants arriving by sea or river).
- **Record types:** Passenger lists (NARA); Spanish-era passport and travel records (Archivo General de Indias).
- **Where held:** NARA holds post-1820 passenger lists. For the 1800 period, formal arrival records are sparse. The FamilySearch wiki notes that the region attracted migrants overland from the Carolinas, Virginia, and Georgia — those migrants left few formal arrival records but may appear in land entry files.
- **Content note:** Passenger lists record every person aboard, including infants and young children traveling with parents.

### Tax records
- **Types:** Territorial and county-level property and poll tax lists.
- **Date range:** Territorial tax records begin 1798-1800 in some districts.
- **Where held:** ADAH; county archives.
- **Substitute value:** Tax lists substitute for missing census years and are especially important for 1801-1809 before county marriage records begin.

### Other record types
- **Spanish colonial records:** Census returns, church registers, land grants, and civil records of the Mobile District under Spanish administration (1780-1813) are at the Archivo General de Indias, Seville, with some copies at the Library of Congress and ADAH.
- **French colonial records:** Records of the French colonial period (1702-1763) are at the Archives Nationales d'Outre-Mer, Aix-en-Provence, France, and on microfilm at the Mobile Municipal Archives.
- **Creek and Cherokee records:** Records of Native nations from this period are in specialized collections at NARA and at tribal archives.

## Repository guide

### Online repositories
| Repository | Collections for this place | Access |
|---|---|---|
| FamilySearch | County Marriages 1809-1950 (1598408); Probate Records 1809-1985 (1537764); Compiled Census/Substitutes 1810-1890 (2016756); Church Records 1803-1950 (1986396); Mississippi Territorial and State Land Records 1798-1907 (1919694); Mississippi County Court Records 1799-1920 (1855293); Mississippi Census Substitutes 1792-1890 (1927171); Mississippi Church Records 1800-1950 (2034891); Browse-only volumes 004512889 and 004512890 | Free |
| BLM General Land Office | Federal land patents for Alabama public-land sales | Free (glorecords.blm.gov) |
| Ancestry.com | U.S. Federal Census Collection (includes 1810 and 1820) | Subscription |
| Fold3 | Military service records and pension files | Subscription |
| Find A Grave | Cemetery records | Free |
| NARA (archives.gov) | Military records, pension files | Free finding aids; some records online via Fold3/Ancestry |

**Coverage of this survey:** The FamilySearch volume_search returned 2 digitized but browse-only image volumes matching Alabama for 1780-1820 (total results: 2; this is the complete set for that query). These are the only named volumes in tool results; additional holdings will exist in physical or partially described form at ADAH and county courthouses.

### Physical repositories
| Repository | Holdings | Access method |
|---|---|---|
| Alabama Department of Archives and History (ADAH), Montgomery, AL | Territorial censuses 1801/1805/1808/1810; county records microfilm; militia records; tax lists; newspapers | In-person; some digitized at adah.alabama.gov |
| County courthouses | Deed books, probate records, marriage bonds (from county formation date) | In-person or mail |
| Archdiocese of Mobile Archives | Catholic parish registers (Mobile area) | Contact archive for access |
| Mobile Municipal Archives | French colonial church register microfilm; early city records | In-person |
| Archives Nationales d'Outre-Mer, Aix-en-Provence, France | French colonial records 1702-1763 | In-person or correspondence |
| Archivo General de Indias, Seville, Spain | Spanish colonial records 1780-1813 (church, land, census) | In-person; partial digitization at pares.mcu.es |
| Library of Congress, Washington DC | Copies of Spanish colonial records | In-person; some online |
| NARA (Atlanta regional facility and Washington DC) | Federal land entry files, military records, 1810 and 1820 federal census originals | In-person; many records online |

## Records NOT online
- Territorial tax lists (1798-1819): primarily physical at ADAH.
- Spanish-era church registers and land grants: primarily at Archivo General de Indias with partial digitization; copies at Library of Congress.
- French colonial records: at Archives Nationales d'Outre-Mer; microfilm at Mobile Municipal Archives.
- Most pre-1809 county-level records (where counties existed): physical at county courthouses or ADAH microfilm.
- Creek and Cherokee nation records from this period: specialized collections at NARA and tribal archives.

## Known record losses
- Many early Alabama county courthouses suffered fire and flood damage in the 19th century, destroying deed books, probate files, and court minutes. Specific losses vary by county — check ADAH's county records survey before assuming a record survives.
- The mobile area's records changed hands (France to Britain to Spain to United States) and some records were removed or lost during each transition.
- No single known catastrophic loss is named in tool results for this period, but the multiple-jurisdiction transitions mean scattered survival.

## Research tips
- **Think in three layers:** For any person in Alabama around 1800, you need to search Mississippi Territory records (not Alabama records), then Alabama Territory records, then early Alabama state records — three different filing systems. The FamilySearch wiki notes territorial censuses (1801, 1805, 1808, 1810) and colonial records are at ADAH (https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Alabama_Genealogy#Territorial_Records).
- **Mobile-area ancestors:** Spanish colonial records are the primary source; search the Archivo General de Indias and its copies at the Library of Congress before assuming records don't exist (https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Alabama_Genealogy#Colonial_Records).
- **Land as a finding tool:** Because civil vital registration did not exist, the federal land entry files at BLM GLO and NARA are often the first documentary record placing a settler in Alabama. Land entries name the individual, the date, and the land description.
- **Tax and militia substitutes:** Territorial tax lists and militia muster rolls (at ADAH) name adult white males in years before county marriage or probate records begin — use them as census substitutes.
- **County formation sequencing:** Identify when the specific county was formed. Baldwin, Madison, Washington, and other early counties were formed 1799-1810 under territorial authority. Any event before that county's formation must be sought in the parent county or territorial records.
- **FamilySearch browse-only volumes:** Volumes 004512889 (territorial court and land, 1808-1819) and 004512890 (Washington County deed and probate, 1803-1820) are online but 0% name-indexed and not full-text searchable — browse image by image.
- **Cross-border research:** Settlers who arrived through Tennessee, Georgia, or the Carolinas may have left records in those states en route. Search the origin state's records alongside Alabama territorial records.

subagents.description: Locality guide for pre-1800 Arkansas under Spanish control

output.text_response:
Here is what the locality-guide agent found:

---

**Locality Guide: Arkansas Before 1800 (Spanish Colonial Period)**

**Locality guide written as loc_001.**

The Arkansas region before 1800 was first a French colonial outpost centered on Arkansas Post (founded 1686), then a Spanish colonial garrison from 1763 until Spain quietly ceded it back to France in 1800. European settlement was tiny throughout this period, so surviving records are few and scattered across three countries.

**What records exist:**
- **Spanish colonial household censuses (padrones)** — population enumerations naming heads of household
- **Land concessions** — grants of land under Spanish rule
- **Military post papers** — garrison records at Arkansas Post
- **Catholic sacramental registers** — baptisms, marriages, and burials at Arkansas Post, covering 1763–1800, in Spanish

None of these are name-indexed online.

**Key repositories:**
| Repository | What they hold |
|---|---|
| **Archivo General de Indias** (Seville, Spain) | Primary colonial records — padrones, land concessions, military papers |
| **Arkansas History Commission** (Little Rock, AR) | Microfilm copies of AGI materials |
| **Library of Congress** | Additional microfilm of Spanish colonial records |
| **Roman Catholic Diocese of Little Rock** | Church sacramental registers |
| **FamilySearch** | 64 digitized images of Arkansas Post sacramental registers (1763–1800), unindexed — browse only |
| **Louisiana State Archives** (Baton Rouge, LA) | Louisiana colonial records; settlers at Arkansas Post frequently appear here before any Arkansas series begins |

**Critical caveat:** Searching only U.S. repositories will miss most of what survives. Much of the colonial record series was sent to Spain and never returned. The **PARES portal** (pares.mcu.es) is the online access point for the Archivo General de Indias and should be a first stop.
