# Locality Guide: Arkansas (Pre-1800, Spanish Colonial Era)

## Jurisdiction overview
- **Formed:** Arkansas Post established 1686 (French); transferred to Spain by Treaty of Paris 1763; secretly ceded back to France 1800; acquired by U.S. via Louisiana Purchase 1803; Arkansas Territory formed 1819; state of Arkansas admitted 1836
- **County seat / administrative center:** Arkansas Post (post commandant's headquarters during colonial era)
- **Parent jurisdiction:** French La Louisiane (1686-1763); Spanish Provincia de Luisiana (1763-1800)
- **Population during period:** Extremely sparse — Arkansas Post was the only significant European settlement before 1800; no population data was returned by place_population for this period
- **Economy:** Fur trade, small-scale agriculture, military garrison
- **Ethnic composition:** French Creole settlers, Spanish military personnel and administrators, enslaved Africans, and neighboring Native American peoples (Quapaw, Osage)
- **Religious denominations:** Roman Catholic (the only organized church in the colonial era; French Franciscan and later Spanish Capuchin missionaries served Arkansas Post)
- **Key historical events:** Treaty of Paris 1763 (France cedes territory to Spain); 1779 Spanish military expansion during American Revolution; Spain secretly cedes back to France via Treaty of San Ildefonso 1800; Louisiana Purchase 1803

## Boundary changes
- **1686-1762:** Arkansas Post exists as part of French La Louisiane, nominally subordinate to the provincial capital in New Orleans
- **1763:** Treaty of Paris transfers all French territory west of the Mississippi, including Arkansas Post, to Spain. Authority now runs: post commandant → Governor of Spanish Louisiana → Capitán General of Cuba (Havana) → Council of the Indies (Madrid). Records created under this chain can appear in repositories along it.
- **1800:** Spain secretly cedes the territory back to France (Treaty of San Ildefonso); actual U.S. transfer follows the Louisiana Purchase in 1803
- **After 1800:** The territory passes through successive U.S. jurisdictions (Territory of Orleans/District of Louisiana 1804, Missouri Territory 1812, Arkansas Territory 1819, state 1836). Records created after 1803 are U.S. territorial or state records, a distinct break from the colonial series.
- There was no county structure during the colonial period; the post commandant exercised all civil and military authority.

## Available record types

### Vital records (civil registration)
- **Start date:** No civil vital registration existed in Arkansas during the colonial period. The FamilySearch Wiki pages for Arkansas Vital Records returned only generic content on this retrieval; the FamilySearch Wiki does not appear to have a dedicated page covering colonial-era registration levels for Arkansas.
- **What exists:** No civil birth, marriage, or death records before 1803. Church sacramental registers are the only vital-event records.
- **Where held:** See Church Records below.
- **Gaps:** The entire pre-1800 period is without civil registration.
- **Pre-registration alternatives:** Catholic sacramental registers at Arkansas Post; Spanish colonial census lists (padrones)

### Church records
- **Denominations present:** Roman Catholic only (Franciscan missionaries from ca. 1700; Capuchin missionaries under Spanish rule from 1763)
- **Record types:** Baptisms, marriages, burials; possibly confirmations
- **Where held:** The FamilySearch wiki search result ([Arkansas Genealogy — Church Records](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Arkansas_Genealogy#Church_Records)) identifies two repositories: (1) Roman Catholic Diocese of Little Rock (original or copy registers); (2) Arkansas History Commission, Little Rock (transcribed form). FamilySearch holds 1 digitized volume covering Arkansas Post sacramental registers 1763-1800 (imageGroupNumber 008814402, 64 images).
- **Language:** Spanish (records created under Spanish administration after 1763); French (records created before 1763). Researchers must be able to read 18th-century ecclesiastical Latin/Spanish/French script.
- **Digitization level:** Browse-only images — FamilySearch volume 008814402 is 0% name-indexed and not full-text searchable. Must be browsed image by image.
- **Note:** French-era registers (pre-1763) survive in transcription at the Arkansas History Commission; their digitization status at FamilySearch is not confirmed by tool results.

### Census records (padrones)
- **Spanish colonial censuses (padrones):** Spain conducted household censuses of its Louisiana settlements, including Arkansas Post, periodically during 1763-1800. These list heads of household, family members, ages, occupations, and sometimes origins.
- **Where held:** Archivo General de Indias, Seville (primary holding); Arkansas History Commission microfilm; Library of Congress microfilm. Per the FamilySearch wiki search result ([Arkansas Genealogy — Colonial Records](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Arkansas_Genealogy#Colonial_Records)), these three repositories are named as holders of surviving Spanish colonial records.
- **Federal/national census:** The first U.S. federal census covering Arkansas was in 1820 (territorial). The 1790 census did not cover the Arkansas region (foreign territory at the time). FamilySearch collection 2085124 (Arkansas, Compiled Census and Census Substitutes Index, 1819-1870) covers 178,345 records beginning 1819 and is indexed with no images.
- **Digitization level:** Spanish colonial padrones — physical or microfilm only (no FamilySearch indexed collection found for this period). U.S. territorial/state census (1820+) — indexed, no images in the compiled substitutes index.

### Probate and court records
- **Types:** Under Spanish colonial administration, the post commandant served as judge for civil disputes and estate matters. Formal probate proceedings were rudimentary given the small population.
- **Where held:** Surviving records are in the Archivo General de Indias and at the Arkansas History Commission. No FamilySearch collection or volume was returned for colonial-era probate in Arkansas.
- **Digitization level:** Physical/microfilm only based on tool results — no FamilySearch digitized probate volumes were found for this period.
- **Note:** The FamilySearch Wiki page for Arkansas Probate Records returned only generic content; no Arkansas-specific probate guidance was available on this retrieval.

### Land records
- **Survey system:** Metes-and-bounds (Spanish colonial concession system); distinct from the later U.S. rectangular survey system.
- **Land-distribution jurisdiction:** Spanish post commandant (granted concessions); confirmed or rejected after U.S. acquisition by the U.S. Board of Land Commissioners for the Territory of Arkansas. Per the FamilySearch wiki search result ([Arkansas Genealogy — Colonial Records](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Arkansas_Genealogy#Colonial_Records)), land concessions are among the record types at the Arkansas History Commission and Archivo General de Indias.
- **Types:** Land concessions (Spanish grants), later U.S. confirmations of Spanish/French grants
- **Date range:** Spanish concessions from ca. 1763
- **Where held:** Archivo General de Indias, Seville; Arkansas History Commission; U.S. General Land Office records (for post-1803 confirmations) via BLM GLO website (glorecords.blm.gov)
- **Digitization level:** Original Spanish concessions — physical or microfilm only based on tool results. U.S. GLO confirmed patents — searchable online at glorecords.blm.gov.
- **Note:** The FamilySearch Wiki page for Arkansas Land and Property returned only generic content.

### Military records
- **Relevant conflicts:** Spanish military at Arkansas Post throughout 1763-1800; Spanish participation in actions during the American Revolutionary War (1779-1783)
- **Record types:** Spanish military post records (muster rolls, service records, correspondence), Spanish Louisiana Governor's papers
- **Where held:** Archivo General de Indias, Seville (primary); Archivo General de Simancas, Spain (military section); Library of Congress microfilm of Louisiana colonial records
- **U.S. military records (post-1803):** NARA, fold3.com
- **Digitization level:** Spanish military records — physical only in Spanish archives based on tool results. Some have been microfilmed at the Library of Congress.

### Cemetery records
- **Major cemeteries:** Arkansas Post had a Catholic burial ground; records of interments are within the sacramental registers noted above
- **Online coverage:** FindAGrave (findagrave.com) covers some Arkansas cemeteries, but colonial-era burials are rarely inscribed on surviving markers
- **Physical records:** Burial entries in Catholic registers at the Arkansas History Commission and Diocese of Little Rock

### Newspaper records
- **Local papers:** No newspapers were published in the Arkansas region before 1800
- **Content value:** Not applicable for this period

### Immigration/emigration records
- **Relevant ports:** New Orleans was the primary port of entry for Spanish Louisiana; settlers arriving at Arkansas Post typically came upriver from New Orleans
- **Record types:** Spanish passport and travel records (licencias de paso) issued to travelers entering Spanish Louisiana; these are in the Archivo General de Indias and Louisiana colonial collections
- **Where held:** Archivo General de Indias; Louisiana State Archives (which holds substantial Spanish Louisiana records pertaining to the entire province, including settlers who later moved upriver to Arkansas Post)
- **Content note:** The Louisiana State Archives in Baton Rouge holds many Spanish-era records for the broader Louisiana Province; researchers should search there for ancestors before they appear at Arkansas Post.

### Tax records
- **Types:** Spanish colonial tax and tribute assessments
- **Date range:** 1763-1800
- **Where held:** Archivo General de Indias; Arkansas History Commission
- **Substitute value:** Can help place settlers at Arkansas Post in years without a surviving census

### Other record types
- **Notarial records:** The post commandant acted as notary; commercial contracts, manumissions, and other legal instruments survive in the colonial record series at the Arkansas History Commission and Archivo General de Indias
- **Correspondence and administrative papers:** The commandant's correspondence with the Governor of Louisiana survives in the Louisiana colonial collections (Louisiana State Archives; Library of Congress microfilm). These name settlers, describe local events, and identify individuals not in any other record type.
- **Published local histories and transcriptions:** Morris S. Arnold's work on colonial Arkansas ("Colonial Arkansas 1686-1804") and the Colonial Arkansas Project have published and transcribed many surviving records; these are available in research libraries and at the Arkansas History Commission.

## Repository guide

### Online repositories
| Repository | Collections for this place | Access |
|---|---|---|
| FamilySearch | 1 digitized volume: Arkansas Post sacramental registers 1763-1800, 64 images, browse-only (Spanish), imageGroupNumber 008814402 | Free |
| FamilySearch | Arkansas, Compiled Census and Census Substitutes Index, 1819-1870 (178,345 records; covers period after 1800 only) | Free |
| FamilySearch | Arkansas, County Marriages, 1837-1957 (covers period after 1800 only) | Free |
| Ancestry.com | U.S. Federal Census Collection (earliest Arkansas coverage: 1820) | Subscription |
| BLM GLO (glorecords.blm.gov) | U.S. land patent confirmations of Spanish/French grants (post-1803 confirmations) | Free |
| Fold3 | Military records (post-1803 U.S. military; Spanish records not online) | Subscription |
| NARA (archives.gov) | National Archives holdings — Louisiana Purchase territorial records | Free finding aids; in-person or reproduction fees for records |

**Coverage of this survey:** FamilySearch volume_search returned 1 total digitized volume matching Arkansas, 1680-1800; that single result is detailed above. This is the complete result set (nextPageToken was not returned). FamilySearch collections_search returned 3 collections for Arkansas, none covering the colonial period (all date from 1819 or later). The pre-1800 record base is not meaningfully represented in FamilySearch's indexed collections.

### Physical repositories
| Repository | Holdings | Access method |
|---|---|---|
| Arkansas History Commission, Little Rock, AR | Spanish colonial records on microfilm; French and Spanish sacramental register transcriptions; Arkansas Post records | In-person; some finding aids online (ahc.arkansas.gov) |
| Roman Catholic Diocese of Little Rock, AR | Original or copy sacramental registers from Arkansas Post | Contact diocese archives |
| Archivo General de Indias, Seville, Spain | Primary repository for Spanish colonial Louisiana records: padrones, land concessions, military papers, administrative correspondence | In-person; some records on Portal de Archivos Espanoles (PARES, pares.mcu.es) — free online |
| Archivo General de Simancas, Valladolid, Spain | Spanish military service records for Louisiana troops | In-person; some records on PARES |
| Louisiana State Archives, Baton Rouge, LA | Spanish Louisiana provincial records covering the entire province (Arkansas Post settlers often appear here before Arkansas records begin) | In-person; some finding aids online |
| Library of Congress, Washington, DC | Microfilm of Louisiana colonial records including Arkansas Post series | In-person; some reproductions available |
| NARA (Southwest Region / College Park) | Post-1803 territorial records | In-person; online NARA catalog (catalog.archives.gov) |

## Records NOT online
- Spanish colonial padrones (censuses) for Arkansas Post — physical/microfilm only at Arkansas History Commission and Archivo General de Indias
- Spanish land concession records — physical/microfilm only
- Spanish military post records and commandant correspondence — physical or microfilm only
- French-era sacramental registers (pre-1763) — transcriptions at Arkansas History Commission; original digitization status unconfirmed
- Notarial records and civil legal instruments from the commandant's court — physical/microfilm only
- Spanish passport and travel records (licencias de paso) — physical in Archivo General de Indias

## Known record losses
- Record survival for pre-1800 Arkansas is sparse because Arkansas Post was a very small garrison settlement with a minimal civilian population. The volume of records created was inherently small.
- Many Spanish colonial records were never deposited locally but were sent directly to New Orleans or to Spain, so gaps in U.S. repositories do not necessarily mean destruction — the records may simply be in Spain.
- No specific courthouse fires or disasters destroying Arkansas colonial records were identified in tool results; the primary gap is dispersal across multiple countries rather than destruction.

## Research tips
- **Start in Spain.** The Archivo General de Indias in Seville is the single most important repository for pre-1800 Arkansas ancestors. Its PARES portal (pares.mcu.es) provides free online access to digitized documents and finding aids. Per the FamilySearch wiki search result covering Arkansas colonial records ([Arkansas Genealogy — Colonial Records](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Arkansas_Genealogy#Colonial_Records)), this archive is explicitly identified as a primary holder.
- **Search Louisiana records before Arkansas records.** Most settlers at Arkansas Post arrived from or through New Orleans. The Louisiana State Archives holds Spanish provincial records that predate their appearance in any Arkansas-specific series. Search Louisiana before narrowing to Arkansas.
- **The single FamilySearch volume (imageGroupNumber 008814402) must be browsed in Spanish.** It is 0% name-indexed and not full-text searchable. A researcher must navigate 64 images manually and read 18th-century ecclesiastical Spanish script.
- **Use published transcriptions.** Morris S. Arnold's scholarly work on Colonial Arkansas and the Colonial Arkansas Project have produced transcribed and published versions of many surviving records. These are far more accessible than the originals and are held at the Arkansas History Commission and major research libraries.
- **Spanish naming customs.** Under Spanish colonial practice, children took both a paternal and maternal surname (compound surname). Women kept their birth surname at marriage. Searching only the paternal surname misses entries filed under the maternal surname. Researchers must track both lines.
- **The 1790 federal census does not exist for Arkansas** — the region was foreign territory. The earliest U.S. enumeration is 1820. For the gap between 1800 and 1820, substitute the compiled census and substitutes index (FamilySearch collection 2085124) and territorial land records.
- **French-era ancestors (1686-1763) require reading French records.** The sacramental registers from the French period are in French and ecclesiastical Latin. French Catholic naming customs (godparents named in baptismal registers) can extend pedigrees significantly.
- **Cross to Louisiana.** Arkansas Post lay on the Arkansas River near its confluence with the Mississippi. Settlers moved freely between Arkansas Post and the lower Mississippi settlements (Natchitoches, New Orleans, Pointe Coupee). Ancestors may appear in Louisiana Catholic registers or Louisiana colonial civil records even if they were based at Arkansas Post.

| FamilySearch | Arkansas, Compiled Census and Census Substitutes Index, 1819-1870 (178,345 records; covers period after 1800 only) | Free |
| FamilySearch | Arkansas, County Marriages, 1837-1957 (covers period after 1800 only) | Free |
| Ancestry.com | U.S. Federal Census Collection (earliest Arkansas coverage: 1820) | Subscription |
| BLM GLO (glorecords.blm.gov) | U.S. land patent confirmations of Spanish/French grants (post-1803 confirmations) | Free |
| Fold3 | Military records (post-1803 U.S. military; Spanish records not online) | Subscription |
| NARA (archives.gov) | National Archives holdings — Louisiana Purchase territorial records | Free finding aids; in-person or reproduction fees for records |

**Coverage of this survey:** FamilySearch volume_search returned 1 total digitized volume matching Arkansas, 1680-1800; that single result is detailed above. This is the complete result set (nextPageToken was not returned). FamilySearch collections_search returned 3 collections for Arkansas, none covering the colonial period (all date from 1819 or later). The pre-1800 record base is not meaningfully represented in FamilySearch's indexed collections.

### Physical repositories
| Repository | Holdings | Access method |
|---|---|---|
| Arkansas History Commission, Little Rock, AR | Spanish colonial records on microfilm; French and Spanish sacramental register transcriptions; Arkansas Post records | In-person; some finding aids online (ahc.arkansas.gov) |
| Roman Catholic Diocese of Little Rock, AR | Original or copy sacramental registers from Arkansas Post | Contact diocese archives |
| Archivo General de Indias, Seville, Spain | Primary repository for Spanish colonial Louisiana records: padrones, land concessions, military papers, administrative correspondence | In-person; some records on Portal de Archivos Espanoles (PARES, pares.mcu.es) — free online |
| Archivo General de Simancas, Valladolid, Spain | Spanish military service records for Louisiana troops | In-person; some records on PARES |
| Louisiana State Archives, Baton Rouge, LA | Spanish Louisiana provincial records covering the entire province (Arkansas Post settlers often appear here before Arkansas records begin) | In-person; some finding aids online |
| Library of Congress, Washington, DC | Microfilm of Louisiana colonial records including Arkansas Post series | In-person; some reproductions available |
| NARA (Southwest Region / College Park) | Post-1803 territorial records | In-person; online NARA catalog (catalog.archives.gov) |

## Records NOT online
- Spanish colonial padrones (censuses) for Arkansas Post — physical/microfilm only at Arkansas History Commission and Archivo General de Indias
- Spanish land concession records — physical/microfilm only
- Spanish military post records and commandant correspondence — physical or microfilm only
- French-era sacramental registers (pre-1763) — transcriptions at Arkansas History Commission; original digitization status unconfirmed
- Notarial records and civil legal instruments from the commandant's court — physical/microfilm only
- Spanish passport and travel records (licencias de paso) — physical in Archivo General de Indias

## Known record losses
- Record survival for pre-1800 Arkansas is sparse because Arkansas Post was a very small garrison settlement with a minimal civilian population. The volume of records created was inherently small.
- Many Spanish colonial records were never deposited locally but were sent directly to New Orleans or to Spain, so gaps in U.S. repositories do not necessarily mean destruction — the records may simply be in Spain.
- No specific courthouse fires or disasters destroying Arkansas colonial records were identified in tool results; the primary gap is dispersal across multiple countries rather than destruction.

## Research tips
- **Start in Spain.** The Archivo General de Indias in Seville is the single most important repository for pre-1800 Arkansas ancestors. Its PARES portal (pares.mcu.es) provides free online access to digitized documents and finding aids. Per the FamilySearch wiki search result covering Arkansas colonial records ([Arkansas Genealogy — Colonial Records](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Arkansas_Genealogy#Colonial_Records)), this archive is explicitly identified as a primary holder.
- **Search Louisiana records before Arkansas records.** Most settlers at Arkansas Post arrived from or through New Orleans. The Louisiana State Archives holds Spanish provincial records that predate their appearance in any Arkansas-specific series. Search Louisiana before narrowing to Arkansas.
- **The single FamilySearch volume (imageGroupNumber 008814402) must be browsed in Spanish.** It is 0% name-indexed and not full-text searchable. A researcher must navigate 64 images manually and read 18th-century ecclesiastical Spanish script.
- **Use published transcriptions.** Morris S. Arnold's scholarly work on Colonial Arkansas and the Colonial Arkansas Project have produced transcribed and published versions of many surviving records. These are far more accessible than the originals and are held at the Arkansas History Commission and major research libraries.
- **Spanish naming customs.** Under Spanish colonial practice, children took both a paternal and maternal surname (compound surname). Women kept their birth surname at marriage. Searching only the paternal surname misses entries filed under the maternal surname. Researchers must track both lines.
- **The 1790 federal census does not exist for Arkansas** — the region was foreign territory. The earliest U.S. enumeration is 1820. For the gap between 1800 and 1820, substitute the compiled census and substitutes index (FamilySearch collection 2085124) and territorial land records.
- **French-era ancestors (1686-1763) require reading French records.** The sacramental registers from the French period are in French and ecclesiastical Latin. French Catholic naming customs (godparents named in baptismal registers) can extend pedigrees significantly.
- **Cross to Louisiana.** Arkansas Post lay on the Arkansas River near its confluence with the Mississippi. Settlers moved freely between Arkansas Post and the lower Mississippi settlements (Natchitoches, New Orleans, Pointe Coupee). Ancestors may appear in Louisiana Catholic registers or Louisiana colonial civil records even if they were based at Arkansas Post.

---

**Ohio circa 1790 — Pre-Statehood Locality Guide** *(logged as loc_001)*

**Jurisdictional Context**

In 1790, Ohio did not yet exist as a state — it was part of the federally administered **Northwest Territory**. Civil government was minimal and limited to just two counties:

- **Washington County** (est. 1788, centered on Marietta)
- **Hamilton County** (est. July 1790, centered on Cincinnati)

For most of present-day Ohio, there was **no courthouse, no court, and no civil record registration** of any kind.

**Boundary Complexity — The Biggest Trap**

Ohio's early territory was carved out of competing land-grant systems:

- **Virginia Military District** — records are held in *Virginia*, not Ohio
- **Connecticut Western Reserve** — records are held in *Cleveland*-area repositories, not the Ohio State Archives

Researchers who go straight to Ohio archives for this period will miss the most important records.

**What Records Exist (1787–~1800)**

| Record Type | Notes |
|---|---|
| Federal land grants (GLO) | Searchable; FamilySearch collection starts 1787 |
| County marriage records | Begin 1789 (Washington Co.) |
| Church records | Pioneer congregations; survival varies |
| Tax lists | Begin ~1799 |
| Territorial volumes on FamilySearch | Digitized but not fully indexed — must be browsed image by image |

**Best Sources for This Period**

Often the most useful records are **not Ohio records at all**:

1. **Origin-state records** — Virginia, Pennsylvania, and New England (where most early Ohio settlers came from)
2. **Revolutionary War pension files** — held at NARA
3. **19th-century published county histories** — many transcribed early territorial records before originals deteriorated

**Recommended Next Step**

Run a research plan for your specific ancestor now that the record landscape is mapped. The agent can continue from here — just say the word.

Washington County (est. 1788) and Hamilton County (est. 1790) were the only organized counties in the territory through 1790. Records created in these years for events anywhere in present-day Ohio could be under either of these two counties depending on geographic location — determine which county had jurisdiction at the event location and date before searching.

The Virginia Military District (between the Scioto and Little Miami rivers) used a metes-and-bounds survey system distinct from the rest of Ohio. Land warrants for this district are at the Virginia State Library, not Ohio repositories.

Ohio is a federal-land state: original land patents were issued by the federal government and recorded through the General Land Office (now searchable at the BLM GLO website, glorecords.blm.gov) — not by a state land office.

entry.guide_markdown:
# Locality Guide: Ohio, United States — Pre-Statehood Era (ca. 1785–1803)

## Jurisdiction overview

- **Formed:** Ohio became the 17th state on 1 March 1803, carved from the Northwest Territory established by the Northwest Ordinance of 1787.
- **County seat / administrative center:** Chillicothe was the territorial and early state capital. Marietta (Washington County seat) and Cincinnati (Hamilton County seat) were the principal administrative centers in 1790.
- **Parent jurisdiction:** Northwest Territory, United States (1787–1803). The Northwest Territory itself was a federal jurisdiction administered by a governor and judges appointed by Congress.
- **Population during period:** Population data tools returned no figures for Ohio at this date range; the region was very sparsely settled by Euro-American colonists in 1790. The 1800 federal census returned a total territorial population for the Northwest Territory.
- **Economy:** Subsistence agriculture, fur trade, military land grants, and early land speculation. The Ohio Company of Associates and the Symmes Purchase drove early colonization.
- **Ethnic composition:** Euro-American settlers (primarily New England, Virginia, and Pennsylvania origin); significant Indigenous populations (Shawnee, Delaware/Lenape, Wyandot, Miami) who are rarely named in surviving Euro-American records.
- **Religious denominations:** Congregationalist and Presbyterian (New England settlers), Methodist and Baptist (Virginia/Kentucky migrants), Quaker (some Pennsylvania settlers). Formal church infrastructure was minimal in 1790.
- **Key historical events:** Northwest Ordinance (1787), organization of Washington County (1788) and Hamilton County (1790), Harmar's Defeat (1790), St. Clair's Defeat (1791), Battle of Fallen Timbers (1794), Treaty of Greenville (1795), statehood (1803).

## Boundary changes

This is the central challenge for 1790 Ohio research. The entire region in 1790 was the Northwest Territory — a federally administered jurisdiction with no state government. County organization was just beginning:

- **Washington County** was established 1788 from the Northwest Territory, covering roughly the southeastern quadrant of present-day Ohio (the Ohio Company's land around Marietta). This was the only county with any functioning civil courts in 1788–1789.
- **Hamilton County** was established July 1790, covering the southwestern quadrant (the Symmes Purchase around Cincinnati). Events in that part of the territory after mid-1790 would fall under Hamilton County.
- **The rest of present-day Ohio** had no county organization in 1790. There was no courthouse, no court of record, and no civil registration infrastructure for most of the territory.
- After statehood in 1803, dozens of new counties were carved from Washington and Hamilton counties, and from federal unorganized territory. A record created in "Washington County" in 1791 may describe land now within a completely different county.
- **Temporal split rule:** For any event before 1803, the applicable jurisdiction is Washington County (southeastern Ohio) or Hamilton County (southwestern Ohio), not the modern county. Search under the 1790 county first; records were not transferred to successor counties when they formed — they stayed in the originating county's books.

## Available record types

### Vital records (civil registration)

- **Start date:** The FamilySearch Wiki Ohio Vital Records page returned only generic content in this survey run — no Ohio-specific civil registration start date was confirmed by any tool result. Do not assume a specific statewide date. What is certain: there was **no statewide civil registration in 1790** — Ohio did not exist as a state. County-level recording of marriages began in Washington County (1789) and Hamilton County (1790) per the FamilySearch-indexed collection "Ohio, County Marriages, 1789–2013" (collection 1803785), which begins in 1789.
- **What exists:** FamilySearch has an indexed collection of county marriages starting 1789 (1,523,678 records, 761,839 images — collection 1803785). No comparable indexed birth or death collection for this period was returned by the tools.
- **Where held:** County courthouse for the originating county (Washington County Courthouse, Marietta; Hamilton County Courthouse, Cincinnati). Ohio History Connection, Columbus, holds territorial-era court records.
- **Gaps:** Birth and death registration in 1790 is essentially nonexistent in civil records. Marriage is the only vital event likely to have a civil record in this period, and only in the two organized counties.
- **Pre-registration alternatives:** Church registers (baptisms, marriages, burials), family Bibles, pension files (which often include family affidavits), and land records naming heirs.

### Church records

- **Denominations present:** Congregationalist, Presbyterian, Methodist, Baptist, Quaker; Catholic missions were operating near the Great Lakes but not in the southern Ohio settlements in 1790.
- **Record types:** Baptisms, marriages, burials. Formal congregations were just forming in 1790 — many settlers had no local church.
- **Where held:** FamilySearch has an indexed collection "Ohio, Church Records, 1787–1950" (collection 2246917, 678,234 records, 339,117 images). Denominational archives (Presbyterian Historical Society in Philadelphia; United Methodist archives; Quaker meetings' own records) hold originals. Western Reserve Historical Society holds some northeastern Ohio church records.
- **Language:** English.
- **Note:** For 1790, church records are the most likely surviving source for baptism/birth and burial/death events. The infrastructure was thin — treat absence of a church record as evidence of underdeveloped local institutions, not evidence of nonexistence of the person.

### Census records

- **Federal census:** The first federal census was taken in 1790, but Ohio/Northwest Territory was not systematically covered at that date — the region's Euro-American population was tiny and dispersed in military settlements and a few river towns. The 1800 federal census is the first with meaningful Ohio coverage.
- **State/provincial census:** None for the territorial period (Ohio had no state government until 1803).
- **Other enumerations:** Tax lists function as a substitute — see Tax records below. Military muster rolls from the 1790s Indian Wars campaigns can serve as substitute enumerations for men.
- **Access:** The 1800 and subsequent federal censuses are indexed and available on FamilySearch and Ancestry. The 1790 Northwest Territory enumeration, where it survives, is very sparse.

### Probate and court records

- **Types:** Wills, administrations, guardianships, inventories — filed at the county level. The Washington County court began functioning in 1788; Hamilton County in 1790.
- **Date range:** From 1788 (Washington County) and 1790 (Hamilton County).
- **Where held:** Ohio History Connection (Columbus) holds territorial-era court records, per the FamilySearch Wiki Ohio Genealogy page (https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Ohio_Genealogy#Northwest_Territory). County courthouses hold records from statehood forward.

In that year only two counties had any civil administration at all: Washington County (formed 1788, centered on Marietta) and Hamilton County (formed July 1790, centered on Cincinnati). ## Jurisdiction overview

- **Formed:** Ohio became the 17th state on 1 March 1803, carved from the Northwest Territory established by the Northwest Ordinance of 1787.
- **County seat / administrative center:** Chillicothe was the territorial and early state capital. Marietta (Washington County seat) and Cincinnati (Hamilton County seat) were the principal administrative centers in 1790.
- **Parent jurisdiction:** Northwest Territory, United States (1787–1803). The Northwest Territory itself was a federal jurisdiction administered by a governor and judges appointed by Congress.
- **Population during period:** Population data tools returned no figures for Ohio at this date range; the region was very sparsely settled by Euro-American colonists in 1790. The 1800 federal census returned a total territorial population for the Northwest Territory.
- **Economy:** Subsistence agriculture, fur trade, military land grants, and early land speculation. The Ohio Company of Associates and the Symmes Purchase drove early colonization.
- **Ethnic composition:** Euro-American settlers (primarily New England, Virginia, and Pennsylvania origin); significant Indigenous populations (Shawnee, Delaware/Lenape, Wyandot, Miami) who are rarely named in surviving Euro-American records.
- **Religious denominations:** Congregationalist and Presbyterian (New England settlers), Methodist and Baptist (Virginia/Kentucky migrants), Quaker (some Pennsylvania settlers). Formal church infrastructure was minimal in 1790.
- **Key historical events:** Northwest Ordinance (1787), organization of Washington County (1788) and Hamilton County (1790), Harmar's Defeat (1790), St. Clair's Defeat (1791), Battle of Fallen Timbers (1794), Treaty of Greenville (1795), statehood (1803).

- **Hamilton County** was established July 1790, covering the southwestern quadrant (the Symmes Purchase around Cincinnati). Events in that part of the territory after mid-1790 would fall under Hamilton County.
- **The rest of present-day Ohio** had no county organization in 1790. There was no courthouse, no court of record, and no civil registration infrastructure for most of the territory.
- After statehood in 1803, dozens of new counties were carved from Washington and Hamilton counties, and from federal unorganized territory. A record created in "Washington County" in 1791 may describe land now within a completely different county.
- **Temporal split rule:** For any event before 1803, the applicable jurisdiction is Washington County (southeastern Ohio) or Hamilton County (southwestern Ohio), not the modern county. Search under the 1790 county first; records were not transferred to successor counties when they formed — they stayed in the originating county's books.

- **Identify the land district.** If a land record is involved, knowing whether the land lies in the Virginia Military District, the Connecticut Western Reserve, or the federal survey area determines which repository holds the original grant and which survey system was used. Source: FamilySearch Wiki, Ohio Genealogy, "Land Records" section (https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Ohio_Genealogy#Land_Records).

Search both together despite different place-name labels.

Here is the locality guide the subagent produced:

---

**California, Gold Rush Era (ca. 1848–1870) — Locality Guide**

**Jurisdictional context**
California had no territorial phase — it went straight to statehood in September 1850, so county records only begin then. County boundaries shifted frequently through the 1850s–1860s as population spread into the gold fields. The mining districts were concentrated in the Sierra Nevada foothills counties: **El Dorado, Placer, Nevada, Calaveras, Tuolumne, Amador, and Mariposa**.

---

**Key warnings before you search**

- The **1850 federal census for California is partially destroyed**. The **1852 California State Census** is the go-to starting point instead — it's 88% name-indexed and free on FamilySearch.
- Civil registration of births and marriages was county-level from 1850, but **coverage is highly incomplete** for this era. Statewide registration didn't begin until 1905.
- Most records are **county-specific**, so knowing which county your ancestor was in before searching makes a large difference.

---

**Best sources, in rough priority order**

| Record type | Details / Repository |
|---|---|
| **1852 California State Census** | Free on FamilySearch; 88% indexed; best substitute for the damaged 1850 federal census |
| **Federal censuses** (1860, 1870) | FamilySearch or Ancestry; El Dorado, Placer, Calaveras, Tuolumne, Nevada counties especially useful |
| **Great Registers (voter rolls)** | Begin 1866; on FamilySearch; gave age, birthplace, occupation, and physical description annually |
| **Ship passenger manifests** | Sea-route arrivals (via Panama or Cape Horn); held at **NARA Pacific Region, San Bruno, CA** |
| **County mining claim registers** | Filed at county recorders' offices; name, claim location, dates |
| **County tax rolls** | Annual; useful for year-by-year placement of an ancestor in a county |
| **County deed and probate records** | County courthouses and California State Archives |
| **Bancroft Library (UC Berkeley)** | Manuscript diaries, letters, overland trail accounts — much not digitized |
| **California State Library** | Similar manuscript holdings plus printed California history collections |

---

**Next step:** Build a research plan targeting the specific ancestor or family you're tracing in California during this period.

Mining Claim Registers for San Francisco (imageGroupNumber 006601002) covering 1849-1855 are browse-only with no name index and no full-text search — must be browsed image by image.
Port Arrival Registers at Sacramento (imageGroupNumber 006601003) covering 1849-1858 are browse-only with no name index and no full-text search — must be browsed image by image.
Ship passenger manifests for San Francisco arrivals are held at the National Archives, Pacific Region (San Bruno, CA) — a major arrival-route record not duplicated in standard indexed databases.
Great Registers (voter registration, 1866-1910) are the best name-indexed source for adult males in California during this period; women were not eligible to vote and do not appear.
Pre-statehood Mission records (1769-1850) document Spanish and Mexican-era inhabitants — valuable as background but largely outside the Gold Rush migrant population.
FamilySearch volume_search returned 14 total digitized volumes for this place and period; only 3 were detailed in the first page — additional volumes remain unexamined.
Gold Rush migrants arrived by both sea (Pacific routes via Cape Horn or Panama) and overland trails; passenger records and overland diaries are separate record sets requiring separate searches.

The California State Library and the Bancroft Library at UC Berkeley hold extensive Gold Rush-era manuscript collections not available online — consult these for diaries, letters, and unpublished materials. (Source: FamilySearch Wiki, https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/California_Genealogy#Gold_Rush_Records)
entry.guide_markdown:
# Locality Guide: California, United States (1848–1870)

## Jurisdiction overview
- **Formed:** California achieved statehood on September 9, 1850, bypassing territorial status entirely. The original 27 counties were created at the same time.
- **County seat / administrative center:** Sacramento (state capital); San Francisco (commercial hub during Gold Rush)
- **Parent jurisdiction:** None — admitted directly as a state; previously under Mexican sovereignty (Treaty of Guadalupe Hidalgo, 1848)
- **Population during period:** An estimated 14,000 non-indigenous residents in 1848 swelled to approximately 92,000 by the 1850 federal census, with 380,000 by 1860 (Wikipedia: California Gold Rush). The population was predominantly transient, young, and male.
- **Economy:** Placer and hard-rock gold mining dominated 1848–1855; agriculture, commerce, and transport infrastructure developed alongside and after the initial rush.
- **Ethnic composition:** Migrants came from across the United States, Latin America (especially Chile and Mexico), China, Australia, and Europe (particularly from Ireland, Germany, and France). Indigenous Californian peoples were present but often excluded from formal record systems.
- **Religious denominations:** Catholic (dominant among earlier Spanish/Mexican settlers and many Irish and Italian immigrants), Protestant (Methodist, Presbyterian, Baptist, Episcopal), and later Jewish congregations in San Francisco and Sacramento.
- **Key historical events:** Gold discovery at Sutter's Mill (January 24, 1848); California statehood (September 9, 1850); peak Gold Rush migration (1849–1852); decline of placer mining and transition to quartz mining (mid-1850s); completion of the First Transcontinental Railroad (1869).

## Boundary changes
- California became a state in 1850 with no prior territorial phase — there are no territorial-era county records to search before statehood.
- The original 27 counties were established in 1850. Many new counties were carved out of these originals through the 1850s and 1860s as population spread. When researching a specific locality, verify which county it belonged to at the event date, as county lines shifted frequently.
- Before 1848, California was under Mexican jurisdiction. Spanish colonial and Mexican-era records are held primarily by the Catholic Church (Mission archives) and by Mexican governmental archives, not California county offices.

## Available record types

### Vital records (civil registration)
- **Start date:** County-level civil registration of births began in 1850 (with the establishment of counties). Statewide registration was not required until 1905. Coverage for the 1848–1870 period is highly incomplete — many births, marriages, and deaths went unrecorded or records have not survived. The FamilySearch wiki pages for California Vital Records returned only a generic page; the specific start dates given here reflect what `collections_search` confirms (county births from 1850, county marriages from 1850).
- **What exists:**
  - Births: FamilySearch collection "California, County Births, 1850-1919" (collection 2017276) — 789,456 indexed records with images. Covers counties individually, not uniformly.
  - Marriages: FamilySearch collection "California, County Marriages, 1850-1952" (collection 1452832) — 567,890 indexed records (1,135,780 persons) with images.
  - Deaths: No FamilySearch indexed death collection for this period appeared in `collections_search`. County death registers may exist at county courthouses or the California State Archives but are not confirmed as a named indexed collection here.
- **Where held:** County clerk or county recorder offices (originals); California State Archives (Sacramento); FamilySearch (digitized and indexed portions online, free)
- **Gaps:** Statewide coverage is absent before 1905 at the state level. Individual counties have varying completeness. Many Gold Rush-era deaths among transient miners were never recorded.
- **Pre-registration alternatives:** Church baptismal and burial records; the 1852 California State Census; newspaper notices; cemetery records.

### Church records
- **Denominations present:** Catholic Church (Franciscan mission system, and later diocesan parishes); Methodist; Presbyterian; Baptist; Episcopal; Jewish congregations.
- **Record types:** Baptisms, marriages, burials; confirmations in Catholic and Episcopal churches.
- **Where held:** The Archdiocese of San Francisco Archives and the Diocese of Sacramento Archives hold Catholic parish registers. The California State Library and the Bancroft Library (UC Berkeley) hold some copies or transcriptions. FamilySearch microfilm holds portions of California Mission Records (collection 1804372: 98,765 records covering 1769–1850 — largely pre-Gold Rush but essential for long-resident families).
- **Language:** Catholic mission records through 1850 are in Spanish or Latin. Post-statehood Catholic parish records are generally in English, though some immigrant-community parishes (Irish, Italian, German) occasionally used heritage languages.
- **Note:** The FamilySearch wiki pages for California Church Records returned only a generic page. Researchers should consult the Archdiocese of San Francisco Archives and individual county historical societies for specific parish holdings.

### Census records
- **Federal census:** 1850 (partially destroyed — some county returns are missing) and 1860 are the two federal enumerations in this period. The 1850 returns for California are incomplete; the 1860 census is more complete. Mortality schedules (recording deaths in the prior year) exist for 1850 and 1860 and are particularly useful for Gold Rush mortality.
- **State census:** The California State Census of 1852 is the critical substitute for the incomplete 1850 federal returns. FamilySearch digitized volume (imageGroupNumber 006601001): 522 images, 88% name-indexed, and full-text searchable — one of the most accessible Gold Rush-era sources available.
- **Access:** The 1852 state census is searchable by name on FamilySearch (88% indexed). The 1850 and 1860 federal censuses are indexed on FamilySearch and Ancestry.

### Probate and court records
- **Types:** Wills, administrations, guardianships, inventories, estate distributions; naturalization petitions; civil and criminal cases.
- **Date range:** From county formation in 1850 onward.
- **Where held:** County superior courts (originals at county courthouses). The California State Archives holds some transferred county records. Pre-1906 naturalization petitions could be filed in any court of record — search county superior courts, the U.S. District Courts in San Francisco and Sacramento, and the U.S. Circuit Court.
- **Digitization:** No specifically indexed probate collection for this period appeared in `collections_search`. Records are largely physical-only or microfilm. The FamilySearch Catalog should be consulted for specific county microfilm holdings.

### Land records

- **Types:** County property tax assessment rolls (annually from 1850 onward); personal property assessments.

(Source: FamilySearch Wiki — California Genealogy, https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/California_Genealogy#Gold_Rush_Records)

- **Parent jurisdiction:** None — admitted directly as a state; previously under Mexican sovereignty (Treaty of Guadalupe Hidalgo, 1848)

- **Economy:** Placer and hard-rock gold mining dominated 1848–1855; agriculture, commerce, and transport infrastructure developed alongside and after the initial rush.
- **Ethnic composition:** Migrants came from across the United States, Latin America (especially Chile and Mexico), China, Australia, and Europe (particularly from Ireland, Germany, and France). Indigenous Californian peoples were present but often excluded from formal record systems.
- **Religious denominations:** Catholic (dominant among earlier Spanish/Mexican settlers and many Irish and Italian immigrants), Protestant (Methodist, Presbyterian, Baptist, Episcopal), and later Jewish congregations in San Francisco and Sacramento.
- **Key historical events:** Gold discovery at Sutter's Mill (January 24, 1848); California statehood (September 9, 1850); peak Gold Rush migration (1849–1852); decline of placer mining and transition to quartz mining (mid-1850s); completion of the First Transcontinental Railroad (1869).

- California became a state in 1850 with no prior territorial phase — there are no territorial-era county records to search before statehood.

- Sexton records for Gold Rush-era camp cemeteries

## Known record losses

- **1850 federal census:** Partially destroyed — some county returns for California are missing. Use the 1852 California State Census as the primary substitute.
- **San Francisco earthquake and fire (1906):** Destroyed many records held in San Francisco, including some county vital records and court files. This is outside the research period but affects survival of records created in the 1850s–1860s that were still held in the city.
- **Mining camp records:** Many informal mining camp records were never formally kept or have been lost. No systematic inventory of surviving camp records exists.
- **Courthouse losses:** Individual county courthouses experienced fires and losses in the 19th century; specific county record losses should be verified before concluding a record does not exist.

## Research tips
- The 1852 California State Census is the single most important starting point for Gold Rush-era research — it is 88% name-indexed on FamilySearch and full-text searchable, and it covers the peak migration period that the partially-destroyed 1850 federal census misses. (Source: FamilySearch Wiki — California Genealogy, https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/California_Genealogy#Gold_Rush_Records)
- Ship passenger manifests for San Francisco arrivals are a key source for sea-route migrants. These are held at NARA Pacific Region (San Bruno) and partially indexed on Ancestry. Search these before assuming an ancestor's arrival cannot be documented. (Source: FamilySearch Wiki — California Genealogy, https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/California_Genealogy#Gold_Rush_Records)
- The Great Registers (collection 1923340) begin in 1866 — they do not cover the first 18 years of the Gold Rush, but they are the most reliable name-indexed source for confirming a male ancestor's presence and county of residence from 1866 onward.
- Determine which specific county your ancestor was in before searching: mining was concentrated in the Sierra Nevada foothills counties (El Dorado, Placer, Nevada, Calaveras, Tuolumne, Amador, Mariposa). County-level record keeping means a statewide search is not sufficient — you need the right county.
- California is a federal-land state. Use BLM GLO (glorecords.blm.gov, free) to search federal land patents for miners who transitioned to farming or town lots.
- For naturalization, search county superior courts, the U.S. District Court in San Francisco, and the U.S. District Court in Sacramento. Pre-1906 naturalizations could be filed in any court of record and are scattered widely.
- The Bancroft Library at UC Berkeley holds the most extensive collection of Gold Rush primary manuscripts (diaries, letters, mining district records) not available anywhere online. A visit or a paid research request is worthwhile when documentary sources are exhausted. (Source: FamilySearch Wiki — California Genealogy, https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/California_Genealogy#Gold_Rush_Records)
- Mining claim registers and county deed records are an underused source — they place a named individual in a specific mining district at a specific date, which is often the only way to confirm a transient miner's presence when census and vital records are absent.
- Tax rolls, while largely physical-only, provide annual coverage 1850 onward and fill the gap between the 1852 state census and the 1860 federal census.
- When searching across counties, note that many Gold Rush miners moved frequently between mining districts — expect to search multiple counties for a single ancestor.

---

This guide covers New York City during the 1700s, a century divided between British colonial rule (as New York Province, through 1776) and early statehood. The most important thing to know upfront: **there was no civil vital registration anywhere in colonial New York**, so church registers are the only documents recording births, baptisms, marriages, and deaths.

**Church Records**
The Dutch Reformed Church has the oldest continuous register series, going back to 1639, but those records from 1700 to 1776 are in Dutch, unindexed, and must be browsed image by image — a researcher needs to read 18th-century Dutch script to use them.

**Online Resources**
FamilySearch holds five indexed collections covering church records, land, probate, and tax rolls, all searchable online and free.

**Physical Repositories**
For deeper research you will need to work with physical repositories:
- **New York State Archives** (Albany) — colonial government records and land patents
- **New York City Municipal Archives** — Mayor's Court files
- **New-York Historical Society** — the essential *Abstracts of Wills* index and Loyalist material
- **New York Genealogical and Biographical Society** — transcribed colonial church and court records not available on major platforms

When you are ready, a research plan can be built around a specific family or question using this locality guide as its foundation.

entry.guide_markdown:
# Locality Guide: New York City (1700–1800)

## Jurisdiction overview
- **Formed:** New Amsterdam established 1626 by the Dutch West India Company; seized by England 1664 and renamed New York City
- **Administrative center:** City Hall (lower Manhattan); New York City served as the capital of New York Province under British rule
- **Parent jurisdiction during 1700s:** New York Province (British colonial, 1664-1776), then New York State (1776-)
- **Population during period:** Population data for this specific place and period was not returned by the population tool; Wikipedia notes the city was the largest in British North America by the late 1700s, with estimates of roughly 5,000 in 1700 rising to approximately 33,000 by 1790 (per the first federal census).
- **Economy:** Major commercial port and trading hub; merchant shipping, maritime trades, artisan crafts, and retail. The fur trade was a earlier driver; by the 1700s, Atlantic commerce dominated.
- **Ethnic composition:** Predominantly Dutch-descended families in the early part of the century, with growing English, Huguenot (French Protestant), German, and African populations. Enslaved Africans formed a significant share of the population.
- **Religious denominations:** Dutch Reformed (oldest continuous series of registers), Anglican/Church of England (Trinity Church, founded 1697), Presbyterian, Lutheran, French Reformed (Huguenot), Quaker, Jewish (Congregation Shearith Israel, the oldest synagogue in North America).
- **Key historical events:** 1712 and 1741 slave insurrections and trials (court records survive); Seven Years' War (1756-1763); British occupation of the city 1776-1783; the city briefly served as the first U.S. capital 1789-1790.

## Boundary changes
- The city occupied the southern tip of Manhattan Island throughout the 1700s. Its political parent changed from British colonial Province of New York (until 1776) to New York State (from 1776).
- Record custody follows this split: pre-1776 colonial court records, land patents, and administrative records are in the New York Colonial Manuscripts series at the New York State Archives; post-1776 records shift to state and city repositories.
- The city's five modern boroughs did not exist in this period. All 1700s records concern Manhattan only.

## Available record types

### Vital records (civil registration)
- **Start date:** There was no civil vital registration system in New York City during the 1700s. The FamilySearch Wiki pages for New York Vital Records redirected to a generic page and did not return jurisdiction-specific registration dates for this period — do not assume a civil start date from memory. What is established by the wiki_search result is that civil registration did not exist during this period and church records are the substitute.
- **What exists:** No civil birth, marriage, or death certificates for the 1700s.
- **Where held:** N/A for civil records in this period.
- **Pre-registration alternatives:** Church registers of baptism, marriage, and burial are the primary vital-event records. See Church Records below.

### Church records
- **Denominations present and their record series:**
  - **Dutch Reformed Church** — oldest continuous register series beginning 1639. FamilySearch volume 007733180 (211 images) covers 1700-1776. Records are in **Dutch** and are 0% name-indexed and not full-text searchable; they must be browsed image by image. A researcher must be able to read 18th-century Dutch script.
  - **Anglican / Church of England** — Trinity Church (founded 1697) maintained registers of baptisms, marriages, and burials. Trinity's records are among the best-preserved for the English-speaking population.
  - **Presbyterian** — First Presbyterian Church of New York records survive for part of this period.
  - **French Reformed (Huguenot)** — Congregation records document the Huguenot community that arrived in large numbers after 1685.
  - **Lutheran** — German and Dutch Lutheran registers.
  - **Jewish** — Congregation Shearith Israel kept records of births, marriages, and deaths in the Sephardic Jewish community.
- **FamilySearch indexed collection:** "New York, Church Records, 1640-1940" (collection id 1469062) covers the period and is name-indexed. This is the broadest digital starting point.
- **Where originals are held:** Individual congregational archives, the New York Genealogical & Biographical Society (NYGBS), and the New-York Historical Society. The Reformed Church in America archives (New Brunswick Theological Seminary) holds many Dutch Reformed registers.
- **Language:** Dutch Reformed records are in Dutch. Anglican records are in English. French Reformed records may be in French.

### Census records
- **Federal/national census:** The first federal census was 1790 — it is the only federal census that falls near this period and captures families who were present in the 1780s-1790s. It is indexed and available online (FamilySearch, Ancestry).
- **Colonial enumerations:** The Province of New York took several censuses during the colonial period. These are not standard federal enumerations and coverage is uneven. The New York State Archives holds surviving colonial census lists.
- **Other enumerations:** Tax assessment lists survive for some years and city wards, and are accessible through the New York State Archives and published transcriptions. Militia rolls list men of military age and can serve as a rough census substitute.
- **Access:** The 1790 federal census is indexed + images online. Colonial-era lists are largely physical-only or microfilm.

### Probate and court records
- **Types:** Wills, administrations, inventories, guardianships. During the British colonial period, wills were proved before the **Prerogative Court of New York** (a provincial court). After independence, probate shifted to the New York Surrogate's Court.
- **Key finding aid:** The *Abstracts of Wills* series, published by the New-York Historical Society, indexes wills proved before the Prerogative Court. This is the essential starting index for colonial-era probate.
- **FamilySearch collection:** "New York, Probate Records, 1629-1971" (collection id 1542780) covers the period.
- **Where held:** New York State Archives (colonial-era originals); New York County Surrogate's Court (post-1776); the New-York Historical Society (published abstracts and microfilm).
- **Mayor's Court:** The Mayor's Court of New York City heard civil and some criminal matters throughout the colonial period. Records are at the New York City Municipal Archives.

### Land records
- **Survey system:** Metes and bounds (colonial New York used the English metes-and-bounds system; Dutch-era lot descriptions also appear).
- **Land-distribution jurisdiction:** Land patents and grants during the colonial period were issued under the authority of the Province of New York (the Royal Governor). The New York State Archives holds the New York Colonial Manuscripts, which include land patents.
- **Types:** Deeds, grants, patents, conveyances, mortgages.
- **FamilySearch collection:** "New York, Land Records, 1630-1975" (collection id 2078654) covers the full colonial period.
- **Where held:** New York State Archives (colonial patents); New York City Register's Office (deeds recorded at the city level); the New-York Historical Society.

### Military records
- **Relevant conflicts:** Queen Anne's War (1702-1713), King George's War (1744-1748), Seven Years' War/French and Indian War (1756-1763), American Revolution (1775-1783).
- **Record types:** Colonial militia rolls (Province of New York); Continental Army service records; Loyalist claims (for families who remained loyal to the Crown during the Revolution, extensive records were filed with British authorities).
- **Where held:** New York State Archives (colonial militia); National Archives (NARA) for Continental service records and pension files; the New-York Historical Society for Loyalist material; the Public Record Office (now The National Archives, UK) for British military records involving New York.
- **Note on Loyalists:** Many established Dutch and English colonial families in New York City were Loyalists. Their records (including property confiscation proceedings after 1776) are a valuable genealogical source and can be found at the New York State Archives and British repositories.

### Cemetery records
- **Major burial grounds:** Trinity Church Churchyard (lower Manhattan, still extant; burials dating to the late 1600s); St. Paul's Chapel Churchyard; Dutch Reformed Church burying grounds; Congregation Shearith Israel's oldest cemetery (Chatham Square, 1683, the oldest Jewish cemetery in the U.S.).
- **Online coverage:** FindAGrave and BillionGraves have transcriptions of Trinity and some other churchyards. Coverage is incomplete for the 1700s.
- **Physical records:** Sexton records and burial registers survive for some congregations at their archives or at NYGBS.

### Newspaper records
- **Local papers:** The *New-York Gazette* (founded 1725, the city's first newspaper) and later the *New-York Weekly Journal* (1733) and *New-York Mercury* (1752). Multiple papers operated through the later 18th century.
- **Content value:** Marriage and death notices, legal notices (estate administration, land sales), runaway servant/slave advertisements (which name enslaved and indentured people), and political news identifying community figures.
- **Where held:** The New-York Historical Society and the New York Public Library hold microfilm runs. America's Historical Newspapers (Readex) and Newspapers.com have partial digital coverage.

### Immigration/emigration records
- **Relevant port:** The Port of New York was the primary Atlantic entry point.
- **Record types:** Passenger lists (colonial-era lists are fragmentary compared to post-1820 arrivals); naturalization proceedings before the Mayor's Court or other courts of record.
- **Where held:** NARA (post-1820 passenger lists are more complete); the New York City Municipal Archives and New York State Archives for colonial naturalization records; the *Denizations and Naturalizations* series published by NYGBS covers colonial-period proceedings.
- **Note:** Colonial-era passenger lists are sparse. The strongest substitute is church records of newly-arrived immigrants presenting for membership.

This guide covers New York City during the 1700s, a century divided between British colonial rule (as New York Province, through 1776) and early statehood. The most important thing to know upfront: there was no civil vital registration anywhere in colonial New York, so church registers are the only documents recording births, baptisms, marriages, and deaths. The Dutch Reformed Church has the oldest continuous register series, going back to 1639, but those records from 1700 to 1776 are in Dutch, unindexed, and must be browsed image by image — a researcher needs to read 18th-century Dutch script to use them. FamilySearch holds five indexed collections covering church records, land, probate, and tax rolls, all searchable online and free. For deeper research you will need to work with physical repositories: the New York State Archives in Albany for colonial government records and land patents, the New York City Municipal Archives for Mayor's Court files, the New-York Historical Society for the essential Abstracts of Wills index and Loyalist material, and the New York Genealogical and Biographical Society for transcribed colonial church and court records not available on major platforms.

When you are ready, a research plan can be built around a specific family or question using this locality guide as its foundation.

# Locality Guide: New York City (1700–1800)

## Jurisdiction overview
- **Formed:** New Amsterdam established 1626 by the Dutch West India Company; seized by England 1664 and renamed New York City
- **Administrative center:** City Hall (lower Manhattan); New York City served as the capital of New York Province under British rule
- **Parent jurisdiction during 1700s:** New York Province (British colonial, 1664-1776), then New York State (1776-)
- **Population during period:** Population data for this specific place and period was not returned by the population tool; Wikipedia notes the city was the largest in British North America by the late 1700s, with estimates of roughly 5,000 in 1700 rising to approximately 33,000 by 1790 (per the first federal census).
- **Economy:** Major commercial port and trading hub; merchant shipping, maritime trades, artisan crafts, and retail. The fur trade was a earlier driver; by the 1700s, Atlantic commerce dominated.
- **Ethnic composition:** Predominantly Dutch-descended families in the early part of the century, with growing English, Huguenot (French Protestant), German, and African populations. Enslaved Africans formed a significant share of the population.
- **Religious denominations:** Dutch Reformed (oldest continuous series of registers), Anglican/Church of England (Trinity Church, founded 1697), Presbyterian, Lutheran, French Reformed (Huguenot), Quaker, Jewish (Congregation Shearith Israel, the oldest synagogue in North America).
- **Key historical events:** 1712 and 1741 slave insurrections and trials (court records survive); Seven Years' War (1756-1763); British occupation of the city 1776-1783; the city briefly served as the first U.S. capital 1789-1790.

## Boundary changes
- The city occupied the southern tip of Manhattan Island throughout the 1700s. Its political parent changed from British colonial Province of New York (until 1776) to New York State (from 1776).
- Record custody follows this split: pre-1776 colonial court records, land patents, and administrative records are in the New York Colonial Manuscripts series at the New York State Archives; post-1776 records shift to state and city repositories.
- The city's five modern boroughs did not exist in this period. All 1700s records concern Manhattan only.

## Available record types

### Vital records (civil registration)
- **Start date:** There was no civil vital registration system in New York City during the 1700s. The FamilySearch Wiki pages for New York Vital Records redirected to a generic page and did not return jurisdiction-specific registration dates for this period — do not assume a civil start date from memory. What is established by the wiki_search result is that civil registration did not exist during this period and church records are the substitute.
- **What exists:** No civil birth, marriage, or death certificates for the 1700s.
- **Where held:** N/A for civil records in this period.
- **Pre-registration alternatives:** Church registers of baptism, marriage, and burial are the primary vital-event records. See Church Records below.

### Church records
- **Denominations present and their record series:**
  - **Dutch Reformed Church** — oldest continuous register series beginning 1639. FamilySearch volume 007733180 (211 images) covers 1700-1776. Records are in **Dutch** and are 0% name-indexed and not full-text searchable; they must be browsed image by image. A researcher must be able to read 18th-century Dutch script.
  - **Anglican / Church of England** — Trinity Church (founded 1697) maintained registers of baptisms, marriages, and burials. Trinity's records are among the best-preserved for the English-speaking population.
  - **Presbyterian** — First Presbyterian Church of New York records survive for part of this period.
  - **French Reformed (Huguenot)** — Congregation records document the Huguenot community that arrived in large numbers after 1685.
  - **Lutheran** — German and Dutch Lutheran registers.
  - **Jewish** — Congregation Shearith Israel kept records of births, marriages, and deaths in the Sephardic Jewish community.
- **FamilySearch indexed collection:** "New York, Church Records, 1640-1940" (collection id 1469062) covers the period and is name-indexed. This is the broadest digital starting point.
- **Where originals are held:** Individual congregational archives, the New York Genealogical & Biographical Society (NYGBS), and the New-York Historical Society. The Reformed Church in America archives (New Brunswick Theological Seminary) holds many Dutch Reformed registers.
- **Language:** Dutch Reformed records are in Dutch. Anglican records are in English. French Reformed records may be in French.

### Census records
- **Federal/national census:** The first federal census was 1790 — it is the only federal census that falls near this period and captures families who were present in the 1780s-1790s. It is indexed and available online (FamilySearch, Ancestry).
- **Colonial enumerations:** The Province of New York took several censuses during the colonial period. These are not standard federal enumerations and coverage is uneven. The New York State Archives holds surviving colonial census lists.
- **Other enumerations:** Tax assessment lists survive for some years and city wards, and are accessible through the New York State Archives and published transcriptions. Militia rolls list men of military age and can serve as a rough census substitute.
- **Access:** The 1790 federal census is indexed + images online. Colonial-era lists are largely physical-only or microfilm.

### Probate and court records
- **Types:** Wills, administrations, inventories, guardianships. During the British colonial period, wills were proved before the **Prerogative Court of New York** (a provincial court). After independence, probate shifted to the New York Surrogate's Court.
- **Key finding aid:** The *Abstracts of Wills* series, published by the New-York Historical Society, indexes wills proved before the Prerogative Court. This is the essential starting index for colonial-era probate.
- **FamilySearch collection:** "New York, Probate Records, 1629-1971" (collection id 1542780) covers the period.
- **Where held:** New York State Archives (colonial-era originals); New York County Surrogate's Court (post-1776); the New-York Historical Society (published abstracts and microfilm).
- **Mayor's Court:** The Mayor's Court of New York City heard civil and some criminal matters throughout the colonial period. Records are at the New York City Municipal Archives.

### Land records
- **Survey system:** Metes and bounds (colonial New York used the English metes-and-bounds system; Dutch-era lot descriptions also appear).
- **Land-distribution jurisdiction:** Land patents and grants during the colonial period were issued under the authority of the Province of New York (the Royal Governor). The New York State Archives holds the New York Colonial Manuscripts, which include land patents.
- **Types:** Deeds, grants, patents, conveyances, mortgages.
- **FamilySearch collection:** "New York, Land Records, 1630-1975" (collection id 2078654) covers the full colonial period.
- **Where held:** New York State Archives (colonial patents); New York City Register's Office (deeds recorded at the city level); the New-York Historical Society.

### Military records

- **Note on Loyalists:** Many established Dutch and English colonial families in New York City were Loyalists. Their records (including property confiscation proceedings after 1776) are a valuable genealogical source and can be found at the New York State Archives and British repositories.

### Cemetery records

- **Where held:** The New-York Historical Society and the New York Public Library hold microfilm runs. America's Historical Newspapers (Readex) and Newspapers.com have partial digital coverage.

### Immigration/emigration records
- **Relevant port:** The Port of New York was the primary Atlantic entry point.
- **Record types:** Passenger lists (colonial-era lists are fragmentary compared to post-1820 arrivals); naturalization proceedings before the Mayor's Court or other courts of record.
- **Where held:** NARA (post-1820 passenger lists are more complete); the New York City Municipal Archives and New York State Archives for colonial naturalization records; the *Denizations and Naturalizations* series published by NYGBS covers colonial-period proceedings.

- **Content note:** Passenger lists (arrival manifests) record every person aboard, including infants and young children traveling with parents. When researching a family, examine the full manifest for all family members.

### Tax records
- **Types:** Provincial tax lists; city ward assessment rolls.
- **Date range:** Some colonial tax lists survive from the early 1700s.
- **FamilySearch collection:** "New York, Tax Assessment Rolls of Real and Personal Estates, 1799-1804" (collection id 1678432) falls at the very end of the period.

The subagent produced locality guide **`loc_001`** and offers this survey:

---

### Key Context to Know Up Front

- **No 1790 Virginia federal census exists** — it was destroyed in 1814. The **1782–1787 state personal property and land tax lists** are the primary substitute for placing families in Virginia during and just after the war.
- **No civil vital registration** existed in this era. Births, marriages, and burials appear only in **church registers** (Anglican/Episcopal vestry books especially) and **county court records**.

---

### Best Record Types for Military Families

| Record Type | What It Contains | Where to Find It |
|---|---|---|
| **Revolutionary War pension files** | Names soldier's wife, children, neighbors, county; often the richest biographical source | NARA (National Archives) — also on FamilySearch and Fold3 |
| **Bounty land warrants** | Issued to veterans for service; names county of residence | Library of Virginia (LOV); FamilySearch has a browse-only volume |
| **Virginia militia records** | Muster rolls, pay records, commissions | Library of Virginia, Richmond |
| **County deed & court order books** | Land transactions, estate settlements, court actions | Individual county courthouses; microfilm at LOV |
| **1782–1787 tax lists** | Personal property and land — census substitute | Library of Virginia; FamilySearch indexed collection |
| **Anglican/Episcopal vestry books** | Baptisms, marriages, burials, poor relief | LOV; individual churches; some on FamilySearch |

---

### Key Repositories

- **Library of Virginia (Richmond)** — anchor repository for militia records, bounty warrants, county records on microfilm
- **NARA** — pension files (pension application series W, S, R, BLW numbers)
- **FamilySearch** — five indexed collections: church records, land & wills, military records (1775–1783 specifically), tax records, county court records; plus digitized volumes including full-text-searchable tax lists

---
