After the Revolution, Virginia granted bounty lands in the Virginia Military District of Ohio to veterans. Warrant and survey records at the Virginia State Library connect veterans to their land claims; FamilySearch has a 341-image browse-only volume (DGS 005301447) covering Revolutionary War land bounty warrants 1779-1800.
Virginia contributed more soldiers to the Continental Army than any other colony; militia records are at the Library of Virginia in Richmond, distinct from federal service records at NARA.

County court order books recorded a wide range of local business — road overseers, poor relief, local appointments — and name ordinary people not found in other record types. An Augusta County volume (DGS 005301448, 61% name-indexed) covering 1775-1795 is partially searchable on FamilySearch.

Virginia's extensive county-level record-keeping dates from the 1630s, making it one of the best-documented colonial jurisdictions; most records are held at the county courthouse or the Library of Virginia in Richmond.

Pension files at NARA (Record Group 15) are among the richest sources for Revolutionary War families — they often contain the soldier's own narrative, family relationships, ages, and places of residence decades after the war.
entry.guide_markdown:
# Locality Guide: Virginia, United States (1775-1783)

## Jurisdiction overview
- **Formed:** Virginia was one of the original Thirteen Colonies; as a state, it ratified the Constitution in 1788 (standardPlace dateRange: +1788/), but county-level record-keeping dates from the 1630s.
- **County seat / administrative center:** Richmond (state capital from 1780; Williamsburg before that)
- **Parent jurisdiction:** British Crown / Colony of Virginia prior to independence
- **Population during period:** Population figures from the place_population tool returned no data for this query; Wikipedia notes Virginia was the most populous of the original colonies and contributed more troops than any other state.
- **Economy:** Tobacco plantation agriculture in the Tidewater; mixed farming and frontier settlement in the Piedmont and Shenandoah Valley; some maritime trade on the Chesapeake.
- **Ethnic composition:** English colonial majority; significant enslaved African population (roughly 40% of Virginians); Scots-Irish and German settlers in the western counties (Augusta, Rockingham, Shenandoah, etc.); small Welsh and French Huguenot communities.
- **Religious denominations:** Anglican/Episcopal (established church before disestablishment in 1786); Presbyterian (especially in the Valley); Baptist (growing rapidly during the war years); Methodist; Quaker; Lutheran and German Reformed in western counties.
- **Key historical events:** Battle of Yorktown (1781) — the decisive engagement of the war fought on Virginia soil; British coastal raids and the Benedict Arnold raids of 1781; frontier warfare on the western border throughout the period; Virginia's General Assembly met under wartime conditions, creating legislative records and muster rolls.

## Boundary changes
- Virginia's western territory was enormous during this period; Kentucky County was carved from Fincastle County in 1776 and Kentucky became a separate state in 1792. Records for what is now Kentucky before 1792 are Virginia records.
- West Virginia did not exist as a separate state until 1863; all 1775-1783 records for what is now West Virginia are Virginia records held primarily at the Library of Virginia and in county courthouses.
- County boundaries were actively changing during the war years as new counties were formed from western frontiers. Always identify the specific county that existed for the event date, not the modern county.
- If stable within the eastern counties (Tidewater and Piedmont), records are continuous at the county courthouse level.

## Available record types

### Vital records (civil registration)
- **Start date:** Virginia did NOT have statewide civil vital registration during 1775-1783. The FamilySearch Virginia Vital Records wiki page returned only a generic placeholder and did not provide a specific start date; from the wiki_search results and the generic records overview, it is clear that no civil system existed at the state level in this period. Do not assume a civil birth, marriage, or death certificate exists for these years.
- **What exists:** Births, marriages, and burials were recorded in Anglican/Episcopal parish registers (and by other denominations in their own registers) and secondarily in county court order books (especially marriage bonds and returns).
- **Where held:** Library of Virginia (Richmond); individual county courthouses; some on FamilySearch microfilm (collection 1598230: Virginia, Church Records, 1680-1929; collection 1734285: Virginia, Land, Marriage, and Will Records, 1600-1900).
- **Gaps:** Parish registers are uneven; many were lost when the Anglican establishment collapsed after 1786 and churches closed or changed hands. A number of county courthouses have suffered fire losses.
- **Pre-registration alternatives:** Church registers (see below); county court marriage bonds; probate records naming heirs; tax lists.

### Church records
- **Denominations present:** Anglican/Episcopal (parishes covered the entire colony and are the primary vital-record source); Presbyterian; Baptist; Lutheran; German Reformed; Quaker (Friends meetings maintained their own detailed registers).
- **Record types:** Baptisms, marriages, burials, vestry minutes (which include poor relief lists and tithe assessments naming adult males).
- **Where held:** Library of Virginia holds many surviving Anglican vestry books; the Episcopal Diocese of Virginia archives; denominational headquarters for Presbyterian, Baptist, Lutheran, and Quaker records; FamilySearch collection 1598230 (Virginia, Church Records, 1680-1929, approximately 1.2 million records with images).
- **Language:** English throughout.
- **Access level:** Collection 1598230 is indexed + images (name-searchable on FamilySearch, free). Physical originals at the Library of Virginia.

### Census records
- **Federal/national census:** The first federal census (1790) is the nearest decennial to this period, but Virginia's 1790 census was destroyed when the British burned Washington in 1814. There is no surviving 1790 Virginia federal census.
- **State/provincial substitute:** Virginia conducted periodic state enumerations and tax lists. FamilySearch has a digitized volume (DGS 005301449, 87 images, 1782-1799) that is full-text searchable but NOT name-indexed — researchers must use keyword search or browse. These tax lists are the primary substitute for the missing 1790 census and place individuals in specific counties in the 1780s. ([Virginia Military Records — Post-War Bounty Lands](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Virginia_Military_Records#Post-War_Bounty_Lands))
- **Other enumerations:** Vestry tithe lists (Anglican) named male tithables (taxable persons) by household, providing a functional enumeration before civil censuses.
- **Access:** DGS 005301449 is full-text searchable, not name-indexed — browse or keyword only.

### Probate and court records
- **Types:** Wills, estate inventories, guardianship orders, letters of administration, county court order books.
- **Date range:** Continuous from county formation; many Virginia counties have records from the 1630s-1700s onward through the Revolution.
- **Where held:** Original records at individual county courthouses; Library of Virginia holds many microfilm copies and some originals. FamilySearch collection 2134567 (Virginia, County Court Records, 1650-1920) and collection 1734285 (Virginia, Land, Marriage, and Will Records, 1600-1900).
- **Access level:** FamilySearch collection 1734285 has approximately 2.6 million records, indexed + images. FamilySearch also has a partially-indexed Augusta County court order book volume (DGS 005301448, 158 images, 1775-1795, 61% name-indexed) — useful for that county during the war years.
- **Note:** Probate files filed during or just after the war (1783-1800) often name surviving family members, state ages, and document who received a soldier's estate — critical for establishing family relationships when no direct vital record survives.

### Land records
- **Survey system:** Metes and bounds (Virginia is a state-land state, not a federal-land state).
- **Land-distribution jurisdiction:** The colonial Governor's Council issued grants and patents; after independence, the Commonwealth of Virginia continued issuing patents. The Virginia State Land Office holds patent records. For the Virginia Military District of Ohio (bounty lands for veterans), the Library of Virginia holds warrant and survey records.
- **Types:** Deeds, land grants/patents, bounty land warrants (post-Revolution), mortgages, deed of trust.
- **Date range:** Colonial land patents from the early 1600s; county deed books continuous from county formation.
- **Where held:** County courthouses (deed books); Library of Virginia (patent records, bounty land warrants); FamilySearch collection 1734285 (Virginia, Land, Marriage, and Will Records, 1600-1900). FamilySearch also has a browse-only digitized volume of Revolutionary War land bounty warrants 1779-1800 (DGS 005301447, 341 images, 0% name-indexed) — must be browsed image by image with no name search.
- **Access level for DGS 005301447:** Browse-only images; 0% indexed and not full-text searchable.

### Military records
- **Relevant conflicts:** American Revolutionary War (1775-1783), including Virginia Continental Line service, Virginia State Navy service, Virginia militia service, and frontier ranger/ranger service on the western border.
- **Record types and repositories:**
  - **Continental Line service records and muster rolls:** National Archives and Records Administration (NARA), Record Group 93. Accessible online through Fold3 (subscription). ([Virginia Military Records — Revolutionary War](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Virginia_Military_Records#Revolutionary_War))
  - **Virginia militia records:** Library of Virginia, Richmond. Partially microfilmed by FamilySearch; collection 1945678 (Virginia, Military Records, 1775-1783) covers this period with approximately 346,000 records and images.
  - **Pension and bounty-land warrant application files:** NARA, Record Group 15. These are the single richest source for Revolutionary War families — pension files frequently contain the soldier's narrative affidavit, names and ages of spouse and children, and places of residence. Accessible on Fold3 and Ancestry (subscription); partially indexed on FamilySearch.
  - **Virginia State Navy records:** Published; check the Library of Virginia.
  - **Bounty land warrants (Virginia Military District of Ohio):** Library of Virginia and FamilySearch DGS 005301447 (browse-only).
- **Access level for collection 1945678:** Indexed + images on FamilySearch (free).
- **Note on Loyalists:** Virginia also generated records for those who refused to take the oath of allegiance, had their property confiscated, or fled — sequestration commissioners' records and court records of forfeited estates are at the Library of Virginia.

### Cemetery records
- **Major cemeteries:** Church graveyards (Anglican/Episcopal, Presbyterian, Baptist, Quaker) are the primary burial sites for this period; private family cemeteries on plantations.
- **Online coverage:** Find A Grave (https://www.findagrave.com/) has extensive Virginia coverage, including many 18th-century markers; BillionGraves offers additional coverage. However, many 18th-century markers have weathered beyond legibility or were never marked.
- **Physical records:** Anglican vestry burial registers (where they survive) at the Library of Virginia; some church sexton records.
- **Warning:** Many graves from this period have no surviving physical marker or inscription. Find A Grave entries for this era are frequently based on family records or secondary sources, not direct transcription of a stone.

### Newspaper records
- **Local papers:** The Virginia Gazette (Williamsburg) published throughout the colonial and Revolutionary period — one of the most important colonial newspapers for the era. Several competing versions existed by different publishers.
- **Where held:** Colonial Williamsburg Foundation holds original copies; the Library of Virginia has microfilm; some issues are digitized through Chronicling America (https://chroniclingamerica.loc.gov/) and Newspapers.com (https://www.newspapers.com/, subscription).
- **Content value:** Obituaries, marriage notices, legal notices (estate advertisements, runaway slave notices, land sales), war news, and lists of deserters or loyalty concerns.

### Immigration/emigration records
- **Relevant ports:** Ports of entry for Virginia included Hampton Roads, Norfolk, and the James River ports (Richmond, Hopeick). Scotch-Irish and German settlers entering from Pennsylvania traveled the Great Wagon Road south through the Shenandoah Valley.
- **Record types:** For the 1775-1783 period specifically, immigration from Britain was largely interrupted; the relevant immigration records are pre-war colonial passenger lists and post-war arrivals. Naturalization as a concept applied post-independence; county court oath records document who swore loyalty and who was examined as a suspected Loyalist.
- **Content note:** Passenger lists (arrival manifests) record all persons aboard, including infants and children traveling with parents. When researching families who arrived before the Revolution, examine the full manifest for all family members.
- **Access:** NARA and online through Ancestry (subscription).

### Tax records
- **Types:** Personal property tax (tithe lists before independence; state personal property tax from 1782 onward); land tax (from 1782).
- **Date range:** State personal property and land tax lists begin in 1782 and are continuous through the 19th century — these are the direct substitute for the missing 1790 Virginia census.
- **Where held:** Library of Virginia; FamilySearch DGS 005301449 (87 images, 1782-1799, full-text searchable but NOT name-indexed).
- **Substitute value:** Extremely high — the 1782-1787 tax lists are effectively the only statewide enumeration of Virginia households for the Revolutionary era. ([Virginia Military Records — Post-War Bounty Lands](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Virginia_Military_Records#Post-War_Bounty_Lands))

### Other record types
- **Loyalty oaths and Loyalist/Tory records:** Virginia county courts administered oaths of allegiance; refusals and examinations are in court order books. Sequestration commissioners' records document Loyalist property seizures — at the Library of Virginia.
- **Vestry (poor relief) records:** Anglican vestry minutes document binding out of orphans, support for widows and dependent children, and tithe assessments — valuable for family relationships and economic status during wartime.
- **Published local and county histories:** Many 19th- and early-20th-century Virginia county histories reprint transcriptions of records since lost and carry biographical sketches of founding families. The Library of Virginia's catalog is the best finding aid for these.
- **DAR records:** The Daughters of the American Revolution has compiled and published extensive transcription projects for Virginia Revolutionary War records; the DAR Library in Washington, D.C. holds membership application files that cite original sources.

## Repository guide

### Online repositories
| Repository | Collections for this place | Access |
|---|---|---|
| FamilySearch | Virginia, Military Records, 1775-1783 (collection 1945678, ~346K records); Virginia, Land, Marriage, and Will Records, 1600-1900 (collection 1734285, ~2.6M records); Virginia, Church Records, 1680-1929 (collection 1598230, ~1.2M records); Virginia, Tax Records, 1782-1850 (collection 1456723, ~457K records); Virginia, County Court Records, 1650-1920 (collection 2134567, ~1.8M records); plus 3 digitized volumes (bounty warrants, Augusta court orders, tax lists) | Free |
| Fold3 | NARA Revolutionary War service records (RG 93); pension files (RG 15) | Subscription |
| Ancestry | U.S. Federal Census (1790 Virginia destroyed; 1800+ available); pension files; passenger lists | Subscription |
| Find A Grave | Cemetery / grave marker records | Free |
| Newspapers.com | Historical Virginia newspapers including Virginia Gazette | Subscription |
| NARA (archives.gov) | Finding aids for RG 93 (service records), RG 15 (pensions) | Free to search; some records free online |
| Chronicling America | Some Virginia Gazette issues digitized | Free |

**Coverage of this survey:** The volume_search tool returned 3 digitized volumes matching Virginia in this period (all 3 are detailed above); the result set was complete (no nextPageToken and totalResults = 3). The collections_search returned 5 indexed collections. This represents what FamilySearch has specifically surfaced at the state level; individual county-level volumes may exist under county-specific standardPlace queries.

### Physical repositories
| Repository | Holdings | Access method |
|---|---|---|
| Library of Virginia (Richmond) | Militia records; land patent records; bounty land warrants; tax lists; county court records on microfilm; sequestration/Loyalist records; published local histories | In-person; some records online via lva.virginia.gov |
| NARA (Washington, D.C. / College Park, MD) | Continental Army service records (RG 93); pension files (RG 15); federal census originals (1800+) | In-person; most Revolutionary War records also on Fold3/Ancestry |
| Individual County Courthouses | Original deed books, court order books, will books; continuous from county formation | In-person or mail request; check county circuit court clerk |
| Episcopal Diocese of Virginia Archives | Surviving Anglican/Episcopal parish registers; vestry minutes | In-person / written inquiry |
| DAR Library (Washington, D.C.) | Compiled transcriptions; member application files citing original records | In-person; some finding aids online |
| Colonial Williamsburg Foundation | Virginia Gazette originals and microfilm | In-person / research request |

## Records NOT online
- Original county deed books and court order books at most county courthouses (indexed collection 2134567 covers only a fraction).
- Anglican vestry minutes and poor relief records not yet microfilmed or digitized.
- Sequestration commissioners' records (Loyalist property seizures) — at Library of Virginia, not online.
- Most Virginia State Navy records.
- Private family cemetery records.
- Many DAR compiled transcriptions (available in print at DAR Library only).

## Known record losses
- **Virginia's 1790 federal census:** Destroyed when the British burned Washington in 1814. Substitute with 1782-1787 state tax lists. ([Virginia Military Records — Post-War Bounty Lands](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Virginia_Military_Records#Post-War_Bounty_Lands))
- **Anglican parish registers:** After disestablishment (1786), many parishes dissolved and registers were lost, dispersed, or neglected. Coverage is uneven; some counties have no surviving colonial/Revolutionary-era church registers.
- **County courthouse fires:** A number of Virginia county courthouses burned at various points in the 19th century (and some during the Civil War), destroying deed books, court order books, and will records. Check the Courthouse Disasters page for the specific county you are researching before concluding a record does not exist.

## Research tips
- **Start with pension files.** NARA pension files (RG 15, searchable on Fold3) are the richest source for Revolutionary War military families. A pension application routinely contains the soldier's affidavit naming his wife, children, and county of residence, plus sworn statements from neighbors — essentially a biographical sketch filed decades after the war. ([Virginia Military Records — Revolutionary War](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Virginia_Military_Records#Revolutionary_War))
- **Use tax lists in place of the missing 1790 census.** The 1782-1787 Virginia personal property and land tax lists are available on microfilm and partially online (DGS 005301449 is full-text searchable on FamilySearch). They list heads of household by county and can establish residence during the war years. ([Virginia Military Records — Post-War Bounty Lands](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Virginia_Military_Records#Post-War_Bounty_Lands))
- **Distinguish Continental Line from militia service.** Continental Line records are at NARA; Virginia militia records are at the Library of Virginia. A man might appear in both, or in one but not the other. The FamilySearch collection 1945678 covers both to varying degrees, but verify against the original repositories.
- **Check bounty land warrants for post-war location.** After the Revolution, Virginia veterans could claim land in the Virginia Military District of Ohio. The warrant application and survey record names the veteran and sometimes family members, and the act of claiming land tells you the veteran was alive and where he was living at claim time. FamilySearch DGS 005301447 covers 1779-1800 but is browse-only (0% indexed) — no name search, must browse image by image.
- **Search vestry records for non-combatants.** Women, children, the elderly, and the poor appear in vestry minute books (tithe lists, orphan bindings, poor relief) that are not accessible through military searches. These records name family members not found in any military source.
- **Kentucky and West Virginia records are Virginia records.** For families in what is now Kentucky (before 1792) or West Virginia (before 1863), the records are Virginia county records — search under the Virginia county that existed at the time, not the modern state.
- **County boundary changes are frequent.** Before searching a courthouse, verify which county existed for the specific event date and place. The Library of Virginia's county formation records and published guides to Virginia county boundaries are the authoritative reference.
- **The Virginia Gazette is a primary research tool.** Legal notices, estate advertisements, loyalty matters, and community news were published in the Gazette throughout the war. Partially online through Chronicling America (free) and Newspapers.com (subscription).
- **DAR compiled sources supplement originals.** The DAR has transcribed thousands of Virginia Revolutionary War records; their published volumes and member application files (at the DAR Library, Washington, D.C.) often cite records that have since been lost.

Locality guide written as `loc_001`.

---

Virginia records are extensive for the 1775-1783 period because the colony had maintained county-level courts, Anglican parish registers, and land-grant systems since the 1630s. The two most important warnings: Virginia's 1790 federal census was destroyed in 1814, so the 1782-1787 state personal property and land tax lists are the primary substitute for placing families in the state during and just after the war; and there was no civil vital registration system at all in this period, so births, marriages, and burials appear only in church registers (Anglican/Episcopal vestry books above all) and in county court records. The richest military source is the pension file series at NARA, which routinely names the soldier's wife, children, neighbors, and county of residence. The Library of Virginia in Richmond is the anchor repository for militia records, bounty land warrants, and many county records on microfilm, while individual county courthouses hold the original deed and court order books. FamilySearch has five indexed collections covering church records, land and wills, military records (1775-1783 specifically), tax records, and county court records, plus three digitized volumes including a full-text-searchable tax-list volume and a browse-only bounty-warrant volume. If you want to move from this survey into a concrete research plan for a specific ancestor or family, say the word and the research-plan skill runs next.

Virginia contributed more soldiers to the Continental Army than any other colony; militia records are at the Library of Virginia in Richmond, distinct from federal service records at NARA.

Virginia's extensive county-level record-keeping dates from the 1630s, making it one of the best-documented colonial jurisdictions; most records are held at the county courthouse or the Library of Virginia in Richmond.

Pension files at NARA (Record Group 15) are among the richest sources for Revolutionary War families — they often contain the soldier's own narrative, family relationships, ages, and places of residence decades after the war.
added.guide_markdown:
# Locality Guide: Virginia, United States (1775-1783)

## Jurisdiction overview
- **Formed:** Virginia was one of the original Thirteen Colonies; as a state, it ratified the Constitution in 1788 (standardPlace dateRange: +1788/), but county-level record-keeping dates from the 1630s.
- **County seat / administrative center:** Richmond (state capital from 1780; Williamsburg before that)
- **Parent jurisdiction:** British Crown / Colony of Virginia prior to independence
- **Population during period:** Population figures from the place_population tool returned no data for this query; Wikipedia notes Virginia was the most populous of the original colonies and contributed more troops than any other state.
- **Economy:** Tobacco plantation agriculture in the Tidewater; mixed farming and frontier settlement in the Piedmont and Shenandoah Valley; some maritime trade on the Chesapeake.
- **Ethnic composition:** English colonial majority; significant enslaved African population (roughly 40% of Virginians); Scots-Irish and German settlers in the western counties (Augusta, Rockingham, Shenandoah, etc.); small Welsh and French Huguenot communities.
- **Religious denominations:** Anglican/Episcopal (established church before disestablishment in 1786); Presbyterian (especially in the Valley); Baptist (growing rapidly during the war years); Methodist; Quaker; Lutheran and German Reformed in western counties.
- **Key historical events:** Battle of Yorktown (1781) — the decisive engagement of the war fought on Virginia soil; British coastal raids and the Benedict Arnold raids of 1781; frontier warfare on the western border throughout the period; Virginia's General Assembly met under wartime conditions, creating legislative records and muster rolls.

## Boundary changes
- Virginia's western territory was enormous during this period; Kentucky County was carved from Fincastle County in 1776 and Kentucky became a separate state in 1792. Records for what is now Kentucky before 1792 are Virginia records.
- West Virginia did not exist as a separate state until 1863; all 1775-1783 records for what is now West Virginia are Virginia records held primarily at the Library of Virginia and in county courthouses.
- County boundaries were actively changing during the war years as new counties were formed from western frontiers. Always identify the specific county that existed for the event date, not the modern county.
- If stable within the eastern counties (Tidewater and Piedmont), records are continuous at the county courthouse level.

## Available record types

### Vital records (civil registration)
- **Start date:** Virginia did NOT have statewide civil vital registration during 1775-1783. The FamilySearch Virginia Vital Records wiki page returned only a generic placeholder and did not provide a specific start date; from the wiki_search results and the generic records overview, it is clear that no civil system existed at the state level in this period. Do not assume a civil birth, marriage, or death certificate exists for these years.
- **What exists:** Births, marriages, and burials were recorded in Anglican/Episcopal parish registers (and by other denominations in their own registers) and secondarily in county court order books (especially marriage bonds and returns).
- **Where held:** Library of Virginia (Richmond); individual county courthouses; some on FamilySearch microfilm (collection 1598230: Virginia, Church Records, 1680-1929; collection 1734285: Virginia, Land, Marriage, and Will Records, 1600-1900).
- **Gaps:** Parish registers are uneven; many were lost when the Anglican establishment collapsed after 1786 and churches closed or changed hands. A number of county courthouses have suffered fire losses.
- **Pre-registration alternatives:** Church registers (see below); county court marriage bonds; probate records naming heirs; tax lists.

### Church records
- **Denominations present:** Anglican/Episcopal (parishes covered the entire colony and are the primary vital-record source); Presbyterian; Baptist; Lutheran; German Reformed; Quaker (Friends meetings maintained their own detailed registers).
- **Record types:** Baptisms, marriages, burials, vestry minutes (which include poor relief lists and tithe assessments naming adult males).
- **Where held:** Library of Virginia holds many surviving Anglican vestry books; the Episcopal Diocese of Virginia archives; denominational headquarters for Presbyterian, Baptist, Lutheran, and Quaker records; FamilySearch collection 1598230 (Virginia, Church Records, 1680-1929, approximately 1.2 million records with images).
- **Language:** English throughout.
- **Access level:** Collection 1598230 is indexed + images (name-searchable on FamilySearch, free). Physical originals at the Library of Virginia.

### Census records
- **Federal/national census:** The first federal census (1790) is the nearest decennial to this period, but Virginia's 1790 census was destroyed when the British burned Washington in 1814. There is no surviving 1790 Virginia federal census.
- **State/provincial substitute:** Virginia conducted periodic state enumerations and tax lists. FamilySearch has a digitized volume (DGS 005301449, 87 images, 1782-1799) that is full-text searchable but NOT name-indexed — researchers must use keyword search or browse. These tax lists are the primary substitute for the missing 1790 census and place individuals in specific counties in the 1780s. ([Virginia Military Records — Post-War Bounty Lands](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Virginia_Military_Records#Post-War_Bounty_Lands))
- **Other enumerations:** Vestry tithe lists (Anglican) named male tithables (taxable persons) by household, providing a functional enumeration before civil censuses.
- **Access:** DGS 005301449 is full-text searchable, not name-indexed — browse or keyword only.

### Probate and court records
- **Types:** Wills, estate inventories, guardianship orders, letters of administration, county court order books.
- **Date range:** Continuous from county formation; many Virginia counties have records from the 1630s-1700s onward through the Revolution.
- **Where held:** Original records at individual county courthouses; Library of Virginia holds many microfilm copies and some originals. FamilySearch collection 2134567 (Virginia, County Court Records, 1650-1920) and collection 1734285 (Virginia, Land, Marriage, and Will Records, 1600-1900).
- **Access level:** FamilySearch collection 1734285 has approximately 2.6 million records, indexed + images. FamilySearch also has a partially-indexed Augusta County court order book volume (DGS 005301448, 158 images, 1775-1795, 61% name-indexed) — useful for that county during the war years.
- **Note:** Probate files filed during or just after the war (1783-1800) often name surviving family members, state ages, and document who received a soldier's estate — critical for establishing family relationships when no direct vital record survives.

### Land records
- **Survey system:** Metes and bounds (Virginia is a state-land state, not a federal-land state).
- **Land-distribution jurisdiction:** The colonial Governor's Council issued grants and patents; after independence, the Commonwealth of Virginia continued issuing patents. The Virginia State Land Office holds patent records. For the Virginia Military District of Ohio (bounty lands for veterans), the Library of Virginia holds warrant and survey records.
- **Types:** Deeds, land grants/patents, bounty land warrants (post-Revolution), mortgages, deed of trust.
- **Date range:** Colonial land patents from the early 1600s; county deed books continuous from county formation.
- **Where held:** County courthouses (deed books); Library of Virginia (patent records, bounty land warrants); FamilySearch collection 1734285 (Virginia, Land, Marriage, and Will Records, 1600-1900). FamilySearch also has a browse-only digitized volume of Revolutionary War land bounty warrants 1779-1800 (DGS 005301447, 341 images, 0% name-indexed) — must be browsed image by image with no name search.
- **Access level for DGS 005301447:** Browse-only images; 0% indexed and not full-text searchable.

### Military records
- **Relevant conflicts:** American Revolutionary War (1775-1783), including Virginia Continental Line service, Virginia State Navy service, Virginia militia service, and frontier ranger/ranger service on the western border.
- **Record types and repositories:**
  - **Continental Line service records and muster rolls:** National Archives and Records Administration (NARA), Record Group 93. Accessible online through Fold3 (subscription). ([Virginia Military Records — Revolutionary War](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Virginia_Military_Records#Revolutionary_War))
  - **Virginia militia records:** Library of Virginia, Richmond. Partially microfilmed by FamilySearch; collection 1945678 (Virginia, Military Records, 1775-1783) covers this period with approximately 346,000 records and images.
  - **Pension and bounty-land warrant application files:** NARA, Record Group 15. These are the single richest source for Revolutionary War families — pension files frequently contain the soldier's narrative affidavit, names and ages of spouse and children, and places of residence. Accessible on Fold3 and Ancestry (subscription); partially indexed on FamilySearch.
  - **Virginia State Navy records:** Published; check the Library of Virginia.
  - **Bounty land warrants (Virginia Military District of Ohio):** Library of Virginia and FamilySearch DGS 005301447 (browse-only).
- **Access level for collection 1945678:** Indexed + images on FamilySearch (free).
- **Note on Loyalists:** Virginia also generated records for those who refused to take the oath of allegiance, had their property confiscated, or fled — sequestration commissioners' records and court records of forfeited estates are at the Library of Virginia.

### Cemetery records
- **Major cemeteries:** Church graveyards (Anglican/Episcopal, Presbyterian, Baptist, Quaker) are the primary burial sites for this period; private family cemeteries on plantations.
- **Online coverage:** Find A Grave (https://www.findagrave.com/) has extensive Virginia coverage, including many 18th-century markers; BillionGraves offers additional coverage. However, many 18th-century markers have weathered beyond legibility or were never marked.
- **Physical records:** Anglican vestry burial registers (where they survive) at the Library of Virginia; some church sexton records.
- **Warning:** Many graves from this period have no surviving physical marker or inscription. Find A Grave entries for this era are frequently based on family records or secondary sources, not direct transcription of a stone.

### Newspaper records
- **Local papers:** The Virginia Gazette (Williamsburg) published throughout the colonial and Revolutionary period — one of the most important colonial newspapers for the era. Several competing versions existed by different publishers.
- **Where held:** Colonial Williamsburg Foundation holds original copies; the Library of Virginia has microfilm; some issues are digitized through Chronicling America (https://chroniclingamerica.loc.gov/) and Newspapers.com (https://www.newspapers.com/, subscription).
- **Content value:** Obituaries, marriage notices, legal notices (estate advertisements, runaway slave notices, land sales), war news, and lists of deserters or loyalty concerns.

### Immigration/emigration records
- **Relevant ports:** Ports of entry for Virginia included Hampton Roads, Norfolk, and the James River ports (Richmond, Hopeick). Scotch-Irish and German settlers entering from Pennsylvania traveled the Great Wagon Road south through the Shenandoah Valley.
- **Record types:** For the 1775-1783 period specifically, immigration from Britain was largely interrupted; the relevant immigration records are pre-war colonial passenger lists and post-war arrivals. Naturalization as a concept applied post-independence; county court oath records document who swore loyalty and who was examined as a suspected Loyalist.
- **Content note:** Passenger lists (arrival manifests) record all persons aboard, including infants and children traveling with parents. When researching families who arrived before the Revolution, examine the full manifest for all family members.
- **Access:** NARA and online through Ancestry (subscription).

### Tax records
- **Types:** Personal property tax (tithe lists before independence; state personal property tax from 1782 onward); land tax (from 1782).
- **Date range:** State personal property and land tax lists begin in 1782 and are continuous through the 19th century — these are the direct substitute for the missing 1790 Virginia census.
- **Where held:** Library of Virginia; FamilySearch DGS 005301449 (87 images, 1782-1799, full-text searchable but NOT name-indexed).
- **Substitute value:** Extremely high — the 1782-1787 tax lists are effectively the only statewide enumeration of Virginia households for the Revolutionary era. ([Virginia Military Records — Post-War Bounty Lands](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Virginia_Military_Records#Post-War_Bounty_Lands))

### Other record types
- **Loyalty oaths and Loyalist/Tory records:** Virginia county courts administered oaths of allegiance; refusals and examinations are in court order books. Sequestration commissioners' records document Loyalist property seizures — at the Library of Virginia.
- **Vestry (poor relief) records:** Anglican vestry minutes document binding out of orphans, support for widows and dependent children, and tithe assessments — valuable for family relationships and economic status during wartime.
- **Published local and county histories:** Many 19th- and early-20th-century Virginia county histories reprint transcriptions of records since lost and carry biographical sketches of founding families. The Library of Virginia's catalog is the best finding aid for these.
- **DAR records:** The Daughters of the American Revolution has compiled and published extensive transcription projects for Virginia Revolutionary War records; the DAR Library in Washington, D.C. holds membership application files that cite original sources.

## Repository guide

### Online repositories
| Repository | Collections for this place | Access |
|---|---|---|
| FamilySearch | Virginia, Military Records, 1775-1783 (collection 1945678, ~346K records); Virginia, Land, Marriage, and Will Records, 1600-1900 (collection 1734285, ~2.6M records); Virginia, Church Records, 1680-1929 (collection 1598230, ~1.2M records); Virginia, Tax Records, 1782-1850 (collection 1456723, ~457K records); Virginia, County Court Records, 1650-1920 (collection 2134567, ~1.8M records); plus 3 digitized volumes (bounty warrants, Augusta court orders, tax lists) | Free |
| Fold3 | NARA Revolutionary War service records (RG 93); pension files (RG 15) | Subscription |
| Ancestry | U.S. Federal Census (1790 Virginia destroyed; 1800+ available); pension files; passenger lists | Subscription |
| Find A Grave | Cemetery / grave marker records | Free |
| Newspapers.com | Historical Virginia newspapers including Virginia Gazette | Subscription |
| NARA (archives.gov) | Finding aids for RG 93 (service records), RG 15 (pensions) | Free to search; some records free online |
| Chronicling America | Some Virginia Gazette issues digitized | Free |

**Coverage of this survey:** The volume_search tool returned 3 digitized volumes matching Virginia in this period (all 3 are detailed above); the result set was complete (no nextPageToken and totalResults = 3). The collections_search returned 5 indexed collections. This represents what FamilySearch has specifically surfaced at the state level; individual county-level volumes may exist under county-specific standardPlace queries.

### Physical repositories
| Repository | Holdings | Access method |
|---|---|---|
| Library of Virginia (Richmond) | Militia records; land patent records; bounty land warrants; tax lists; county court records on microfilm; sequestration/Loyalist records; published local histories | In-person; some records online via lva.virginia.gov |
| NARA (Washington, D.C. / College Park, MD) | Continental Army service records (RG 93); pension files (RG 15); federal census originals (1800+) | In-person; most Revolutionary War records also on Fold3/Ancestry |
| Individual County Courthouses | Original deed books, court order books, will books; continuous from county formation | In-person or mail request; check county circuit court clerk |
| Episcopal Diocese of Virginia Archives | Surviving Anglican/Episcopal parish registers; vestry minutes | In-person / written inquiry |
| DAR Library (Washington, D.C.) | Compiled transcriptions; member application files citing original records | In-person; some finding aids online |
| Colonial Williamsburg Foundation | Virginia Gazette originals and microfilm | In-person / research request |

## Records NOT online
- Original county deed books and court order books at most county courthouses (indexed collection 2134567 covers only a fraction).
- Anglican vestry minutes and poor relief records not yet microfilmed or digitized.
- Sequestration commissioners' records (Loyalist property seizures) — at Library of Virginia, not online.
- Most Virginia State Navy records.
- Private family cemetery records.
- Many DAR compiled transcriptions (available in print at DAR Library only).

## Known record losses
- **Virginia's 1790 federal census:** Destroyed when the British burned Washington in 1814. Substitute with 1782-1787 state tax lists. ([Virginia Military Records — Post-War Bounty Lands](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Virginia_Military_Records#Post-War_Bounty_Lands))
- **Anglican parish registers:** After disestablishment (1786), many parishes dissolved and registers were lost, dispersed, or neglected. Coverage is uneven; some counties have no surviving colonial/Revolutionary-era church registers.
- **County courthouse fires:** A number of Virginia county courthouses burned at various points in the 19th century (and some during the Civil War), destroying deed books, court order books, and will records. Check the Courthouse Disasters page for the specific county you are researching before concluding a record does not exist.

## Research tips
- **Start with pension files.** NARA pension files (RG 15, searchable on Fold3) are the richest source for Revolutionary War military families. A pension application routinely contains the soldier's affidavit naming his wife, children, and county of residence, plus sworn statements from neighbors — essentially a biographical sketch filed decades after the war. ([Virginia Military Records — Revolutionary War](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Virginia_Military_Records#Revolutionary_War))
- **Use tax lists in place of the missing 1790 census.** The 1782-1787 Virginia personal property and land tax lists are available on microfilm and partially online (DGS 005301449 is full-text searchable on FamilySearch). They list heads of household by county and can establish residence during the war years. ([Virginia Military Records — Post-War Bounty Lands](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Virginia_Military_Records#Post-War_Bounty_Lands))
- **Distinguish Continental Line from militia service.** Continental Line records are at NARA; Virginia militia records are at the Library of Virginia. A man might appear in both, or in one but not the other. The FamilySearch collection 1945678 covers both to varying degrees, but verify against the original repositories.
- **Check bounty land warrants for post-war location.** After the Revolution, Virginia veterans could claim land in the Virginia Military District of Ohio. The warrant application and survey record names the veteran and sometimes family members, and the act of claiming land tells you the veteran was alive and where he was living at claim time. FamilySearch DGS 005301447 covers 1779-1800 but is browse-only (0% indexed) — no name search, must browse image by image.
- **Search vestry records for non-combatants.** Women, children, the elderly, and the poor appear in vestry minute books (tithe lists, orphan bindings, poor relief) that are not accessible through military searches. These records name family members not found in any military source.
- **Kentucky and West Virginia records are Virginia records.** For families in what is now Kentucky (before 1792) or West Virginia (before 1863), the records are Virginia county records — search under the Virginia county that existed at the time, not the modern state.
- **County boundary changes are frequent.** Before searching a courthouse, verify which county existed for the specific event date and place. The Library of Virginia's county formation records and published guides to Virginia county boundaries are the authoritative reference.
- **The Virginia Gazette is a primary research tool.** Legal notices, estate advertisements, loyalty matters, and community news were published in the Gazette throughout the war. Partially online through Chronicling America (free) and Newspapers.com (subscription).
- **DAR compiled sources supplement originals.** The DAR has transcribed thousands of Virginia Revolutionary War records; their published volumes and member application files (at the DAR Library, Washington, D.C.) often cite records that have since been lost.

**New Orleans, Early 1800s — Record Survival and Substitutes**

New Orleans sits at the center of one of the most dramatic record-survival stories in American genealogy. Here's the picture:

**What was lost**
Two catastrophic fires (1788 and 1794) destroyed much of colonial New Orleans and many of its earliest records. Yellow fever epidemics and periodic flooding caused further losses later.

**What survived — and where to find it**

- **St. Louis Cathedral sacramental registers** (baptisms, marriages, burials from 1731, with gaps) came through the fires. Four indexed FamilySearch collections cover church records, parish marriages, probate ("successions"), and a statewide death index for this period.

- **New Orleans Notarial Archives Research Center** holds over 30 million pages of notarial acts dating to 1734. In Louisiana's civil-law system, nearly every major life event — property transfers, wills, birth/death declarations, manumissions of enslaved persons, marriage contracts — had to pass through a notary. This makes notarial acts the single most important *substitute* for the vital records that simply didn't exist; Louisiana didn't require statewide civil registration until 1914.

- **Federal census records** survived local fires entirely because they were held in Washington.

- **Tax assessment rolls** at the Louisiana State Archives and City Archives fill the gaps between censuses.

- One browse-only digitized volume of Orleans Parish notarial acts (1803–1820) is on FamilySearch but is unindexed — you'd need to scroll image by image with no name search.

**Key caveats**
- Louisiana uses civil-law terminology that differs from every other U.S. state.
- Many pre-1820 records are in French or Spanish.

The guide has been saved to the project. If you'd like a research plan built around these collections, that would be the natural next step.

entry.guide_markdown:
# Locality Guide: New Orleans, Orleans Parish, Louisiana (1800-1860)

## Jurisdiction overview
- **Formed:** New Orleans founded 1718 by the French; Orleans Parish established under Spanish and then U.S. administration; Louisiana became a U.S. state in 1812
- **County seat / administrative center:** New Orleans (city and parish are coterminous)
- **Parent jurisdiction:** Orleans Territory (1803-1812), then State of Louisiana (1812-present)
- **Population during period:** Population data was not returned by place_population for this standardPlace. Wikipedia notes New Orleans was the largest city in the South by mid-century, driven by the cotton and sugar trade.
- **Economy:** Dominant industries were river commerce, cotton and sugar trading, maritime shipping, and enslaved-labor plantation economy. The port of New Orleans was among the busiest in North America.
- **Ethnic composition:** French Creoles, Spanish Creoles, Anglo-Americans (after 1803), free people of color (gens de couleur libres), enslaved Africans and African Americans, German and Irish immigrants (arriving in large numbers from the 1830s-1850s), and smaller communities of Italians and other Europeans.
- **Religious denominations:** Roman Catholic (dominant, via St. Louis Cathedral), Protestant denominations (Episcopal, Presbyterian, Methodist, Baptist), Jewish congregations.
- **Key historical events:** Louisiana Purchase (1803); Louisiana statehood (1812); Battle of New Orleans (1815); repeated yellow fever epidemics (especially 1832, 1853); major floods and hurricanes throughout the period.

## Boundary changes
- New Orleans was French (1718-1763), then Spanish (1763-1800), briefly French again, then became U.S. territory via the Louisiana Purchase on 30 April 1803.
- Before 1803, records were created by French and Spanish colonial authorities. After 1803, U.S. territorial and state authority applied.
- Orleans Parish boundaries were established under the Louisiana territorial period. The city and parish remained coterminous through the early 1800s.
- Records from the pre-1803 period may require reading French or Spanish.

## Known record losses (disasters)

This is the central concern for early New Orleans research. The FamilySearch Wiki page for New Orleans Genealogy (https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/New_Orleans_Genealogy#Records_Surviving_Disasters) states the following:

**Fires of 1788 and 1794:** Two catastrophic fires destroyed most of the French Quarter and many colonial records. These are the most significant losses for researchers of the pre-1800 period.

**What survived despite the fires:**
- Sacramental registers of St. Louis Cathedral: baptisms, marriages, and burials from 1731, though with gaps created by the fires and subsequent disasters.
- Notarial records: The New Orleans Notarial Archives Research Center holds over 30 million pages of notarial acts dating back to 1734. Notarial acts documented property sales, contracts, manumissions, wills, and many other legal transactions that effectively substitute for missing vital and court records.
- Records of the Cabildo (Spanish colonial governing body): survive for the Spanish period.

**Subsequent damage:** Wikipedia notes that repeated yellow fever epidemics, hurricanes, and flooding further damaged archival holdings throughout the 19th century. No specific record sets destroyed by post-1800 events were named in the tool results returned for this survey — verify survival of any specific record set directly with the Louisiana State Archives or the New Orleans Notarial Archives before assuming it exists.

**Substitute sources for destroyed records:**
- Notarial acts (property, contracts, manumissions, wills) — held at the New Orleans Notarial Archives Research Center
- Federal census records (1810, 1820, 1830, 1840, 1850, 1860) — survived independently of local fires
- Succession (probate) records at the Orleans Parish Civil District Court
- Newspaper notices (births, marriages, deaths, estate notices)
- U.S. territorial and early state government records at the Louisiana State Archives, Baton Rouge

## Available record types

### Vital records (civil registration)
- **Start date:** The FamilySearch Wiki page for Louisiana Vital Records returned only a generic fallback page and could not confirm a specific statewide start date. Louisiana is known not to have had statewide civil registration until 1914. For the early 1800s, no statewide civil birth, marriage, or death registration system existed.
- **What exists for 1800-1860:** Church sacramental registers (especially St. Louis Cathedral) are the primary vital record source. Some local civil marriage registration existed in Orleans Parish by the 1840s-1850s — verify dates with the Louisiana State Archives.
- **Where held:** Archdiocese of New Orleans Archives for sacramental registers; Orleans Parish Civil District Court for civil marriages; Louisiana State Archives (Baton Rouge) for territorial and early state records.
- **Gaps:** Pre-1800 records have significant gaps from the 1788 and 1794 fires. Post-1800 gaps occur from yellow fever epidemics and periodic flooding.
- **Pre-registration alternatives:** Notarial acts (especially act-of-birth and act-of-death declarations before a notary), newspaper notices, and federal census records.

### Church records
- **Denominations present:** Roman Catholic (dominant; St. Louis Cathedral served the entire city and surrounding territory), Protestant (Episcopal, Methodist, Presbyterian, Baptist), Jewish congregations from the 1820s onward.
- **Record types:** Baptisms, marriages, burials, confirmations. The FamilySearch collection "Louisiana, Church Records, 1718-1925" (collection ID 1612905) covers this period and is indexed with images on FamilySearch.
- **Where held:** Archdiocese of New Orleans Archives holds original sacramental registers. FamilySearch has microfilmed and digitized much of this material in collection 1612905.
- **Language:** Records from the French and Spanish periods are in French or Spanish. Records from after 1803 are increasingly in English but may still appear in French for Catholic registers into the 1840s.
- **Access level:** Indexed + images (FamilySearch collection 1612905, approximately 987,000 records and 493,000 images).

### Census records
- **Federal census:** 1810, 1820, 1830, 1840, 1850 (with full names), 1860 for New Orleans.
- **State/territorial census:** Louisiana territorial and state censuses exist for some years; the FamilySearch Wiki page for Louisiana Census returned only a generic fallback and could not confirm specific state census years. Consult the Louisiana State Archives directly.
- **Other enumerations:** Spanish colonial censuses (padrones) survive for the pre-1803 period.
- **Access:** Federal censuses are indexed and available on FamilySearch and Ancestry. Pre-1803 Spanish padrones are in physical or microfilm format.

### Probate and court records
- **Types:** In Louisiana's civil-law system, the equivalent of probate is called a "succession." Tutorships (guardianship) and interdictions (incompetency proceedings) are separate record types. Succession records document estate distribution, and often name heirs, debts, and property.
- **Date range:** FamilySearch collection "Louisiana, Probate Records, 1756-1984" (collection ID 2078341) covers this period with approximately 456,000 records and 228,000 images.
- **Where held:** Orleans Parish Civil District Court (originals); FamilySearch (digitized, indexed collection 2078341); Louisiana State Archives (Baton Rouge) for territorial records.
- **Access level:** Indexed + images (FamilySearch collection 2078341).
- **Note:** Because the civil-law succession process required formal court filings even for small estates, succession records are especially rich and often name all heirs, including children and collateral relatives.

### Land records
- **Survey system:** French long-lot system (arpents), not the rectangular U.S. survey system. Land measured in arpents fronting the river with long strips running back. This system persists on modern maps.
- **Land-distribution jurisdiction:** Under French and Spanish rule, colonial land grants were made by the colonial government. After 1803, the U.S. General Land Office confirmed or denied existing grants. The FamilySearch Wiki page for Louisiana Land and Property returned only a generic fallback — consult the BLM General Land Office website (glorecords.blm.gov) for post-1803 federal land patents, and the Louisiana State Land Office for confirmed Spanish and French grants.
- **Types:** Colonial grants, Spanish land grants, U.S. confirmations of prior grants, notarial acts of sale (the primary record of private land transfer), mortgage acts, and donation acts.
- **Date range:** Notarial acts from 1734 survive at the New Orleans Notarial Archives Research Center.
- **Where held:** New Orleans Notarial Archives Research Center (notarial acts of sale and mortgage); Orleans Parish Conveyance Office (deed books from U.S. period); BLM GLO website (federal land patents); Louisiana State Archives (territorial land records).
- **Access level:** Notarial acts are partially digitized; the Notarial Archives Research Center has an online index. Some deeds are in physical repositories only.

### Military records
- **Relevant conflicts:** Battle of New Orleans (1815, War of 1812); Louisiana militia service; Civil War (1861-1865, just outside the period but relevant for families).
- **Record types:** Service records (NARA), pension files (NARA), War of 1812 bounty land warrants, militia muster rolls.
- **Where held:** National Archives (NARA) for federal service and pension records; Louisiana State Archives for state militia records; Fold3 (online, subscription) for digitized military records.

### Cemetery records
- **Major cemeteries:** St. Louis Cemetery No. 1 (1789, oldest extant), St. Louis Cemetery No. 2 (1823), St. Louis Cemetery No. 3 (1854), Metairie Cemetery, Lafayette Cemetery (1833, Garden District). New Orleans' above-ground burial tradition means many tombs survive physically even where paper records do not.
- **Online coverage:** FindAGrave (https://www.findagrave.com) covers many New Orleans cemeteries. Save Our Cemeteries (a local nonprofit) has conducted transcription projects.
- **Physical records:** Sexton records and burial registers at the Archdiocese of New Orleans Archives and at individual cemetery offices.

### Newspaper records
- **Local papers:** The Louisiana Gazette (founded 1804), the New Orleans Picayune (founded 1837), L'Abeille de la Nouvelle-Orléans (bilingual French-English, 1827-1923), and others.
- **Where held:** Newspapers.com (online, subscription, https://www.newspapers.com/); the Louisiana State University Libraries hold microfilm of many titles; the Historic New Orleans Collection.
- **Content value:** Obituaries, marriage notices, death notices (especially important given the yellow fever epidemics), sheriff's sales, estate notices, and ship arrivals (useful for immigration research).

### Immigration and emigration records
- **Relevant ports:** New Orleans was one of the largest ports of entry in the United States; enormous numbers of German and Irish immigrants arrived here in the 1830s-1850s.
- **Record types:** Passenger lists (NARA and online); naturalization records filed in Orleans Parish courts; passport applications.
- **Where held:** NARA (passenger lists and naturalizations); FamilySearch and Ancestry (indexed passenger lists); Orleans Parish Civil District Court (pre-1906 naturalization records).
- **Content note:** Passenger lists record every person aboard, including infants and young children. When researching an immigrant family, examine the full manifest for all family members, not just the head of household.
- **Access level:** Indexed + images for most post-1820 passenger lists on FamilySearch and Ancestry.

### Tax records
- **Types:** Orleans Parish property tax (assessment rolls), poll tax.
- **Date range:** Tax assessment rolls survive from the territorial period.
- **Where held:** Louisiana State Archives (Baton Rouge); the City Archives at the New Orleans Public Library.
- **Substitute value:** Tax rolls are especially valuable for the years 1800-1840 before the federal census included full names (pre-1850 censuses name only the head of household).

### Notarial records (unique to Louisiana)
- **Significance:** Louisiana's civil-law system required nearly all significant legal acts — property sales, wills, contracts, manumissions of enslaved persons, marriage contracts, birth and death declarations — to be recorded by a notary. This makes notarial acts one of the most important record classes for New Orleans research, functioning as a substitute for vital records, land records, and court records simultaneously.
- **Date range:** From 1734, with gaps.
- **Where held:** New Orleans Notarial Archives Research Center (30+ million pages). Partially indexed online.
- **Access:** In-person research or mail inquiries to the Notarial Archives Research Center. Some records partially digitized.

### Enslavement records
- **Significance:** New Orleans was the largest domestic slave market in the United States. Records of enslaved persons appear in notarial acts of sale, succession inventories, manumission acts, newspaper advertisements, and plantation records.
- **Where held:** New Orleans Notarial Archives Research Center; Louisiana State Archives; the Historic New Orleans Collection; Tulane University Special Collections.
- **Online resources:** Enslaved.org and Freedom on the Move (freedom-suit and runaway advertisements) are specialized online databases.

## Repository guide

### Online repositories
| Repository | Collections for this place | Access |
|---|---|---|
| FamilySearch | Louisiana Church Records 1718-1925 (collection 1612905, ~987K records); Louisiana Parish Marriages 1837-1957 (collection 1798054, ~567K records); Louisiana Probate Records 1756-1984 (collection 2078341, ~456K records); Louisiana Statewide Death Index 1819-1964 (collection 1543892, ~2.3M records, index only) | Free |
| Ancestry | U.S. Federal Census Collection (all years); passenger lists; miscellaneous Louisiana records | Subscription |
| Fold3 | Military records (War of 1812, Civil War) | Subscription |
| Newspapers.com | Historical New Orleans newspapers | Subscription |
| FindAGrave | Cemetery records | Free |
| NARA (archives.gov) | Passenger lists, naturalization records, federal military records | Free (some digitized, some in-person) |
| BLM GLO (glorecords.blm.gov) | Federal land patents post-1803 | Free |
| Enslaved.org / Freedom on the Move | Enslavement-related records | Free |

**Coverage of this survey:** The volume_search returned 1 digitized volume (image group 004990115, Orleans Parish notarial acts 1803-1820, 167 images, browse-only). The collections_search returned 4 Louisiana-level indexed collections. These do not represent the complete universe of digitized New Orleans material — additional volumes may exist outside this time-filtered search, and physical repositories hold substantially more.

### Physical repositories
| Repository | Holdings | Access method |
|---|---|---|
| New Orleans Notarial Archives Research Center | 30+ million pages of notarial acts from 1734 | In-person or mail inquiry |
| Orleans Parish Civil District Court | Succession records, naturalization records, civil court files | In-person |
| Orleans Parish Conveyance Office | Deed books (U.S. period) | In-person |
| Archdiocese of New Orleans Archives | Original sacramental registers, St. Louis Cathedral and other parishes | In-person or written request |
| Louisiana State Archives, Baton Rouge | Territorial and state government records, tax rolls, militia records | In-person or online catalog |
| City Archives, New Orleans Public Library | Municipal records, assessment rolls, city council minutes | In-person |
| Historic New Orleans Collection | Manuscripts, newspapers, maps, enslaved-person records | In-person (appointment recommended) |
| Tulane University Special Collections | Plantation records, family papers, business records | In-person |

## Records NOT online
- Original sacramental registers of St. Louis Cathedral (digitized in FamilySearch collection 1612905, but the Archdiocese holds originals with potentially more detail)
- Most Orleans Parish tax assessment rolls
- City council minutes and municipal administrative records
- Many succession case files beyond the digitized index entries
- Records of the Cabildo (Spanish colonial government) — held at the Louisiana State Archives
- Spanish and French colonial land grants — partially online via Louisiana State Archives, but many physical only
- Most pre-1803 notarial acts not captured in online indexes
- Records of individual Protestant and Jewish congregations from this period

## Known record losses
- **Fire of 1788:** Destroyed most of French Quarter and many colonial-era records.
- **Fire of 1794:** Second major fire, further damage to the built environment and archives.
- **Yellow fever epidemics (especially 1832, 1853):** Disrupted record-keeping; mortality was so high that some death records from epidemic years are incomplete.
- **Periodic flooding and hurricanes:** Ongoing damage to records throughout the 19th century.
- **Substitute sources:** Notarial acts at the New Orleans Notarial Archives Research Center; St. Louis Cathedral sacramental registers (survived with gaps); federal census records (held independently in Washington, D.C., surviving the local fires); succession (probate) records; newspaper notices.

## Research tips
- **Use notarial acts as your first stop, not a last resort.** Because civil vital registration did not exist in early Louisiana, notarial acts are the primary record of births, marriages, deaths, property transfers, and manumissions. The New Orleans Notarial Archives Research Center holds over 30 million pages from 1734. This point is drawn from the FamilySearch Wiki search result: https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/New_Orleans_Genealogy#Records_Surviving_Disasters
- **Louisiana uses civil law, not common law.** Terminology differs from every other U.S. state: succession (not probate), tutorship (not guardianship), interdiction (not incompetency), act of sale (not deed). Search for these Louisiana-specific terms, not their common-law equivalents.
- **Check St. Louis Cathedral records first for Catholics.** Sacramental registers from 1731 survive with gaps and are partially indexed in FamilySearch collection 1612905. Even Protestant and Jewish residents sometimes appear in Catholic registers during epidemics.
- **Read French and Spanish.** Records before approximately 1820-1830 are often in French; records from the Spanish period (1763-1800) are in Spanish. Working with an original-language reader or transcription service is essential for this period.
- **Succession records name all heirs.** Because Louisiana's civil-law succession process required formal court filings, succession records are unusually complete and often name all children, including daughters who would disappear under married names in common-law states.
- **Search federal census records to bridge gaps.** The 1810, 1820, 1830, and 1840 censuses were held and microfilmed in Washington, D.C. They survived the New Orleans fires entirely. They name only heads of household before 1850 but place families in place and time.
- **Tax assessment rolls substitute for missing years.** Property tax rolls survive from the territorial period at the Louisiana State Archives and the City Archives at the New Orleans Public Library and can place an ancestor in a specific ward between censuses.
- **The Louisiana Statewide Death Index 1819-1964 (FamilySearch collection 1543892) is index-only** — no images. Use it to identify a death date and then locate the original death certificate or sacramental burial record.
- **Adjoining parishes:** Orleans Parish borders Jefferson Parish (west and east bank), St. Bernard Parish (downriver), and St. Tammany Parish (across Lake Pontchartrain). Families near parish boundaries may have generated records on both sides — the wiki_place_page tool did not return the Neighboring Counties table for New Orleans, so consult the FamilySearch Wiki directly for the full list. Jefferson Parish held its own notarial and succession records independently from Orleans.
- **The FamilySearch Wiki pages for Louisiana (all four sections: home, getting_started, online_records, research_tips) returned only a generic fallback page in this survey run** — their specific content could not be verified. Consult https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Louisiana_Genealogy directly for the full Louisiana research strategy guide.
