entry.guide_markdown:
# Locality Guide: Pennsylvania, United States — Quaker Communities (1750–1800)

## Jurisdiction overview
- **Formed:** 1681 (charter granted to William Penn); achieved statehood 1787
- **Administrative center:** Philadelphia (colonial capital and seat of the Philadelphia Yearly Meeting)
- **Parent jurisdiction (colonial period):** British Crown colony
- **Population during period:** Pennsylvania was one of the most populous colonies/early states; exact figures for 1750–1800 were not returned by the population tool
- **Economy:** Farming (especially in Chester, Bucks, and Lancaster counties), trade, commerce (Philadelphia), iron manufacturing
- **Ethnic composition:** English Quakers (founding settlers), German immigrants, Scots-Irish, Welsh; significant Welsh Quaker communities in Chester County
- **Religious denominations relevant to this period:** Society of Friends (Quakers), German Reformed, Lutheran, Anglican/Episcopal, Presbyterian, Mennonite, Amish
- **Key historical events:** French and Indian War (1754–1763); American Revolution (1775–1783) — Quakers faced particular pressure over pacifism and were sometimes disowned for taking sides; Constitutional Convention (Philadelphia, 1787)

## Boundary changes
- Pennsylvania's external boundaries were largely stable in this period, though the Mason-Dixon Line survey (completed 1767) settled the Maryland border.
- Counties were actively subdivided: new counties created from older ones throughout the late 1700s (e.g., York from Lancaster in 1749, Bedford from Cumberland in 1771, Westmoreland from Bedford in 1773, Washington from Westmoreland in 1781). A family's records may be under the parent county if the county of residence was formed after the event date.
- Quaker records are organized by meeting — not by county — so county boundary changes do not directly disrupt the record series, but they do affect civil records (probate, land, tax) for the same families.

## Available record types

### Vital records (civil registration)
- **Start date:** Pennsylvania did not mandate statewide civil registration until 1906. There was no county-level civil vital registration requirement during the late 1700s.
- **What exists for 1750–1800:** No civil birth, marriage, or death records for this period in any governmental sense. Quaker meeting registers and church registers of other denominations are the primary substitute.
- **Pre-registration alternatives:** Quaker birth, marriage, and burial registers (see Church records below); Pennsylvania Compiled Marriages, 1700–1900 (FamilySearch collection 1502909, 198,765 records, no images); Pennsylvania Civil Marriages, 1677–1950 (FamilySearch collection 1571957, 312,045 records)

### Church records — Quaker meetings (primary focus)
- **Denominations and structure:** The Society of Friends operated a three-tier structure: monthly meetings (local, held the records), quarterly meetings (regional), and the Philadelphia Yearly Meeting (the governing body for nearly all Pennsylvania Friends). Welsh Tract Monthly Meeting (Chester/Delaware County), Abington Monthly Meeting (Montgomery County), Burlington (New Jersey, but closely linked to Chester County Friends), and others served this period.
- **Record types created at the monthly meeting level:**
  - Birth registrations (parents recorded the birth; not a baptism — Friends did not baptize)
  - Marriage certificates (signed by all attendees present — typically 30–100 signatories; the most detailed marriage record type for any denomination in this era)
  - Burial registrations
  - Minutes recording disciplinary proceedings and disownments (naming the individual and often the offense — marrying outside the meeting was the most common cause)
  - Certificates of removal (when a family moved from one monthly meeting to another, a removal certificate was issued naming the family members and the destination meeting)
  - Meeting minute books recording business conducted: poor relief, oversight of members, appointments
- **Primary published abstract:** William Wade Hinshaw, *Encyclopedia of American Quaker Genealogy*, 6 volumes. Volume 2 covers Pennsylvania. This abstracts the minute books of many monthly meetings and is the fastest first stop before working original records. It is available at major genealogical libraries and is partially available on Ancestry. (Source: wiki_search result, https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Pennsylvania_Church_Records#Published_Quaker_Abstracts)
- **Where originals are held:**
  - **Friends Historical Library, Swarthmore College** (Swarthmore, PA): the largest repository of American Quaker records, holding original minute books and registers for many Pennsylvania monthly meetings (confirmed by wiki_search result and Wikipedia). Access: in-person and by correspondence; some records microfilmed.
  - **Quaker and Special Collections, Haverford College** (Haverford, PA): second major repository; holds records for meetings not at Swarthmore (confirmed by Wikipedia extract).
  - **FamilySearch microfilm:** FamilySearch has microfilmed many monthly meeting minutes and registers. Volume 001188322 (Philadelphia Yearly Meeting Minutes, 1750–1800, 145 images) is digitized and browsable on FamilySearch but is 0% name-indexed and not full-text searchable — it must be browsed image by image with no search capability. Additional microfilm may be ordered through FamilySearch or consulted at the Family History Library in Salt Lake City.
- **Language:** English throughout
- **Critical quirk — Quaker calendar:** Records before the British calendar reform of 1752 used a calendar in which March was the First Month. After September 1752, January became the First Month. Always verify the calendar convention in use for any individual record, as this affects date interpretation.

### Census records
- **Federal census:** The first federal census was taken in 1790 — the only one within this period. It listed the head of household by name and enumerated other household members by age and sex category only (no individual names for non-heads). This is valuable for placing a Quaker family geographically in 1790.
- **Pre-1790 enumerations:** No federal census. Pennsylvania did not conduct a formal state census in this period. Tax lists (see below) serve as the primary substitute population record.
- **Access to 1790 census:** Indexed and imaged on FamilySearch and Ancestry.

### Probate and court records
- **Types:** Wills, administrations, inventories, guardianships — held at the county level from formation of each county.
- **FamilySearch collection:** Pennsylvania, Probate Records, 1683–1994 (collection 1999196): 3,200,560 images, 0 indexed records — browse-only. This covers the late 1700s period and is digitized, but requires browsing by county and date range. This is a significant resource for Quaker families who left wills.
- **Access:** Browse on FamilySearch (https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1999196); originals held at county orphans' courts and the Pennsylvania State Archives.
- **Note:** Quaker wills frequently name meeting affiliation, which can confirm a family's meeting membership.

### Land records
- **Survey system:** Metes and bounds (Pennsylvania is a state-land state; the Commonwealth granted land, not the federal government)
- **Land-distribution jurisdiction:** The Pennsylvania Land Office (colonial Proprietors, then the Commonwealth) granted warrants and patents. The Pennsylvania State Archives holds warrant registers and survey books.
- **Types:** Warrants, surveys, patents, deeds (recorded at county courthouse), tax assessment lists
- **Access:** Pennsylvania State Archives (Harrisburg) holds original land records. Some are digitized; deed books are at county courthouses.
- **Value for Quaker research:** Land records place a family in a specific township, which can help identify which monthly meeting served that area.

### Military records
- **Relevant conflicts:** French and Indian War (1754–1763), American Revolution (1775–1783)
- **Quaker-specific note:** Friends were pacifists and officially discouraged military service. Many were disowned by their meetings for enlisting. A Quaker ancestor's name in a military record may be accompanied by a disownment record in the meeting minutes — the two records cross-reference each other. Search both.
- **Record types:** Continental Army service records (NARA); Pennsylvania militia records (Pennsylvania State Archives); pension files (NARA, indexed and imaged on Fold3 and Ancestry)

### Cemetery records
- **Quaker burial grounds:** Friends maintained their own burial grounds, typically adjacent to the meetinghouse. Grave markers were traditionally plain or unmarked; many early Quaker graves have no stone at all. Burial registers in the meeting records are more reliable than physical headstones for this period.
- **Online coverage:** FindAGrave (https://www.findagrave.com) has some Quaker cemetery entries, but coverage is sparse for 18th-century grounds.
- **Physical records:** The burial register kept by the monthly meeting is the authoritative source.

### Tax records
- **Types:** Provincial tax lists (colonial period), county assessment lists (after 1780s), various war tax assessments
- **Date range:** Pennsylvania tax lists survive from the early 1700s
- **Value:** The best substitute for missing census years before 1790. Tax lists name adult male heads of household annually and can track a family year by year through a county.
- **Where held:** Pennsylvania State Archives; many have been published or transcribed by county genealogical societies. Some are on Ancestry.

### Newspaper records
- **Local papers:** *Pennsylvania Gazette* (Philadelphia, 1728–1800) is the dominant paper of the period. Several others operated in Philadelphia and Lancaster.
- **Content value:** Marriage notices (though Quakers rarely advertised in newspapers — check anyway), legal notices, death notices
- **Access:** *Pennsylvania Gazette* is fully digitized and searchable through Accessible Archives and at some library databases. Chronicling America (Library of Congress) has some Pennsylvania papers.

### Immigration and emigration records
- **Relevant ports:** Philadelphia was the primary port of entry for this period
- **Quaker-specific:** Many Quaker families arrived from England, Wales, and Ireland in the late 1600s–early 1700s. Passenger lists for this era are incomplete. The *Welcome Society* (for Penn's 1682 voyage) and published emigrant lists by Hinshaw and others are the best starting points.
- **Certificates of removal from British meetings:** A Quaker emigrating from England or Ireland was expected to carry a removal certificate from their home meeting to the receiving Pennsylvania meeting. These certificates survive in some meeting records and name the immigrant's origin meeting — valuable for tracing English or Irish origins.
- **Record types:** Philadelphia port arrivals (some published and indexed); Pennsylvania State Archives has some early records.

### Other record types
- **Quaker meeting poor relief lists:** Monthly meetings maintained lists of members receiving poor relief. These records name individuals who may not appear in any other series.
- **Disownment records:** Recorded in monthly meeting minutes; they name the individual, the reason, and sometimes family members. The most common reasons in the late 1700s were: marrying outside the meeting ("marrying contrary to discipline"), participating in the Revolutionary War, and later, involvement in the slave trade. Disownment did not always end family connection to the meeting.
- **County histories:** Many 19th-century county histories for Chester, Bucks, Philadelphia, and Delaware counties include biographical sketches of prominent families and reprint early records. These are at the Family History Library, state archives, and local historical societies.

## Repository guide

### Online repositories
| Repository | Collections for this place | Access |
|---|---|---|
| FamilySearch | Philadelphia Yearly Meeting Minutes 1750–1800 (browse-only, 145 images, vol. 001188322); Pennsylvania Probate Records 1683–1994 (browse-only, 3.2M images); Pennsylvania Civil Marriages 1677–1950 (312K records indexed); Pennsylvania Compiled Marriages 1700–1900 (198K records) | Free |
| Ancestry | Hinshaw's *Encyclopedia of American Quaker Genealogy* (partial); U.S. Federal Census 1790; Pennsylvania land and tax records | Subscription |
| Fold3 | Revolutionary War pension files and service records | Subscription |
| FindAGrave | Cemetery records (sparse for 18th-century Quaker grounds) | Free |
| NARA (archives.gov) | Military records, pension files, naturalization | Free browsing; some records by request |
| Newspapers.com / Chronicling America | *Pennsylvania Gazette* and other colonial/early national papers | Subscription (Newspapers.com); Free (Chronicling America) |

**Coverage of this survey:** The `volume_search` returned 1 total result for Pennsylvania religious records in this period (Philadelphia Yearly Meeting Minutes, 001188322). This is the complete result set for that query — no additional pages. The small count reflects that most Quaker meeting records have been microfilmed but many are not yet digitized or indexed as named collections in FamilySearch's volume database.

### Physical repositories
| Repository | Holdings | Access method |
|---|---|---|
| Friends Historical Library, Swarthmore College (Swarthmore, PA) | Original minute books and registers for many PA monthly meetings; the largest American Quaker archive | In-person; correspondence; appointment recommended |
| Quaker and Special Collections, Haverford College (Haverford, PA) | Monthly meeting records for meetings not at Swarthmore; Quaker biography and genealogy | In-person; correspondence |
| Pennsylvania State Archives (Harrisburg, PA) | Land warrants and surveys; colonial-era tax lists; some county records | In-person; some records online |
| Family History Library, Salt Lake City | Microfilmed Quaker meeting minutes and registers; Pennsylvania county records | In-person; microfilm loan through local FamilySearch centers |
| County courthouses (Chester, Bucks, Philadelphia, Delaware, Montgomery) | Deed books; orphans' court/probate records | In-person; some digitized on FamilySearch |
| Local county historical societies | Published abstracts; local histories; transcriptions | In-person or by mail |

## Records NOT online
- Most original monthly meeting minute books and birth/marriage/burial registers held at Swarthmore and Haverford have not been digitized in full; only the Philadelphia Yearly Meeting Minutes volume noted above was found as a digitized FamilySearch volume for 1750–1800.
- Colonial-era Pennsylvania tax lists: many are published in print but the originals are at the Pennsylvania State Archives and are not fully digitized.
- Pennsylvania State Archives land warrant books: available in-person; partial online access.
- Local county history volumes: held physically at the Family History Library, county historical societies, and state archives.

## Known record losses
- No major courthouse fire or disaster specifically affecting Quaker meeting records is documented in the sources returned by this survey.
- Physical Quaker grave markers for this period are frequently absent or illegible — treat burial registers as the authoritative burial record, not headstones.
- Pre-1790 census-equivalent records do not exist; tax lists are the substitute.

## Research tips
- **Start with Hinshaw.** William Wade Hinshaw's *Encyclopedia of American Quaker Genealogy*, vol. 2 (Pennsylvania), abstracts the minute books of many monthly meetings. It is the fastest entry point before working originals. It is available at major genealogical libraries and partially on Ancestry. (Source: https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Pennsylvania_Church_Records#Published_Quaker_Abstracts)
- **Identify the monthly meeting first.** Quaker records are organized by meeting, not by county or township. Before searching, determine which monthly meeting covered the area where the family lived. This requires knowing the township. Land records and tax lists can establish the township; then a meeting directory (available in Hinshaw and at Swarthmore) maps the township to the meeting.
- **Work all three meeting levels.** The monthly meeting kept the vital registers. The quarterly meeting and Philadelphia Yearly Meeting kept broader minutes that can name individuals in discipline cases or committee appointments. Check all three.
- **Certificates of removal are migration documents.** When a Quaker family moved, they carried a removal certificate from the old meeting to the new one. If a family disappears from one set of meeting records, look for a certificate of removal — it will name the destination and often the family members. Conversely, search the receiving meeting's records for the corresponding certificate of arrival. (Source: https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Pennsylvania_Church_Records#Quaker_Records)
- **Marriage certificates named all attendees.** A Quaker marriage certificate was signed by every person present at the meeting when the marriage was solemnized — often 50 to 100 people. This list of signatories can identify neighbors, relatives, and meeting members who would otherwise be invisible. (Source: https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Pennsylvania_Church_Records#Quaker_Records)
- **Cross-reference disownments with other record types.** A man disowned for military service during the Revolution may appear in Pennsylvania militia or Continental Army records. A person disowned for marrying out may have a civil or other-church marriage record.
- **Quaker date conversion.** Records before September 1752 used a calendar in which March = First Month. After the calendar reform, January = First Month. A record reading "11th day, 8th Month, 1745" would be November 11 in old-style reckoning (October being the 8th month). Verify the date convention carefully.
- **Pennsylvania's Quaker-dense counties.** If you do not yet know the county, prioritize Philadelphia, Chester, Bucks, Delaware, and Montgomery counties, which had the heaviest Quaker populations in the late 1700s. (Source: Wikipedia, https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Quakers#Pennsylvania and https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Pennsylvania_Church_Records#Quaker_Records)
- **The 1790 census is the only federal census within this period.** It names heads of household only. Use it to geographically place the family, then work backward and forward through meeting records and tax lists.
- **Statewide civil registration did not begin until 1906.** For any vital event in the late 1700s, there is no civil record to find — the meeting register is the record of first resort, not a substitute. (Source: https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Pennsylvania_Church_Records#Quaker_Records)

- **Content value:** Marriage notices (though Quakers rarely advertised in newspapers — check anyway), legal notices, death notices
- **Access:** *Pennsylvania Gazette* is fully digitized and searchable through Accessible Archives and at some library databases. Chronicling America (Library of Congress) has some Pennsylvania papers.

### Immigration and emigration records
- **Relevant ports:** Philadelphia was the primary port of entry for this period
- **Quaker-specific:** Many Quaker families arrived from England, Wales, and Ireland in the late 1600s–early 1700s. Passenger lists for this era are incomplete. The *Welcome Society* (for Penn's 1682 voyage) and published emigrant lists by Hinshaw and others are the best starting points.
- **Certificates of removal from British meetings:** A Quaker emigrating from England or Ireland was expected to carry a removal certificate from their home meeting to the receiving Pennsylvania meeting. These certificates survive in some meeting records and name the immigrant's origin meeting — valuable for tracing English or Irish origins.
- **Record types:** Philadelphia port arrivals (some published and indexed); Pennsylvania State Archives has some early records.

### Other record types
- **Quaker meeting poor relief lists:** Monthly meetings maintained lists of members receiving poor relief. These records name individuals who may not appear in any other series.
- **Disownment records:** Recorded in monthly meeting minutes; they name the individual, the reason, and sometimes family members. The most common reasons in the late 1700s were: marrying outside the meeting ("marrying contrary to discipline"), participating in the Revolutionary War, and later, involvement in the slave trade. Disownment did not always end family connection to the meeting.
- **County histories:** Many 19th-century county histories for Chester, Bucks, Philadelphia, and Delaware counties include biographical sketches of prominent families and reprint early records. These are at the Family History Library, state archives, and local historical societies.

## Repository guide

### Online repositories
| Repository | Collections for this place | Access |
|---|---|---|
| FamilySearch | Philadelphia Yearly Meeting Minutes 1750–1800 (browse-only, 145 images, vol. 001188322); Pennsylvania Probate Records 1683–1994 (browse-only, 3.2M images); Pennsylvania Civil Marriages 1677–1950 (312K records indexed); Pennsylvania Compiled Marriages 1700–1900 (198K records) | Free |
| Ancestry | Hinshaw's *Encyclopedia of American Quaker Genealogy* (partial); U.S. Federal Census 1790; Pennsylvania land and tax records | Subscription |
| Fold3 | Revolutionary War pension files and service records | Subscription |
| FindAGrave | Cemetery records (sparse for 18th-century Quaker grounds) | Free |
| NARA (archives.gov) | Military records, pension files, naturalization | Free browsing; some records by request |
| Newspapers.com / Chronicling America | *Pennsylvania Gazette* and other colonial/early national papers | Subscription (Newspapers.com); Free (Chronicling America) |

**Coverage of this survey:** The `volume_search` returned 1 total result for Pennsylvania religious records in this period (Philadelphia Yearly Meeting Minutes, 001188322). This is the complete result set for that query — no additional pages. The small count reflects that most Quaker meeting records have been microfilmed but many are not yet digitized or indexed as named collections in FamilySearch's volume database.

### Physical repositories
| Repository | Holdings | Access method |
|---|---|---|
| Friends Historical Library, Swarthmore College (Swarthmore, PA) | Original minute books and registers for many PA monthly meetings; the largest American Quaker archive | In-person; correspondence; appointment recommended |
| Quaker and Special Collections, Haverford College (Haverford, PA) | Monthly meeting records for meetings not at Swarthmore; Quaker biography and genealogy | In-person; correspondence |
| Pennsylvania State Archives (Harrisburg, PA) | Land warrants and surveys; colonial-era tax lists; some county records | In-person; some records online |
| Family History Library, Salt Lake City | Microfilmed Quaker meeting minutes and registers; Pennsylvania county records | In-person; microfilm loan through local FamilySearch centers |
| County courthouses (Chester, Bucks, Philadelphia, Delaware, Montgomery) | Deed books; orphans' court/probate records | In-person; some digitized on FamilySearch |
| Local county historical societies | Published abstracts; local histories; transcriptions | In-person or by mail |

## Records NOT online
- Most original monthly meeting minute books and birth/marriage/burial registers held at Swarthmore and Haverford have not been digitized in full; only the Philadelphia Yearly Meeting Minutes volume noted above was found as a digitized FamilySearch volume for 1750–1800.
- Colonial-era Pennsylvania tax lists: many are published in print but the originals are at the Pennsylvania State Archives and are not fully digitized.
- Pennsylvania State Archives land warrant books: available in-person; partial online access.
- Local county history volumes: held physically at the Family History Library, county historical societies, and state archives.

## Known record losses
- No major courthouse fire or disaster specifically affecting Quaker meeting records is documented in the sources returned by this survey.
- Physical Quaker grave markers for this period are frequently absent or illegible — treat burial registers as the authoritative burial record, not headstones.
- Pre-1790 census-equivalent records do not exist; tax lists are the substitute.

## Research tips
- **Start with Hinshaw.** William Wade Hinshaw's *Encyclopedia of American Quaker Genealogy*, vol. 2 (Pennsylvania), abstracts the minute books of many monthly meetings. It is the fastest entry point before working originals. It is available at major genealogical libraries and partially on Ancestry. (Source: https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Pennsylvania_Church_Records#Published_Quaker_Abstracts)
- **Identify the monthly meeting first.** Quaker records are organized by meeting, not by county or township. Before searching, determine which monthly meeting covered the area where the family lived. This requires knowing the township. Land records and tax lists can establish the township; then a meeting directory (available in Hinshaw and at Swarthmore) maps the township to the meeting.
- **Work all three meeting levels.** The monthly meeting kept the vital registers. The quarterly meeting and Philadelphia Yearly Meeting kept broader minutes that can name individuals in discipline cases or committee appointments. Check all three.
- **Certificates of removal are migration documents.** When a Quaker family moved, they carried a removal certificate from the old meeting to the new one. If a family disappears from one set of meeting records, look for a certificate of removal — it will name the destination and often the family members. Conversely, search the receiving meeting's records for the corresponding certificate of arrival. (Source: https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Pennsylvania_Church_Records#Quaker_Records)
- **Marriage certificates named all attendees.** A Quaker marriage certificate was signed by every person present at the meeting when the marriage was solemnized — often 50 to 100 people. This list of signatories can identify neighbors, relatives, and meeting members who would otherwise be invisible. (Source: https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Pennsylvania_Church_Records#Quaker_Records)
- **Cross-reference disownments with other record types.** A man disowned for military service during the Revolution may appear in Pennsylvania militia or Continental Army records. A person disowned for marrying out may have a civil or other-church marriage record.
- **Quaker date conversion.** Records before September 1752 used a calendar in which March = First Month. After the calendar reform, January = First Month. A record reading "11th day, 8th Month, 1745" would be November 11 in old-style reckoning (October being the 8th month). Verify the date convention carefully.
- **Pennsylvania's Quaker-dense counties.** If you do not yet know the county, prioritize Philadelphia, Chester, Bucks, Delaware, and Montgomery counties, which had the heaviest Quaker populations in the late 1700s. (Source: Wikipedia, https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Quakers#Pennsylvania and https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Pennsylvania_Church_Records#Quaker_Records)
- **The 1790 census is the only federal census within this period.** It names heads of household only. Use it to geographically place the family, then work backward and forward through meeting records and tax lists.
- **Statewide civil registration did not begin until 1906.** For any vital event in the late 1700s, there is no civil record to find — the meeting register is the record of first resort, not a substitute. (Source: https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Pennsylvania_Church_Records#Quaker_Records)

Here is what the locality-guide agent found:

---

This survey covers **Pittsburgh and Allegheny County, Pennsylvania, 1860–1910** — the heart of the steel industry boom. Key findings:

**The critical context:**
Pennsylvania did not require statewide birth or death registration until **1906**, so for most of this period the most important sources are:

1. **Church registers** — especially ethnic Catholic parish registers in Polish, Slovak, Croatian, Italian, or German. These immigrant communities built their own parishes, and baptism/marriage/burial registers are often the only vital records for this era.

2. **Allegheny County local registration** — the county maintained its own vital registration from around 1870, predating the state requirement.

3. **City directories** — annual snapshots giving each worker's name, occupation, and address. These are essential substitutes for the destroyed 1890 federal census.

4. **Company employment records** — Carnegie Steel and other mills do have surviving fragments, but they are held physically at the **Heinz History Center** and the **Rivers of Steel archives** in Pittsburgh and are not systematically indexed or digitized online.

**The biggest access gap:**
The **1890 federal census was destroyed by fire**, making the late 1880s and early 1890s a black hole for most researchers. City directories and tax records from that period are the primary workarounds.

**Recommended next step:**
Identify specific ancestors by ethnic community, approximate arrival date, and the mill town where they lived — that will point to the most likely record series (e.g., a Slovak Catholic worker in Braddock vs. a Welsh Protestant ironworker in Allegheny City).

Marriage records were kept at the county level from the colonial period — search the Allegheny County courthouse for marriage licenses and bonds throughout the target period.

Naturalization records before 1906 could be filed in any court of record — search Allegheny County Court of Common Pleas, the U.S. District Court at Pittsburgh, and the National Archives at Philadelphia. FamilySearch has a partially indexed digitized volume (15% name-indexed, imageGroupNumber 008120443, covering 1790-1915, in English and German).
Company employment records for steel mills are fragmentary — surviving records are held at the Heinz History Center and the Rivers of Steel archives, not at a courthouse or state archive.

Catholic parishes in Pittsburgh served specific ethnic communities (Polish, Slovak, Croatian, Italian) — identify the ethnic parish that served your ancestor's community before searching generic Catholic diocesan archives.

City directories at the Carnegie Library of Pittsburgh list occupations from as early as the 1810s — these are the primary source for confirming an ancestor's occupation and address between census years.
Federal census schedules for 1870, 1880, 1900 list each person's occupation — these are primary sources for industrial workers and should be cross-checked against city directories.

Probate volume 008120441 (1,180 images, 1683-1994) is browse-only with 0% name indexing; probate volume 008120442 for death records (674 images, 1852-1968) is also browse-only. Both must be examined image by image.

Pittsburgh sits near the borders of Washington County (south) and Westmoreland County (east) — mill towns on the Monongahela and Youghiogheny rivers in those counties generated records independently; search those counties if an ancestor worked in outlying mill towns.
entry.guide_markdown:
# Locality Guide: Pittsburgh / Allegheny County, Pennsylvania (1860-1910)

## Jurisdiction overview
- **Formed:** Allegheny County formed in 1788 from parts of Washington and Westmoreland counties. Pittsburgh was incorporated as a borough in 1794 and chartered as a city in 1816.
- **County seat / administrative center:** Pittsburgh
- **Parent jurisdiction:** Pennsylvania
- **Population during period:** Population data was not returned by the place_population tool for this query. Wikipedia notes that Pittsburgh's steel-industry boom drew hundreds of thousands of workers in the late 1800s, making it one of the largest industrial cities in the United States by 1900.
- **Economy:** Steel production (Carnegie Steel and successor firms), iron manufacturing, glass works, coke production, coal mining in surrounding townships. The late 1800s was the peak of heavy industrial growth.
- **Ethnic composition:** Large waves of Irish, German, Polish, Slovak, Croatian, and Italian immigrant workers arrived from the 1870s through the 1900s. Earlier settlers included Scots-Irish and English. Each ethnic group formed distinct community and church structures. (Source: Wikipedia, https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pittsburgh)
- **Religious denominations:** Roman Catholic (multiple ethnic parishes), Presbyterian, Methodist, Episcopal, Lutheran (German), Greek Catholic / Byzantine Catholic (Slovak, Ukrainian, Croatian), Jewish congregations.
- **Key historical events:** Homestead Strike (1892) at Carnegie Steel's Homestead plant; rapid industrialization 1870s-1900s; major immigration waves corresponding to industrial labor demand.

## Boundary changes
- Allegheny County boundaries have been stable since 1788. No county boundary changes during the target period.
- The city of Allegheny (across the Ohio River from Pittsburgh) existed as a separate city until 1907, when it was annexed into Pittsburgh. Records created before 1907 for residents of Allegheny City are filed under "Allegheny City" not "Pittsburgh" — search both when covering the period before 1907.
- Mill towns along the Monongahela River (Homestead, Braddock, McKeesport) are in Allegheny County; those further south and east may fall in Washington or Westmoreland County.

## Available record types

### Vital records (civil registration)
- **Start date:** Pennsylvania did not require **statewide** registration of births and deaths until 1906. Before that, Allegheny County maintained its own local vital registration from approximately 1870. Marriage records were kept at the **county level** from the colonial period. (Source: FamilySearch Wiki, Pennsylvania Vital Records, https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Pennsylvania_Vital_Records)
- **What exists:**
  - Births and deaths (county-level local registration): ca. 1870-1905 for Allegheny County, held at the county or at the Pennsylvania State Archives
  - Births and deaths (statewide): 1906 onward — indexed and digitized in FamilySearch collection "Pennsylvania, Death Certificates, 1906-1968" (collection 2255317; 4,218,763 indexed records with images)
  - Marriages (county level): from colonial period through the entire target period — FamilySearch collections "Pennsylvania, County Marriages, 1885-1950" (collection 1921317; 524,189 records) and "Pennsylvania, Civil Marriages, 1677-1950" (collection 1571957; 312,045 records)
- **Where held:** Allegheny County courthouse; Pennsylvania State Archives (Harrisburg); FamilySearch online for post-1906 deaths and county marriages
- **Gaps:** Births and deaths 1860-1869 have no statewide or reliable county registration — church records are the primary alternative. The 1890 federal census was largely destroyed by fire.
- **Pre-registration alternatives:** Church baptism, marriage, and burial registers; family Bibles; newspaper notices.

### Church records
- **Denominations present:** Roman Catholic (with distinct ethnic parishes — Polish, Slovak, Croatian, Italian, Irish, German), Presbyterian, Methodist, Episcopal, German Lutheran, Byzantine/Greek Catholic, Jewish.
- **Record types:** Baptisms, marriages, burials, confirmations. Ethnic Catholic parishes kept registers in the language of the congregation (Polish, Slovak, Croatian, Italian, German).
- **Where held:** Individual parish offices; Diocese of Pittsburgh archives; FamilySearch microfilm holdings. The FamilySearch wiki_search result specifically notes that Catholic parishes served specific ethnic communities and their registers are often the best source for family data. (Source: https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Allegheny_County,_Pennsylvania_Genealogy#Immigration_Records)
- **Language:** Registers of ethnic Catholic parishes may be in Polish, Slovak, Croatian, Italian, German, or Latin. The researcher must be able to read the original language or obtain a translation.
- **Access:** Identify the specific ethnic parish before searching — searching generic Catholic diocesan indexes without knowing the parish is unlikely to succeed for immigrant workers.

### Census records
- **Federal census:** 1860, 1870, 1880, 1900, 1910 — all available and indexed online. The 1880, 1900, and 1910 schedules list each person's occupation, birthplace, and parents' birthplaces, making them primary sources for identifying immigrant steel workers.
- **1890 federal census:** Almost entirely destroyed by fire in 1921; fragments survive.
- **Mortality schedules:** Exist for 1850, 1860, 1870, 1880 — record deaths in the year preceding the census enumeration.
- **State census:** Pennsylvania did not conduct a state-level census during this period.
- **Access:** 1860-1880 and 1900-1910 are name-indexed and searchable at Ancestry.com (subscription) and FamilySearch (free).

### Probate and court records

| NARA Online (Ancestry/FamilySearch) | Passenger manifests via Ancestry and FamilySearch; post-1906 naturalization records | Free / Subscription |

**Coverage of this survey:** The `volume_search` returned a total of 3 digitized volumes matching Pennsylvania records in this period. All 3 are detailed above — this is the complete result set.

### Physical repositories
| Repository | Holdings | Access method |
|---|---|---|
| Senator John Heinz History Center, Pittsburgh | Steel industry company employment records (fragmentary); Pittsburgh and western PA history collections | In-person; contact for research services |
| Rivers of Steel National Heritage Area Archives | Industrial records, labor history, Homestead Strike materials | In-person by appointment |
| Allegheny County Courthouse (Pittsburgh) | Deed books, marriage licenses, probate files, naturalization records (pre-1906), court records | In-person; some records on FamilySearch microfilm |
| Carnegie Library of Pittsburgh | City directories 1810s-present; local newspapers on microfilm; local history collection | In-person; limited remote access |
| Pennsylvania State Archives (Harrisburg) | State factory inspector reports; state-level military records; patent/warrant records; some county records | In-person; limited online catalog |
| National Archives Mid-Atlantic Region (Philadelphia) | Pre-1906 naturalization records from federal courts; passenger manifests | In-person; some online via Ancestry/FamilySearch |
| Diocese of Pittsburgh Archives | Catholic parish registers; diocesan records | Contact diocese for access; not publicly browsable |
| Pennsylvania State Library (Harrisburg) | Historical newspapers; state publications | In-person; some digital |

## Records NOT online

- Most company employment records for Carnegie Steel and other Pittsburgh mills (held at Heinz History Center and Rivers of Steel archives — not digitized or publicly indexed)
- Union membership rolls and Amalgamated Association of Iron and Steel Workers records
- Allegheny County local vital registration (births and deaths, ca. 1870-1905, before statewide requirement)
- County coroner records and industrial accident inquests
- Ethnic mutual aid society records (Slovak, Polish, Croatian lodges)
- Hospital institutional records
- Orphanage admission and case records
- Most pre-1906 naturalization records from county courts (microfilm only; the one FamilySearch digitized volume is 15% indexed)

## Known record losses

- **1890 U.S. Federal Census:** Largely destroyed by fire in Washington DC in 1921. Substitute sources include the 1880 and 1900 censuses, city directories for 1885-1895, state veterans' schedules that partially survive for 1890, and tax lists.
- **No systematic destruction of courthouse records reported** for Allegheny County during this period — the county courthouse survived intact.
- **Company records:** Many steel company operational records were not preserved when plants changed ownership or closed; what survives is fragmentary and not comprehensively inventoried.

## Research tips

- **Vital registration gap:** Pennsylvania required no statewide birth or death registration until 1906. For 1860-1905, church records and the Allegheny County local registration series (ca. 1870-1905) are the primary vital-record sources. Do not assume a FamilySearch "not found" in the death certificates collection means the person's death is unrecorded before 1906. (Source: FamilySearch Wiki, Pennsylvania Vital Records, https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Pennsylvania_Vital_Records)
- **Identify the ethnic parish first:** For immigrant steel workers, the ethnic Catholic parish is often the richest source of family data — baptisms, marriages, and burials with full family detail. Identify the specific parish that served your ancestor's community (Polish, Slovak, Croatian, Italian) before searching generic indexes. (Source: https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Allegheny_County,_Pennsylvania_Genealogy#Immigration_Records)
- **City directories as annual census substitutes:** The Carnegie Library of Pittsburgh's city directory collection, running from the 1810s, gives annual snapshots of each resident's name, occupation, and address. For a steel worker, consecutive directory years can trace job changes, moves between mill towns, and the arrival of boarders (often relatives).
- **Federal census occupation columns:** The 1870, 1880, 1900, and 1910 census schedules all list each person's occupation. For industrial workers, these directly name the trade ("puddler," "roller," "heater," "laborer in iron works") and are the starting point for identifying mill employment.
- **Naturalization as family-reconstruction tool:** Post-1906 naturalization petitions ("second papers" / final papers) list the petitioner's port and date of arrival, spouse's name and birthplace, and names and ages of all children. Even if you find the ancestor in the 1900 or 1910 census, locate the naturalization petition for the additional family data it provides.
- **Allegheny City annexation:** The city of Allegheny (across the Ohio River from Pittsburgh) was annexed in 1907. Before that date, residents of Allegheny City appear in records under "Allegheny City," not "Pittsburgh." If an ancestor lived in what is now the North Side of Pittsburgh before 1907, search Allegheny City records, not Pittsburgh records.
- **Neighboring counties:** Pittsburgh-area mill towns along the Monongahela River (Clairton, Donora, Monessen) fall in Washington County to the south; towns along the Youghiogheny River may be in Westmoreland County. If an ancestor worked in a mill town and you cannot find the family in Allegheny County records, search Washington and Westmoreland county records. (The Neighboring Counties table from the Allegheny County wiki page was not returned — searching those counties is advised regardless.)
- **Strike and labor records:** The 1892 Homestead Strike generated substantial newspaper coverage, court records (criminal charges against strikers and Pinkerton agents), and congressional testimony. If an ancestor worked at Homestead in 1892, these records may directly name the individual.

Here is what the locality-guide agent found:

---

**Philadelphia, Pennsylvania — 1793 Yellow Fever Epidemic Research Guide**
*(Coverage period: roughly 1780–1810, with the epidemic of August–November 1793 as the core focus)*

---

### Key Context Before You Search

Pennsylvania had **no civil registration of births, marriages, or deaths in 1793** — statewide civil registration didn't begin until 1906. This means:

- **Church burial registers are the primary death record** for epidemic victims.
- Those registers are held by individual congregations and denominational archives, **not** in any central repository.
- A large portion are **not digitized or indexed online** — many require in-person access.
- Families who **fled the city** during the epidemic may have left traces in surrounding counties (Montgomery, Bucks, Delaware, Chester) rather than Philadelphia proper.

---

### Priority Records & Repositories

#### 1. Mathew Carey's Published List of the Dead
The most important starting point. Mathew Carey (a Philadelphia printer) published a list of epidemic dead and survivors in his pamphlet *A Short Account of the Malignant Fever* (1793, multiple editions). It is freely available on **HathiTrust**. Search your surname here first to confirm whether the family appears before investing time in archival visits.

#### 2. Church Burial Registers
The epidemic's death toll (roughly 5,000 in about three months) overwhelmed individual congregations. Key denominations with Philadelphia-area registers from this period:

- **Christ Church (Anglican/Episcopal)** — burial register held at Christ Church; some records microfilmed by FamilySearch
- **Gloria Dei (Old Swedes') Church** — one of the oldest in the city; registers at the church and the Historical Society of Pennsylvania (HSP)
- **St. Mary's Roman Catholic Church** — burial records at the Archdiocese of Philadelphia Archives
- **Mikveh Israel (Jewish congregation)** — burial records at the congregation and HSP
- **First African Church (Mother Bethel AME)** — Richard Allen's congregation played a direct role in epidemic relief; records at Mother Bethel AME Archives
- **German Reformed and Lutheran congregations** — registers held at the Lutheran Theological Seminary (Krauth Memorial Library, Philadelphia) and HSP
- **Presbyterian churches** — Philadelphia Presbytery records at the Presbyterian Historical Society, 425 Lombard Street, Philadelphia

#### 3. Philadelphia City Archives
Holds municipal records from this period, including:
- **Committee of Philadelphia minutes** — the volunteer relief committee organized during the epidemic kept records of relief distributions, names of the sick, and names of the dead
- Early city council minutes and mayor's records

#### 4. Historical Society of Pennsylvania (HSP)
The single most important repository for this research. Holdings include:
- Church registers (originals and microfilm) for dozens of Philadelphia congregations
- Mathew Carey papers
- Benjamin Rush papers (Rush was the leading physician during the epidemic; his patient records and correspondence name many families)
- Philadelphia city directories for 1793–1800 (useful for locating where families lived before and after the epidemic)
- Estate inventories and administration papers

#### 5. Genealogical Society of Pennsylvania (GSP)
Partners closely with HSP; holds indexes and transcriptions of many church registers and compiled records specifically useful for Philadelphia genealogy.

#### 6. Pennsylvania State Archives (Harrisburg)
- **Provincial and state tax lists** (1769–1799) — the 1793–1800 tax lists can show whether a household disappeared from a ward after the epidemic
- **Land records** — useful if property changed hands during or after the epidemic

#### 7. Probate Records — Register of Wills, Philadelphia County
When epidemic deaths were followed by estate settlement:
- Wills, letters of administration, and inventories are at the **Philadelphia Register of Wills** (City Hall Annex)
- Pre-1900 indexes are available on **Ancestry** and **FamilySearch** under Pennsylvania, Philadelphia County, Probate Records
- The spike in probate filings in late 1793 and early 1794 often flags epidemic-related deaths

#### 8. Newspaper Death Notices
Philadelphia had several newspapers in 1793. Death notices and lists of the sick appeared regularly during the epidemic:
- *Dunlap's American Daily Advertiser*, *Federal Gazette*, *General Advertiser* (later renamed *Aurora*)
- **Accessible Archives** (subscription) has digitized Philadelphia newspapers of this era
- **Chronicling America** (Library of Congress, free) covers later years but is worth checking
- HSP holds original and microfilmed copies of the 1793 Philadelphia press

#### 9. Benjamin Rush's Papers and Medical Records
Rush treated hundreds of patients during the epidemic and kept detailed records. His papers at HSP and at the **Library Company of Philadelphia** (a block from HSP) name patients and families. The Library Company also holds a strong collection of epidemic-era pamphlets.

#### 10. Philadelphia City Directories
City directories for 1791, 1793, 1794, and 1796 can bracket a disappearance — a family present in 1791–93 but absent in 1794–96 is a strong indicator of epidemic loss. Available at HSP and on microfilm at the Family History Library (FamilySearch).

---

### Surrounding County Records (Refugees)
Many Philadelphians fled to Germantown (then in Philadelphia County), Bristol (Bucks County), and various taverns and homes in Montgomery and Delaware counties. If your family disappears from city records but doesn't appear in burial registers, check:
- Montgomery County Register of Wills and tax lists (Pennsylvania State Archives / Montgomery County Courthouse)
- Bucks County and Delaware County equivalent records
- Germantown church registers (Germantown was a distinct community; several congregations kept separate registers)

---

### Online Starting Points

| Resource | What's There | Cost |
|---|---|---|
| **FamilySearch.org** | Philadelphia church registers (partial), probate indexes, city directories | Free |
| **Ancestry.com** | Philadelphia probate indexes, city directories, some church records | Subscription |
| **HathiTrust** | Mathew Carey's pamphlet and other epidemic publications | Free |
| **Accessible Archives** | 1793 Philadelphia newspapers | Subscription |
| **PhillyHistory.org** | Philadelphia City Archives photographs and some documents | Free |

---

### Recommended First Steps

1. **Search Mathew Carey's list** on HathiTrust for your surname — this is the fastest single check.
2. **Check FamilySearch** for the family in Philadelphia church burial registers (1790–1800).
3. **Search Ancestry** for the family in Philadelphia probate records (1793–1796 spike).
4. **Check the 1793 and 1794 city directories** at HSP (or FamilySearch microfilm) to bracket a disappearance.
5. If the family isn't found dead, check **surrounding county tax lists** for refugee settlement.
6. For an in-person visit: **HSP and GSP** on Locust Street are your most productive single stop.

---

*This locality entry has been logged to the project research log.*

The 1790 federal census is the only decennial census bracketing 1793; the next is 1800. Neither is name-indexed for every household member — all members other than the head are only tallied as counts by age group.

Roughly 5,000 of Philadelphia's 50,000 residents died in the 1793 epidemic (August–November). Thousands more fled to surrounding counties, so records of those families may appear in Montgomery, Delaware, Bucks, or Chester County repositories.

Mathew Carey's published account 'A Short Account of the Malignant Fever' (1793) includes a named list of the dead — this is a critical finding aid and was held and transcribed by the Historical Society of Pennsylvania.

The Committee of Philadelphia (relief committee) kept minutes naming individuals who received aid, died, or were otherwise documented — held at the Philadelphia City Archives and the Historical Society of Pennsylvania.
Bush Hill hospital (the fever hospital set up during the epidemic) generated patient and death records; these are held at the Historical Society of Pennsylvania.
The Philadelphia Yearly Meeting Minutes (FamilySearch image group 001188322, 145 images, 1750–1800) are digitized but NOT name-indexed and NOT full-text searchable — must be browsed image by image.

Church records in 1793 Philadelphia were kept in multiple languages: English (Anglican/Episcopal, Presbyterian, Methodist, Baptist, Quaker), German (Lutheran, German Reformed), Swedish (Gloria Dei/Old Swedes'), and Latin (Roman Catholic). Non-English records require reading in the original language.
The 1793 epidemic created a surge in probate filings: check Philadelphia County Orphans' Court and Register of Wills records from late 1793 through 1794 for estates of epidemic victims.

Families who fled Philadelphia may have left property behind or had guardianship proceedings filed in the counties where they sheltered — check Montgomery, Bucks, Delaware, and Chester Counties as well.
entry.guide_markdown:
# Locality Guide: Philadelphia, Pennsylvania (1780–1810, focus on 1793 yellow fever epidemic)

## Jurisdiction overview
- **Formed:** Philadelphia was founded 1682; Philadelphia County and Philadelphia City were coextensive through this period.
- **County seat / administrative center:** Philadelphia (city and county seat were the same municipality)
- **Parent jurisdiction:** Pennsylvania (Commonwealth)
- **Population during period:** Approximately 50,000 residents in 1793, making Philadelphia the largest city in the new United States and its temporary capital. The 1790 federal census is the bracketing enumeration just before the epidemic; 1800 follows it.
- **Economy:** Mercantile trade, shipping, artisan crafts, printing and publishing. Philadelphia was the commercial and political capital of the early republic.
- **Ethnic composition:** English Quaker founding population; significant German (Lutheran and Reformed), Scots-Irish Presbyterian, Swedish (Gloria Dei congregation), Irish Catholic, and free Black communities by 1793. Recent Haitian refugee arrivals in 1793 were linked epidemiologically to the yellow fever outbreak.
- **Religious denominations:** Society of Friends (Quakers), Anglican/Episcopal (Christ Church, St. Peter's, St. Paul's), Presbyterian (First Presbyterian, Second Presbyterian), Lutheran (Zion, St. Michael's), German Reformed, Roman Catholic (St. Mary's, St. Joseph's), Methodist, Baptist, Swedish Lutheran (Gloria Dei/Old Swedes'), African Methodist Episcopal (founded 1793–1794 by Richard Allen partly in response to the epidemic).
- **Key historical events:** The 1793 yellow fever epidemic (August–November 1793) killed approximately 5,000 people — one-tenth of the population. Thousands more fled to surrounding counties. This is the central event for this research focus.

## Boundary changes
- Philadelphia County and Philadelphia City were coextensive through this period; no significant boundary changes affected record jurisdiction between 1780 and 1810.
- The formal city-county consolidation into a single jurisdiction came later, in 1854 — outside the target period and not relevant here.
- Families who fled during the epidemic may have generated records in surrounding counties: Montgomery, Bucks, Delaware, and Chester. Search those county repositories for any documented activity in the fall of 1793.

## Available record types

### Epidemic-specific published sources (START HERE)
Before searching any archive, consult the two published finding aids that name 1793 victims directly:

1. **Mathew Carey, *A Short Account of the Malignant Fever* (1793, multiple editions).** Carey compiled a named list of the dead, organized by household and street. Widely reprinted; held by the Historical Society of Pennsylvania and available in early American imprint digitization projects (Evans Digital Edition, Archive.org). This is the single most efficient starting point.
2. **Minutes of the Committee of Philadelphia (the relief committee appointed by citizens under Mayor Matthew Clarkson).** Names individuals who died, received relief, or were otherwise documented. Held at the Philadelphia City Archives and the Historical Society of Pennsylvania. According to Wikipedia's article on the Yellow Fever Epidemic of 1793 (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yellow_fever_epidemic_of_1793), these are the primary manuscript sources for names of the dead.

### Vital records (civil registration)
- **Start date:** Pennsylvania had NO statewide civil registration of births, marriages, or deaths in 1793. Statewide death registration did not begin until 1906. The FamilySearch collection "Pennsylvania, Death Certificates, 1906-1968" (collection 2255317) postdates the epidemic by over a century and has no bearing on 1793 research.
- **What exists for 1793:** No civil death certificates. Church burial registers are the sole systematic record of deaths.
- **Pre-registration sources:** Church registers (see below), Carey's published list, and Committee minutes.
- **Marriage records:** FamilySearch holds "Pennsylvania, Civil Marriages, 1677-1950" (collection 1571957, 312,045 indexed records, images online) and "Pennsylvania, Compiled Marriages, 1700-1900" (collection 1502909, 198,765 indexed records, no images). Both cover the 1793 period and are searchable by name at FamilySearch.org.

### Church records (PRIMARY SOURCE FOR DEATHS AND BURIALS)

| NARA Mid-Atlantic Region, Philadelphia | Naturalization records; federal court records | In-person |

## Records NOT online
- The Committee of Philadelphia minutes (naming epidemic victims and relief recipients)
- Bush Hill hospital patient and death records
- Philadelphia County tax assessment lists for 1793–1794
- Most individual Philadelphia church burial registers (a major gap — these exist physically but most are not yet digitized or indexed online)
- Philadelphia City Archives deed books for this period
- Almshouse records
- The full run of 1793 Philadelphia newspapers (partial digitization only)

## Known record losses
- No courthouse fire or major record destruction is documented for Philadelphia County for this period. The records that do not exist online are largely a digitization gap, not a loss.
- The epidemic itself disrupted record-keeping: some churches suspended normal register entries during August–November 1793 when clergy fled or died. Burial entries may be in irregular formats or consolidated lists rather than individual entries.
- Some families who fled and never returned may have left no Philadelphia-based records after 1793 — track them in the counties where they resettled.

## Research tips
- **Start with Mathew Carey's published list** before searching any archive. It is the fastest path to confirming whether a specific surname appears among the documented dead. Multiple editions exist with slightly different name lists; check more than one.
- **The surge in probate filings is your friend.** Epidemic deaths in 1793 generated a concentrated wave of will probates and administration filings in late 1793 and 1794. Browsing the Philadelphia County probate docket for that window is practical even without a name index.
- **Check both church and civic sources.** A person might appear in a church burial register but not in Carey's list, or vice versa. The overlap between sources is imperfect.
- **Families who fled Philadelphia** during the epidemic (a large portion of the population) may have sheltered in Montgomery County (Germantown was a favored destination), Bucks County, Delaware County, or Chester County. Death, birth, or even church records from the fall of 1793 in those counties may document epidemic refugees.
- **The 1790 and 1800 censuses bracket the epidemic** but name only household heads. Use them to establish presence and household size before and after 1793, then work from church registers for the specific 1793 events.
- **African American families:** The Free African Society and Mother Bethel AME records are essential for African American families. Richard Allen and Absalom Jones published *A Narrative of the Proceedings of the Black People During the Late Awful Calamity in Philadelphia* (1794), which names individuals. Available at HathiTrust.
- **Non-English church records require the original language.** German Lutheran and Reformed registers, Swedish Gloria Dei registers, and Latin Catholic registers cannot be read without knowledge of those languages. Consider hiring a translator or using a transcription service.
- **The Genealogical Society of Pennsylvania** has published compiled indexes to many Philadelphia church records that make browsing the original volumes much faster. Check their published record sets before going to original registers.
- **FamilySearch Wiki note:** The jurisdiction-specific wiki pages for Philadelphia County vital records, church records, and probate records each returned only generic content during this survey. Consult the FamilySearch Catalog directly (https://www.familysearch.org/catalog) and the GSP's published guides for current coverage details.

Locality guide written as **loc_001**.

---

Chicago's Cook County in the 1860–1885 period presents a research situation defined by a single catastrophic event: the Great Fire of October 8–10, 1871, which destroyed the Cook County Courthouse and with it nearly all county-level deed books, vital registers, probate files, court records, and tax rolls filed before that date. The 1870 federal census survived because its originals were held in Washington, not Chicago, making it your essential pre-fire population baseline. Post-fire civil records — births, marriages, and deaths — restart from 1871 and are indexed on FamilySearch with roughly 3 million records across four collections. The most powerful substitutes for destroyed pre-fire records are:

- **Chicago Relief and Aid Society records** (fire victim relief lists, 1871–1874) and the **Chicago Title and Trust Company insurance abstract books**, both held physically at the **Chicago History Museum**
- **Burnt Record Act deed re-filings** (1872) at the **Cook County Recorder of Deeds**
- **Civil War pension files** at **NARA** (compiled in Washington and untouched by the fire)
- **Catholic parish registers** at the **Archdiocese's Bernardin Archives**
- **City directories** from the 1840s onward at the **Newberry Library**

The 1890 federal census is also unavailable nationally due to a 1921 fire at NARA, compounding the gap for Chicago research.

**Recommended next step:** Build a research plan targeting your specific family, starting with the 1870 census and city directories to establish their pre-fire presence, then the Relief Society records to confirm fire impact, and then post-fire civil registrations and church records.

quirks: The Great Chicago Fire (October 8-10, 1871) destroyed the Cook County Courthouse, eliminating most deeds, birth and death registers, court records, and tax rolls filed before that date. There is no complete pre-fire vital record series at the county level.
The 1870 federal census for Chicago survived because the originals were held in Washington, D.C. — not at the courthouse. Use it as a pre-fire population baseline.

The Burnt Record Act of 1872 required property owners to re-register deeds. These reconstructed records are the primary source for pre-fire property ownership and are held at the Cook County Recorder of Deeds and the Chicago History Museum (Chicago Title and Trust Company collection).

FamilySearch collections for Cook County vital records (births, deaths, marriages) begin in 1871 — the post-fire restart date, not the date civil registration began in Illinois. Do not interpret 1871 as the registration start.

Illinois statewide vital registration did not begin until 1916 for births and deaths. Before that, registration was a county-level requirement, and pre-fire Cook County records were largely destroyed in 1871.

Church records are the primary substitute for missing pre-fire vital events. The Archdiocese of Chicago's Joseph Cardinal Bernardin Archives holds Catholic parish registers; many parishes survived the fire or quickly reconstructed their records.

City directories from the 1840s onward survived and are held at the Newberry Library — these can place a person at a specific Chicago address in the years between censuses and before and after the fire.

Pre-1906 naturalizations could be filed in any court of record (federal, state, or local). Cook County Circuit Court naturalizations partially survived the fire; search both the county and federal courts.
Insurance company records, particularly the Chicago Title and Trust Company collection at the Chicago History Museum, are vital substitutes for destroyed pre-fire property records.
The Illinois Regional Archives Depository (IRAD) at Northeastern Illinois University holds Cook County records created after 1871. This is a key repository for post-fire court and land records.
entry.guide_markdown:
# Locality Guide: Chicago, Cook County, Illinois (1860–1885)

## Jurisdiction overview
- **Formed:** Cook County established 1831 from unorganized territory; Chicago incorporated as a town 1833, city 1837
- **County seat / administrative center:** Chicago
- **Parent jurisdiction:** Illinois
- **Population during period:** Chicago grew from approximately 109,000 (1860 census) to 298,977 (1870 census) to 503,185 (1880 census) — one of the fastest-growing cities in the world during this period. No population data was returned by the place_population tool for this query.
- **Economy:** Meatpacking, grain trade, lumber, manufacturing, railroads, and Great Lakes shipping. Chicago was the nation's primary rail hub by the 1860s.
- **Ethnic composition:** Large German, Irish, Scandinavian (Swedish, Norwegian), and Polish immigrant communities by 1870. Significant Bohemian (Czech) and Italian communities growing through the 1880s. African American community concentrated on the Near South Side.
- **Religious denominations:** Roman Catholic (largest single denomination), German Lutheran (several synods), Methodist, Presbyterian, Baptist, Episcopal, Swedish Lutheran, Jewish congregations.
- **Key historical events:** Great Chicago Fire, October 8–10, 1871 — destroyed 3.3 square miles, killed approximately 300 people, left more than 100,000 homeless, and burned the Cook County Courthouse with most of the city's official records. Rapid reconstruction 1871–1873; second major fire (the Chicago Fire of 1874) in a smaller area.

## Boundary changes
- Cook County's geographic boundaries were essentially stable during this period.
- Chicago's city limits expanded significantly through annexation of surrounding townships across the 1860s–1880s (Hyde Park, Lake View, Jefferson, and others fully annexed by 1889). Records for events in these areas before annexation may be under the township, not the city.
- The key jurisdictional break is not a boundary change but a record destruction: October 1871 divides the research period into a pre-fire era (records largely destroyed) and a post-fire era (records begin again from 1871).

## Available record types

### Vital records (civil registration)
- **Registration level and start date:** Illinois did not require statewide registration of births and deaths until 1916. County-level registration was required earlier, but the Cook County pre-fire registers were destroyed in October 1871. FamilySearch's indexed collections (Birth Certificates, 1871–1940; Death Records, 1871–1947; Marriage Records, 1871–1920) begin at the post-fire restart date. The FamilySearch Wiki did not return a jurisdiction-specific vital records page confirming the exact county-level start date before the fire.
- **What exists:** Post-fire: Cook County birth certificates (1871–1940, ~1,450,000 records on FamilySearch, collection 2024189); Cook County death records (1871–1947, ~980,000 records, collection 1913456); Cook County marriage records (1871–1920, ~620,000 records, collection 1756321).
- **Pre-fire:** No systematic county-level vital register survives for the pre-fire period (before October 1871). Church records are the primary substitute.
- **Where held:** Cook County Clerk's Office (originals); FamilySearch (indexed + images, post-fire).
- **Gaps:** All county-level vital records before October 1871 were destroyed in the Great Fire. No pre-fire birth, death, or marriage register series exists at the county courthouse.
- **Pre-registration alternatives:** Church baptism, marriage, and burial registers; mortality schedules from the 1860 and 1870 federal census; newspaper notices.

### Church records
- **Denominations present:** Roman Catholic, German Lutheran (multiple synods), Methodist Episcopal, Presbyterian, Baptist, Episcopal, Swedish Lutheran (Augustana Synod), Jewish.
- **Record types:** Baptisms, marriages, burials, confirmations. Catholic parishes also maintained records of the poor and parish censuses ("status animarum").
- **Where held:** The Archdiocese of Chicago's Joseph Cardinal Bernardin Archives holds Catholic parish registers and is the primary repository for pre- and post-fire Catholic records. Many parishes survived the fire or quickly reconstructed registers from memory and family recollection. German and Scandinavian Lutheran records may be at the Evangelical Lutheran Church in America (ELCA) archives. FamilySearch has microfilmed many registers (collection 1803978: Illinois, Cook County, Chicago, Church Records, 1833–1925, ~285,000 records — indexed + images).
- **Language:** German-language records common in Lutheran, Catholic, and some Reformed parishes serving immigrant communities. Swedish and Norwegian for Scandinavian congregations.

### Census records
- **Federal census:** 1860 (indexed + images, Ancestry and FamilySearch), 1870 (indexed + images — the 1870 Chicago schedules survived the fire because originals were in Washington, D.C.), 1880 (indexed + images). The 1890 federal census was largely destroyed in a 1921 fire at NARA and is not available for Cook County.
- **Mortality schedules:** 1860 and 1870 mortality schedules list persons who died in the year preceding each census — a partial substitute for the missing death registers.
- **State census:** Illinois conducted a state census in 1865. It is less complete than the federal enumerations but covers the gap between 1860 and 1870.
- **Access:** Federal census records 1860–1880 are indexed and searchable by name on both Ancestry and FamilySearch.

### Probate and court records
- **Types:** Wills, estate inventories, letters of administration, guardianships, naturalizations, civil suits, criminal cases.
- **Fire impact:** Cook County Circuit Court records held at the courthouse were largely destroyed in October 1871. Post-fire probate and court records begin again from late 1871.
- **Pre-fire substitute:** Some probate files were reconstructed by claimants presenting copies or affidavits. The Cook County Circuit Court Archives at the Richard J. Daley Center may hold some reconstructed files.
- **Naturalization:** Pre-1906 naturalizations could be filed in any court. Some Cook County naturalizations survived as federal court records (U.S. District Court for the Northern District of Illinois, held at NARA-Great Lakes in Chicago). Search both the county circuit court and the federal court.
- **Where held:** Cook County Circuit Court Archives (post-fire originals); IRAD at Northeastern Illinois University (transferred county records); NARA-Great Lakes (federal court naturalizations).

### Land records
- **Survey system:** Rectangular (Public Land Survey System — Illinois is a federal land state).
- **Land-distribution jurisdiction:** Original patents granted by the federal government through the General Land Office; BLM GLO website (glorecords.blm.gov) holds digitized patent records.
- **Fire impact and the Burnt Record Act:** Pre-fire deed books at the Cook County Recorder of Deeds were destroyed in 1871. The Illinois Burnt Record Act of 1872 required property owners to re-file evidence of ownership. These reconstructed records are a key pre-fire substitute and are held at the Cook County Recorder of Deeds.
- **Insurance company records:** The Chicago Title and Trust Company collection at the Chicago History Museum contains abstract books and insurance maps that document property ownership and transfers both before and after the fire. This is an essential source for pre-fire property research.
- **Types:** Deeds, mortgages, Burnt Record Act re-filings, BLM land patents, Sanborn fire insurance maps (for post-fire property).
- **Where held:** Cook County Recorder of Deeds (originals, including Burnt Record Act volumes); Chicago History Museum (Chicago Title and Trust collection, Sanborn maps); BLM GLO website (federal patents, online and free).

### Military records
- **Relevant conflicts:** Civil War (1861–1865) — many Chicago residents served in Illinois volunteer infantry, cavalry, and artillery regiments.
- **Record types:** Service records (NARA, RG 94), pension files (NARA, RG 15), Illinois adjutant general's regimental rosters (Illinois State Archives), draft registration records (1863 Enrollment Act records at NARA).
- **Where held:** NARA (Washington, D.C. and NARA-Great Lakes, Chicago) for federal records; Illinois State Archives (Springfield) for state-level rosters and pension supplements; Fold3 (indexed + images for service and pension records).
- **Civil War pension files** are especially valuable post-fire because they were compiled in Washington, D.C. and often contain family information (wife's name, children, marriage date and place) that substitutes for destroyed local vital records.

### Cemetery records
- **Major cemeteries:** Graceland Cemetery (1860–present, non-sectarian, North Side), Rosehill Cemetery (1859–present, non-sectarian, North Side), Calvary Cemetery (Catholic, Evanston, just north of the city), St. Boniface (German Catholic), Jewish Graceland section and other Jewish cemeteries.
- **Online coverage:** FindAGrave and BillionGraves have substantial coverage of Chicago-area cemeteries. Graceland and Rosehill have their own online search tools.
- **Physical records:** Sexton's burial registers at each cemetery. The fire did not destroy most North Side and outlying cemeteries, so burial registers from before 1871 often survive.

### Newspaper records
- **Local papers:** The Chicago Tribune (founded 1847) is the major surviving paper. The Tribune's own building was destroyed in the fire but it resumed publication within days. The Chicago Times and Chicago Inter Ocean also covered the period. German-language papers (Illinois Staats-Zeitung) served the immigrant community.
- **Fire coverage:** Newspapers from October–December 1871 carried lists of the dead, missing persons notices, displaced family announcements, and relief distribution records — a unique genealogical source for fire victims.
- **Where held:** Chicago History Museum (extensive newspaper holdings); Newberry Library; ProQuest Historical Newspapers (Chicago Tribune digitized, subscription); Newspapers.com; Illinois Digital Newspaper Collections (state library).
- **Content value:** Obituaries, marriage notices, legal notices (estate proceedings, property transfers), missing persons, and relief lists from the fire period.

### Immigration and emigration records
- **Relevant ports:** Port of New York (Castle Garden, 1855–1890; Ellis Island from 1892), Port of Baltimore, Port of New Orleans, Port of Quebec (for many Scandinavians).
- **Record types:** Passenger arrival lists (NARA and Ancestry/FamilySearch, indexed), declarations of intention and naturalization petitions (Cook County Circuit Court and U.S. District Court), passport applications (NARA), alien registrations.
- **Note on inland filing:** Declarations of intention, naturalizations, and affidavits were all generated in Chicago, far from any port. The U.S. District Court for the Northern District of Illinois at NARA-Great Lakes holds federal naturalization records. Because Cook County's pre-fire court records were destroyed, the federal court series is especially important for naturalizations filed before 1871.
- **Content note:** Passenger lists record every person aboard a vessel, including infants and young children. When researching a family, examine the full manifest for all family members — children as young as newborns are listed.

### Tax records
- **Types:** Real property tax rolls, personal property tax lists.
- **Fire impact:** Pre-fire county tax rolls were destroyed in 1871. Post-fire rolls survive at the Cook County Assessor's Office.
