# Locality Guide: Massachusetts, United States (1620-1700)

## Jurisdiction overview
- **Formed:** Plymouth Colony established 1620; Massachusetts Bay Colony established 1628. The two merged into the Province of Massachusetts Bay in 1691.
- **County seat / administrative center:** Boston (Massachusetts Bay); Plymouth (Plymouth Colony)
- **Parent jurisdiction:** English Crown; after 1691, Province of Massachusetts Bay under the Crown
- **Population during period:** Governor Winthrop's Great Migration brought approximately 20,000 settlers between 1630 and 1640 (per Wikipedia, https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Massachusetts_Bay_Colony). No precise census figures exist for the colonial period; the first federal census is 1790.
- **Economy:** Subsistence farming, fishing, timber, and trade. Boston quickly became a significant Atlantic port.
- **Ethnic composition:** Predominantly English Puritan settlers, with smaller numbers of non-Puritan English. Indigenous peoples (Wampanoag, Massachusett, Nipmuc, and others) interacted with and appear in colonial court and land records.
- **Religious denominations:** Congregationalism was the established church of the colony. Small numbers of Quakers, Baptists, and Anglicans were present but faced legal restrictions in this period.
- **Key historical events:** Mayflower landing 1620; Massachusetts Bay Company charter 1628-1629; Great Migration 1630-1643; King Philip's War 1675-1676 (severely disrupted western communities and destroyed some records); Salem witchcraft trials 1692; merger into Province of Massachusetts Bay 1691.

## Boundary changes
- Plymouth Colony (1620-1691) and Massachusetts Bay Colony (1628-1691) were entirely separate jurisdictions with separate record series. Research the specific town to determine which colony it fell under.
- In 1691 both colonies merged under the Province of Massachusetts Bay charter.
- County formation within Massachusetts Bay began in 1643 (Middlesex, Essex, Suffolk, Norfolk counties). Plymouth Colony formed its own county structure. Knowing the county is essential to locating probate and land records, which were filed at the county level.
- The FamilySearch volume search returned one digitized volume for Suffolk County specifically (1630-1700 Congregational church records). Records for other counties may be held in different series.

## Available record types

### Vital records (civil registration)
- **Start date:** Town-level registration mandated by the colony in 1639 — this is a town-level requirement, not a statewide civil registration system in the modern sense. Statewide civil registration did not begin until 1842. The FamilySearch Wiki topic pages for Massachusetts Vital Records were not accessible in this session; the 1639 town-mandate date comes from the wiki_search result at https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Massachusetts_Genealogy#Colonial_Vital_Records and Wikipedia.
- **What exists:** Births, marriages, and deaths recorded in town books from 1639 (or from the town's founding date, if later). Coverage is uneven — some towns recorded diligently from the start; others have gaps.
- **Where held:** Original town books are held by individual town clerks or, for older records, at the Massachusetts Archives or local historical societies. FamilySearch has indexed these through the collection "Massachusetts, Town Vital Records, 1620-1890" (collection 2061550, 3,456,789 records, images available — indexed + images level of access, https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/2061550).
- **Gaps:** No requirement existed before 1639; the earliest Plymouth settlers (1620-1638) lack civil vital registration. King Philip's War (1675-1676) destroyed some western Massachusetts town records.
- **Pre-registration alternatives:** Congregational church records (baptisms, marriages, burials) from 1630 onward; the Great Migration Study series for arrivals before 1643.

### Church records
- **Denominations present:** Congregationalism was the dominant and established church throughout this period. Quakers and Baptists were present in small numbers but faced legal suppression; their records, where they survive, are scattered.
- **Record types:** Member admission lists, baptisms, marriages, burials, disciplinary proceedings (excommunications and admonishments — these name the person and often describe the offense, making them useful for family context). Confirmations were not a separate event in Congregational practice.
- **Where held:** Many early Congregational records have been published by the Colonial Society of Massachusetts and local historical society publications. FamilySearch holds "Massachusetts, Church Records, 1630-1920" (collection 1921657, 987,654 records, images available — indexed + images, https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1921657). One FamilySearch digitized volume specifically covers Suffolk County Congregational church admissions and baptisms, 1630-1700 (DGS 007612045, 121 images, full-text searchable but 0% name-indexed — must search by full text or browse image by image).
- **Language:** English throughout.

### Census records
- **Federal/national census:** None before 1790. The 1620-1700 period predates all federal enumerations.
- **State/provincial census:** No colonial-era general population census was taken.
- **Other enumerations:** Town proprietors' records and tax lists serve as the closest substitutes. FamilySearch has one digitized browse-only volume of Massachusetts town meeting and proprietors' records, 1620-1698 (DGS 007612044, 188 images, 0% name-indexed, not full-text searchable — must be browsed image by image). Church membership lists ("Half-Way Covenant" rolls and full-member rolls) provide another enumeration substitute.
- **Access:** Both FamilySearch digitized volumes covering this period require hands-on browsing; neither has a name index.

### Probate and court records
- **Types:** Wills, administrations, guardianships, inventories, estate distributions. Probate records begin in the 1630s in Massachusetts.
- **Date range:** From 1635 (FamilySearch collection 1678901 begins this year).
- **Where held:** County probate courts. For the 1620-1691 period, Plymouth Colony had its own probate series (published separately). FamilySearch holds "Massachusetts, Probate Records, 1635-1991" (collection 1678901, 567,890 records, images available, https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1678901 — indexed + images). County court records beyond probate (General Court minutes, quarter sessions) are held at the Massachusetts Archives.
- **Note:** Probate records are especially valuable for this period because they name heirs, describe real and personal property, and often establish family relationships that vital records do not capture.

### Land records
- **Survey system:** Metes and bounds. Massachusetts is a state-land state — the colonial government granted land, not the federal Bureau of Land Management.
- **Land-distribution jurisdiction:** The colonial General Court (Massachusetts Bay) and Plymouth Colony government issued original grants. County registries of deeds recorded subsequent transfers from the 1630s. The FamilySearch wiki_search result states deeds survive in "remarkably complete runs" at county registries of deeds (https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Massachusetts_Genealogy#Colonial_Vital_Records).
- **Types:** Original grants/patents, deeds, mortgages, town proprietors' records (which show original division of common land among founding settlers).
- **Date range:** From 1620s colonial grants onward.
- **Where held:** County registries of deeds (original deeds); Massachusetts Archives (colonial land grants and General Court records). The FamilySearch catalog was not queried in this session — searching the FamilySearch Catalog for individual counties will surface microfilmed deed books.

### Military records
- **Relevant conflicts:** Pequot War (1636-1638); King Philip's War (1675-1676) — the most destructive conflict in 17th-century New England.
- **Record types:** Muster rolls, pay lists, and pension applications. King Philip's War records include lists of men called up by town. Note that pensions for colonial service are distinct from federal pension files (which begin post-Revolution).
- **Where held:** Massachusetts Archives (Boston) holds muster rolls and related colonial military papers. NARA holds no colonial-era Massachusetts service records (those postdate 1775). Some King Philip's War muster lists have been published.

### Cemetery records
- **Major cemeteries:** Burial Hill (Plymouth), Granary Burying Ground and King's Chapel Burying Ground (Boston), and many town burying grounds established in this period. Most 17th-century Massachusetts cemeteries are old-ground burying grounds associated with the town or church.
- **Online coverage:** FindAGrave (https://www.findagrave.com) and BillionGraves include many transcribed colonial-era stones, though weathering has destroyed many 17th-century inscriptions.
- **Physical records:** Sexton records for this period are sparse or nonexistent for most towns; the burying ground was often maintained by the town meeting, not a dedicated sexton. Published gravestone surveys (e.g., by the Association for Gravestone Studies) cover many Massachusetts towns.

### Newspaper records
- **Local papers:** No newspapers were published in Massachusetts before 1704 (the Boston News-Letter, the first continuously published newspaper in the colonies, began that year). This record type does not apply to the 1620-1700 period.

### Immigration and emigration records
- **Relevant ports:** Boston was the primary port of arrival throughout this period. Salem, Plymouth, and other coastal towns also received arrivals.
- **Record types:** Ship passenger lists for colonial arrivals are compiled and reconstructed from multiple sources rather than surviving as uniform government-required manifests (official passenger list requirements came much later). The Great Migration Study series (NEHGS) is the most comprehensive compiled source for arrivals 1620-1643.
- **Where held:** FamilySearch collection "Massachusetts, Passenger Lists, 1820-1891" (collection 1784312) covers 1820 onward — it does not cover the colonial period. For 1620-1700 arrivals, use the Great Migration Study, published ship passenger list compilations (e.g., Filby's Passenger and Immigration Lists Index), and NEHGS databases.
- **Content note:** Passenger lists and compiled arrival records record every person aboard including infants. When researching a family, examine the full ship manifest for all family members.

### Tax records
- **Types:** Property (rateable estate) and poll ("list") taxes assessed by town and colony.
- **Date range:** Colonial tax lists begin from the 1630s, though survival is uneven.
- **Where held:** Massachusetts Archives holds many colonial tax lists. Town archives hold others. Tax lists are a critical substitute for census records in this period.
- **Substitute value:** Because no census exists for 1620-1700, tax lists placing a man in a town in a specific year are among the most useful records for establishing presence and approximate age.

### Other record types
- **Town meeting minutes:** Town government was conducted through the town meeting. Minutes name residents, record actions affecting families (poor relief, road assignments, disputes), and can establish presence and community standing. The FamilySearch digitized volume of Massachusetts town meeting and proprietors' records (DGS 007612044, 1620-1698, browse-only) is an example.
- **Court records (General Court and county courts):** Beyond probate, Massachusetts court records include civil suits, criminal proceedings, and disciplinary actions. They name ordinary people not found elsewhere. Court records for this period are held at the Massachusetts Archives.
- **Published town and county histories:** 19th- and early-20th-century local histories (e.g., the volumes in the Essex Institute Historical Collections, or town histories by authors such as Alonzo Lewis) frequently reprint early records and carry genealogies of founding families. Many are digitized on Google Books and the Internet Archive.
- **The Great Migration Study (NEHGS):** The multi-volume study by Robert Charles Anderson documents every known settler arriving in New England 1620-1643, with full citations. If your ancestor arrived in that window, this is the essential starting point before touching original records.

## Repository guide

### Online repositories
| Repository | Collections for this place | Access |
|---|---|---|
| FamilySearch | Massachusetts, Town Vital Records, 1620-1890 (3,456,789 records, collection 2061550); Massachusetts, Church Records, 1630-1920 (987,654 records, collection 1921657); Massachusetts, Probate Records, 1635-1991 (567,890 records, collection 1678901); plus 2 digitized browse/full-text volumes for 1620-1700 | Free |
| Ancestry.com | U.S. Federal Census Collection and other Massachusetts collections (general subscription link curated by FamilySearch: https://www.ancestry.com/search/collections/census/) | Subscription |
| NARA | Federal records post-1775 only; colonial-era Massachusetts records are not held at NARA | Free to search online; some records require in-person |
| FindAGrave | Cemetery transcriptions including colonial burying grounds (https://www.findagrave.com) | Free |
| Fold3 | Military records post-Revolution (https://www.fold3.com) — not applicable to 1620-1700 period | Subscription |

**Coverage of this survey:** The `volume_search` returned a total of 2 digitized volumes matching Massachusetts for 1620-1700, both detailed above. This is a complete result set for this query (no nextPageToken returned). The `collections_search` returned 5 collections total for Massachusetts; of those, 3 overlap the 1620-1700 target period (Town Vital Records, Church Records, Probate Records). The Passenger Lists collection begins 1820 and Naturalization Records begin 1790 — both postdate the target period and are listed for context only.

### Physical repositories
| Repository | Holdings | Access method |
|---|---|---|
| Massachusetts Archives, Boston | Original colony records, General Court minutes, governor's correspondence, court records, tax lists, military records from 1620s onward | In-person; some records available via correspondence; catalog at www.sec.state.ma.us/arc |
| New England Historic Genealogical Society (NEHGS), Boston | Largest genealogical library in New England; manuscript collections, published genealogies, Great Migration Study series | In-person and online (americanancestors.org, subscription); some collections free |
| County Registries of Deeds | Deed books from 1630s at county level; remarkably complete runs per FamilySearch wiki_search result | In-person or online (many counties have digitized deed books at the county website) |
| County Probate Courts | Original probate files supplementing FamilySearch digitized collection | In-person or mail request |
| Individual town clerks / town archives | Original town vital records books, town meeting minutes | In-person or mail; some towns have deposited older records at the Massachusetts Archives or county historical society |
| Colonial Society of Massachusetts | Published transcriptions of many early church and court records | Published volumes available at major research libraries |

## Records NOT online
- Original town meeting minutes for most towns (the FamilySearch volume covers only a subset; most remain at town archives or the Massachusetts Archives).
- County court records (quarter sessions, general sessions) beyond probate — held at the Massachusetts Archives, not digitized for 1620-1700.
- Most colonial tax lists — held at the Massachusetts Archives.
- Congregational church records not yet filmed or digitized (many local churches retain their own early registers).
- King Philip's War muster rolls — held at the Massachusetts Archives; some published but not in a major online database.
- Manuscript genealogies and family papers at NEHGS — searchable through americanancestors.org but not broadly digitized.

## Known record losses
- King Philip's War (1675-1676) destroyed several western Massachusetts towns and their records. Communities in the Connecticut River Valley (Springfield, Deerfield, Northampton) suffered the most severe losses.
- Some early town records were lost to fire, water damage, or simple neglect during the 17th and 18th centuries before archival preservation became systematic.
- No systematic record of what was lost exists; when a town's early records are sparse, consult the published 'Vital Records of [Town Name] to 1850' series, which may have captured data from records since lost.

## Research tips
- **Two colonies, two record series.** Plymouth Colony (1620-1691) and Massachusetts Bay Colony (1628-1691) kept separate records and have been separately published. The Plymouth Colony records are published and indexed independently. Determine which colony your ancestor's town fell under before searching.
- **The Old Style calendar.** Until 1752, England and its colonies used the Julian calendar, and the new year began on March 25. Colonial records often use double-date notation for January through March (e.g., '14 February 1688/89'). Do not assume the year without checking which convention the clerk used.
- **Start with compiled sources, then go to originals.** The Great Migration Study (NEHGS) and the Vital Records to 1850 series are well-indexed and will save significant browsing time. Use them as a roadmap to the original record.
- **Church membership is genealogically rich.** Congregational admission records name the person, often their spouse, and sometimes their children. Disciplinary records name witnesses and describe relationships. These are not just event records — they are community records.
- **Town proprietors' records.** The original proprietors of a town (those who shared in the division of common land) are listed in proprietors' books, which predate most deed transfers. If your ancestor was a founding settler, this is often the earliest documentary evidence placing them in the town.
- **Probate records for family reconstruction.** In the absence of census records, probate inventories and estate distributions naming heirs are often the best tool for reconstructing a complete family unit.
- **NEHGS americanancestors.org.** The New England Historic Genealogical Society's website has significant Massachusetts colonial-era databases, some free and some subscription, not replicated on FamilySearch or Ancestry. Check it independently.
- **wiki_search source:** https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Massachusetts_Genealogy#Colonial_Vital_Records and https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Massachusetts_Church_Records#Congregational

- **Substitute value:** Because no census exists for 1620-1700, tax lists placing a man in a town in a specific year are among the most useful records for establishing presence and approximate age.

### Other record types
- **Town meeting minutes:** Town government was conducted through the town meeting. Minutes name residents, record actions affecting families (poor relief, road assignments, disputes), and can establish presence and community standing. The FamilySearch digitized volume of Massachusetts town meeting and proprietors' records (DGS 007612044, 1620-1698, browse-only) is an example.
- **Court records (General Court and county courts):** Beyond probate, Massachusetts court records include civil suits, criminal proceedings, and disciplinary actions. They name ordinary people not found elsewhere. Court records for this period are held at the Massachusetts Archives.
- **Published town and county histories:** 19th- and early-20th-century local histories (e.g., the volumes in the Essex Institute Historical Collections, or town histories by authors such as Alonzo Lewis) frequently reprint early records and carry genealogies of founding families. Many are digitized on Google Books and the Internet Archive.
- **The Great Migration Study (NEHGS):** The multi-volume study by Robert Charles Anderson documents every known settler arriving in New England 1620-1643, with full citations. If your ancestor arrived in that window, this is the essential starting point before touching original records.

## Repository guide

### Online repositories
| Repository | Collections for this place | Access |
|---|---|---|
| FamilySearch | Massachusetts, Town Vital Records, 1620-1890 (3,456,789 records, collection 2061550); Massachusetts, Church Records, 1630-1920 (987,654 records, collection 1921657); Massachusetts, Probate Records, 1635-1991 (567,890 records, collection 1678901); plus 2 digitized browse/full-text volumes for 1620-1700 | Free |
| Ancestry.com | U.S. Federal Census Collection and other Massachusetts collections (general subscription link curated by FamilySearch: https://www.ancestry.com/search/collections/census/) | Subscription |
| NARA | Federal records post-1775 only; colonial-era Massachusetts records are not held at NARA | Free to search online; some records require in-person |
| FindAGrave | Cemetery transcriptions including colonial burying grounds (https://www.findagrave.com) | Free |
| Fold3 | Military records post-Revolution (https://www.fold3.com) — not applicable to 1620-1700 period | Subscription |

**Coverage of this survey:** The `volume_search` returned a total of 2 digitized volumes matching Massachusetts for 1620-1700, both detailed above. This is a complete result set for this query (no nextPageToken returned). The `collections_search` returned 5 collections total for Massachusetts; of those, 3 overlap the 1620-1700 target period (Town Vital Records, Church Records, Probate Records). The Passenger Lists collection begins 1820 and Naturalization Records begin 1790 — both postdate the target period and are listed for context only.

### Physical repositories
| Repository | Holdings | Access method |
|---|---|---|
| Massachusetts Archives, Boston | Original colony records, General Court minutes, governor's correspondence, court records, tax lists, military records from 1620s onward | In-person; some records available via correspondence; catalog at www.sec.state.ma.us/arc |
| New England Historic Genealogical Society (NEHGS), Boston | Largest genealogical library in New England; manuscript collections, published genealogies, Great Migration Study series | In-person and online (americanancestors.org, subscription); some collections free |
| County Registries of Deeds | Deed books from 1630s at county level; remarkably complete runs per FamilySearch wiki_search result | In-person or online (many counties have digitized deed books at the county website) |
| County Probate Courts | Original probate files supplementing FamilySearch digitized collection | In-person or mail request |
| Individual town clerks / town archives | Original town vital records books, town meeting minutes | In-person or mail; some towns have deposited older records at the Massachusetts Archives or county historical society |
| Colonial Society of Massachusetts | Published transcriptions of many early church and court records | Published volumes available at major research libraries |

## Records NOT online
- Original town meeting minutes for most towns (the FamilySearch volume covers only a subset; most remain at town archives or the Massachusetts Archives).
- County court records (quarter sessions, general sessions) beyond probate — held at the Massachusetts Archives, not digitized for 1620-1700.
- Most colonial tax lists — held at the Massachusetts Archives.
- Congregational church records not yet filmed or digitized (many local churches retain their own early registers).
- King Philip's War muster rolls — held at the Massachusetts Archives; some published but not in a major online database.
- Manuscript genealogies and family papers at NEHGS — searchable through americanancestors.org but not broadly digitized.

## Known record losses
- King Philip's War (1675-1676) destroyed several western Massachusetts towns and their records. Communities in the Connecticut River Valley (Springfield, Deerfield, Northampton) suffered the most severe losses.
- Some early town records were lost to fire, water damage, or simple neglect during the 17th and 18th centuries before archival preservation became systematic.
- No systematic record of what was lost exists; when a town's early records are sparse, consult the published 'Vital Records of [Town Name] to 1850' series, which may have captured data from records since lost.

## Research tips
- **Two colonies, two record series.** Plymouth Colony (1620-1691) and Massachusetts Bay Colony (1628-1691) kept separate records and have been separately published. The Plymouth Colony records are published and indexed independently. Determine which colony your ancestor's town fell under before searching.
- **The Old Style calendar.** Until 1752, England and its colonies used the Julian calendar, and the new year began on March 25. Colonial records often use double-date notation for January through March (e.g., '14 February 1688/89'). Do not assume the year without checking which convention the clerk used.
- **Start with compiled sources, then go to originals.** The Great Migration Study (NEHGS) and the Vital Records to 1850 series are well-indexed and will save significant browsing time. Use them as a roadmap to the original record.
- **Church membership is genealogically rich.** Congregational admission records name the person, often their spouse, and sometimes their children. Disciplinary records name witnesses and describe relationships. These are not just event records — they are community records.
- **Town proprietors' records.** The original proprietors of a town (those who shared in the division of common land) are listed in proprietors' books, which predate most deed transfers. If your ancestor was a founding settler, this is often the earliest documentary evidence placing them in the town.
- **Probate records for family reconstruction.** In the absence of census records, probate inventories and estate distributions naming heirs are often the best tool for reconstructing a complete family unit.
- **NEHGS americanancestors.org.** The New England Historic Genealogical Society's website has significant Massachusetts colonial-era databases, some free and some subscription, not replicated on FamilySearch or Ancestry. Check it independently.
- **wiki_search source:** https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Massachusetts_Genealogy#Colonial_Vital_Records and https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Massachusetts_Church_Records#Congregational

Locality guide written as **loc_001**.

---

Oklahoma Territory and the Indian Territory that stood alongside it from 1889 to statehood in 1907 are two distinct jurisdictions with completely different record systems, so the most important first step for any family is pinning down **which territory they lived in**.

**For Land Run settlers in the Unassigned Lands (Oklahoma Territory):**

- **Homestead application files at NARA (Record Group 49)** — often contain the settler's full name, age, origin state, and testimony from neighbors. The BLM GLO website ([glorecords.blm.gov](https://glorecords.blm.gov)) lets you search patents for free.
- **1890 Oklahoma special territorial census** — While the 1890 federal census was destroyed by fire, Oklahoma Territory's own 1890 special territorial census survived and is held at the **Oklahoma Historical Society**. This is one of the few places in the country where you can find people in that decade.
- **Church records and early newspapers** — Civil vital registration didn't exist statewide until after 1907, so territorial-era births and deaths are found in church registers, early Guthrie-area newspapers (which began publishing within days of the Land Run), and family affidavits filed in homestead proofs.

**For families in Indian Territory or with Native heritage:**

- **Dawes Commission enrollment jackets on FamilySearch** — essential for any family with possible Native heritage or residence in Indian Territory. Note these must be browsed image by image without a name index.

If you'd like to move from this survey to an actual research plan for a specific family who participated in the Land Run, that would be the natural next step.

quirks: Oklahoma Territory (1890-1907) and Indian Territory were two separate jurisdictions existing side by side; records were created in different systems. At statehood (1907) both merged into the State of Oklahoma — but pre-1907 records remain filed under whichever territory produced them.

The 1890 federal census was almost entirely destroyed by fire; Oklahoma Territory's special territorial census (1890) is one of the few surviving 1890-era enumerations in the nation and is held at the Oklahoma Historical Society.

Homestead land-entry case files are partially name-indexed on FamilySearch (collection 005221388, 74% searchable) and fully available at the Bureau of Land Management's GLO Records site (glorecords.blm.gov); rejected applications survive and often contain family details.

Dawes Commission enrollment jackets (FamilySearch volume 005221389) are browse-only — 0% name-indexed, not full-text searchable — and cover Indian Territory residents 1898-1910; they are essential for any ancestor with Native heritage or who lived in Indian Territory.
Territorial court records for Oklahoma Territory (1890-1907) are split between the National Archives at Fort Worth and the Oklahoma State Archives — search both.
Many Land Run settlers came from Kansas, Texas, Missouri, and Arkansas; tracing origins requires following them back to their departure-state records.

The Organic Act of May 2, 1890 established formal Oklahoma Territory government; records before that date were generated under informal or federal authority, and civil infrastructure was sparse in 1889-1890.
Civil vital registration (statewide) did not begin in Oklahoma until 1908 (after statehood); for 1889-1907 events, church records and territorial court records are the primary substitutes.
Land offices at Guthrie and Kingfisher received the original Land Run homestead applications in April 1889 — these records are at NARA (Record Group 49, General Land Office).
entry.guide_markdown:
# Locality Guide: Oklahoma Territory / Oklahoma (1889-1910)

## Jurisdiction overview
- **Formed:** Oklahoma Territory established by the Organic Act of May 2, 1890, from the former Unassigned Lands and adjoining areas. Indian Territory existed alongside it as a separate jurisdiction until both merged at Oklahoma statehood on November 16, 1907.
- **County seat / administrative center:** Guthrie was the territorial capital (1890-1907); Oklahoma City became the state capital at statehood.
- **Parent jurisdiction:** Federal authority (U.S. Department of the Interior) over territories; Kansas and Arkansas bounded the region to the north and east.
- **Population during period:** An estimated 50,000 settlers entered during the Land Run of April 22, 1889 alone (Wikipedia, Land Run of 1889). Population data from place_population returned no results for this jurisdiction, so census-year figures are not available from tools for this survey.
- **Economy:** Subsistence homesteading, small-scale agriculture, cattle ranching, and early commercial development in newly platted towns (Guthrie, Kingfisher, Norman, Stillwater). Indian Territory had established farming communities among the Five Civilized Tribes.
- **Ethnic composition:** Euro-American settlers from Kansas, Texas, Missouri, Arkansas, and beyond; members of the Five Civilized Tribes (Cherokee, Choctaw, Creek/Muscogee, Chickasaw, Seminole) in Indian Territory; freedmen (formerly enslaved people of tribal members); smaller numbers of African American settlers who founded all-Black towns.
- **Religious denominations:** Methodist, Baptist, Presbyterian, and Catholic missions had operated in Indian Territory from the 1820s onward; denominations established new congregations sporadically in Oklahoma Territory from 1889 forward.
- **Key historical events:** Land Run of 1889 (April 22); subsequent runs in 1891, 1892, 1893 (Cherokee Outlet), and 1895; Organic Act creating Oklahoma Territory (May 2, 1890); Dawes Commission enrollment of tribal members (1898-1914); Oklahoma statehood (November 16, 1907).

## Boundary changes
- Prior to April 22, 1889: the Unassigned Lands were part of Indian Territory with no non-Indian settlement permitted.
- May 2, 1890: Oklahoma Territory formally constituted from the Unassigned Lands and surrounding strips, with Guthrie as capital. Indian Territory remained a separate jurisdiction to the east.
- 1893-1906: Additional land runs and allotment acts progressively transferred land from tribal ownership and opened new counties in both territories.
- November 16, 1907: Oklahoma Territory and Indian Territory merged as the State of Oklahoma. Records created before that date remain under whichever territorial jurisdiction produced them — a searcher must know whether an ancestor lived in Oklahoma Territory or Indian Territory to find the right record series.

## Available record types

### Vital records (civil registration)
- **Start date:** Oklahoma did not have statewide civil registration during the territorial period. The FamilySearch Wiki pages for Oklahoma-specific vital records returned only a generic page and did not provide exact start-date details; the wiki should be consulted directly at https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Oklahoma_Vital_Records. Based on the wiki_search result noting that civil infrastructure was sparse in 1889-1890, statewide civil registration is documented to have begun after statehood (1907/1908), but the exact level and date must be confirmed on the Oklahoma Vital Records wiki page.
- **What exists:** County marriages from 1890 are indexed on FamilySearch (collection 2134789, 456,789 records, 228,394 images). This is the strongest civil vital record series for the period.
- **Where held:** County-level marriage registers at the county courthouse (county clerk); FamilySearch collection 2134789 is the online resource.
- **Gaps:** No statewide birth or death registration during most of the territorial period. The 1890 federal census is destroyed nationally — see Census section.
- **Pre-registration alternatives:** Church records (mission and church records, FamilySearch collection 1654321, 1820-1965); territorial court filings; homestead proof affidavits naming family members.

### Church records
- **Denominations present:** Methodist and Baptist missionaries were active in Indian Territory from the 1820s; Presbyterian and Catholic missions followed. Protestant denominations spread into Oklahoma Territory rapidly after 1889.
- **Record types:** Baptisms, marriages, burials, and mission correspondence.
- **Where held:** FamilySearch collection 1654321 (Oklahoma, Mission and Church Records, 1820-1965) holds 123,456 indexed records with 61,728 images. Denominational archives (e.g., Oklahoma United Methodist Archives, Baptist Historical Collection) hold additional records. The Oklahoma Historical Society also holds church records.
- **Language:** English for most records; some early mission records may be in tribal languages or contain transliterated names.

### Census records
- **Federal census:** The 1890 federal census was nearly entirely destroyed by fire — this is the most critical gap for Land Run research. The 1900 federal census (available on Ancestry and FamilySearch) and 1910 federal census are the first complete federal snapshots of the population after settlement.
- **Oklahoma Territory special census (1890):** This is one of the few surviving 1890-era enumerations in the nation. It is held at the Oklahoma Historical Society and partially available through Ancestry. This is an essential substitute for the destroyed federal census and should be the first census searched for Land Run settlers. (Source: FamilySearch wiki_search result, https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Oklahoma_Land_Records#Land_Run)
- **Indian Censuses and Rolls:** FamilySearch collection 1987432 (Oklahoma, Indian Censuses and Rolls, 1851-1959) contains 567,890 records with 283,945 images. These cover tribal members and freedmen in Indian Territory and are essential for any ancestor with Native heritage or who lived in Indian Territory.
- **Other enumerations:** County-level tax rolls from the 1890s document early settlers; held at county courthouses and the Oklahoma State Archives.
- **Access:** 1900 and 1910 federal censuses are indexed + images on both Ancestry and FamilySearch. The 1890 Oklahoma Territory special census is partially indexed. Indian censuses are indexed + images on FamilySearch (collection 1987432).

### Probate and court records
- **Types:** Wills, administrations, guardianships, inventories; territorial district court civil and criminal cases; naturalizations.
- **Date range:** Oklahoma Territory territorial courts from 1890; county-level probate from county formation dates (most counties formed 1890-1907).
- **Where held:** Territorial court records (1890-1907) are split between the National Archives at Fort Worth (RG 21, territorial district courts) and the Oklahoma State Archives in Oklahoma City. County probate records are at the county courthouse. The wiki_search result at https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Oklahoma_Territorial_Records#Courts confirms this dual custody.
- **Naturalization:** Pre-1906 naturalizations could be filed in any court of record, including territorial district courts. Check both Fort Worth NARA and the Oklahoma State Archives.

### Land records
- **Survey system:** Rectangular survey (federal public domain land state).
- **Land-distribution jurisdiction:** The U.S. General Land Office administered homestead entries. Original land offices for the 1889 Land Run were at Guthrie and Kingfisher. Records are in Record Group 49 at NARA in Washington, D.C.
- **Types:** Homestead applications, final certificate proofs (with witnesses and family details), land patents, and rejected applications. BLM GLO patents are searchable at glorecords.blm.gov.
- **FamilySearch coverage:** Collection 1541872 (Oklahoma and Indian Territory, Early Land Records, 1834-1907) holds 234,567 records and 117,283 images. Volume 005221388 (land-entry case files / homestead final proofs, 1889-1907) has 402 images and is 74% name-indexed — indexed + images level. (Source: https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Oklahoma_Land_Records#Land_Run)

Locality guide written as **loc_001**.

---

Oklahoma Territory and the Indian Territory that stood alongside it from 1889 to statehood in 1907 are two distinct jurisdictions with completely different record systems, so the most important first step for any family is pinning down which territory they lived in. For Land Run settlers in the Unassigned Lands (future Oklahoma Territory), land records are the most reliable surviving source: the homestead application file at NARA (Record Group 49) often contains the settler's full name, age, origin state, and testimony from neighbors, and the BLM GLO website (glorecords.blm.gov) lets you search patents for free. For families in Indian Territory or with Native heritage, the Dawes Commission enrollment jackets on FamilySearch are essential, though they must be browsed image by image with no name index.

If you would like to move from this survey to an actual research plan for a specific family who participated in the Land Run, that would be the natural next step.

- **Parent jurisdiction:** Federal authority (U.S. Department of the Interior) over territories; Kansas and Arkansas bounded the region to the north and east.

- **Economy:** Subsistence homesteading, small-scale agriculture, cattle ranching, and early commercial development in newly platted towns (Guthrie, Kingfisher, Norman, Stillwater). Indian Territory had established farming communities among the Five Civilized Tribes.
- **Ethnic composition:** Euro-American settlers from Kansas, Texas, Missouri, Arkansas, and beyond; members of the Five Civilized Tribes (Cherokee, Choctaw, Creek/Muscogee, Chickasaw, Seminole) in Indian Territory; freedmen (formerly enslaved people of tribal members); smaller numbers of African American settlers who founded all-Black towns.
- **Religious denominations:** Methodist, Baptist, Presbyterian, and Catholic missions had operated in Indian Territory from the 1820s onward; denominations established new congregations sporadically in Oklahoma Territory from 1889 forward.
- **Key historical events:** Land Run of 1889 (April 22); subsequent runs in 1891, 1892, 1893 (Cherokee Outlet), and 1895; Organic Act creating Oklahoma Territory (May 2, 1890); Dawes Commission enrollment of tribal members (1898-1914); Oklahoma statehood (November 16, 1907).

Here's what the locality-guide agent found:

---

**Alabama Before Statehood (~1780–1819): Locality Research Guide**

The most important framing: **"Alabama" didn't exist as a jurisdiction in 1800.** The territory was split between two completely different record systems:

1. **The interior** — eastern Mississippi Territory (organized 1798). Records at the Alabama Department of Archives and History (ADAH) in Montgomery and NARA's Atlanta facility: territorial census lists, tax records, court records, land office records. Almost none are digitized online.

2. **The Mobile area** — Spanish colonial territory until 1813. Records are Spanish colonial documents at the Archivo General de Indias in Seville (copies at the Library of Congress and Mobile Municipal Archives), plus Mobile Catholic parish registers back to 1703.

---

**On digitized/browsable volumes specifically:** FamilySearch's volume search returned **zero** digitized browsable image volumes for Alabama in this period — a genuine digitization gap, not a missing-records gap. The four FamilySearch indexed collections for Alabama all begin at 1803–1810 at the earliest, only touching the tail end of the territorial period.

---

**Best online substitutes:**

- **BLM General Land Office** (glorecords.blm.gov) — free, name-searchable federal land patents from ~1803 onward, with patent images
- **War of 1812 / Creek War pension files** at NARA (many indexed at Fold3) — pension applications often contain family affidavits with marriage dates and children's names

---

**Bottom line:** For this place and period, serious research will require physical or microfilm access at ADAH or NARA Atlanta. If you want to go further, share who you're looking for and a targeted research plan can be built from here.

quirks: Alabama did not exist as a jurisdiction in 1800 — the region was then the eastern part of the Mississippi Territory (1798-1817). Records created before 1817 were generated under Mississippi Territory authority, not Alabama authority. Search Mississippi Territory sources first for any event before 1817.

The Mobile area was under Spanish rule (as part of the Mobile District of Spanish West Florida) from 1780 until 1813 — not under U.S. or territorial authority. Vital, land, and church records for Mobile-area events in this window are Spanish colonial records, held primarily at the Archivo General de Indias in Seville, with copies at the Library of Congress and the Mobile Municipal Archives.

FamilySearch volume_search returned zero digitized browsable volumes for Alabama with date ranges overlapping 1780-1830. This is a digitization gap, not evidence that records do not exist — pre-statehood records exist but are largely undigitized or held in physical repositories.

FamilySearch's four Alabama indexed collections all begin in 1803 or later (marriages 1809, probate 1809, church 1803, census substitutes 1810). No FamilySearch indexed collection covers the full pre-statehood territorial window.

Mississippi Territory territorial censuses of 1801, 1805, 1808, and 1810 enumerated settlers in present-day Alabama. These are held at the Alabama Department of Archives and History (ADAH) in Montgomery, per FamilySearch Wiki (https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Alabama_Genealogy#Territorial_Records).

French colonial records (1702-1763) are held at the Archives Nationales d'Outre-Mer in Aix-en-Provence, France, with microfilm copies at the Mobile Municipal Archives, per FamilySearch Wiki (https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Alabama_Genealogy#Colonial_Records).

Land grants in the pre-statehood period come from three distinct systems: Spanish/British colonial grants (physical archives overseas or at the Library of Congress), Mississippi Territory grants (ADAH and NARA), and post-1817 U.S. federal land patents (Bureau of Land Management GLO website). A single family may have records across all three systems.

There was no civil vital registration (births, deaths) in the Alabama region during the pre-statehood period. Church records are the only vital-events source for this window, and even those are sparse outside the Mobile Catholic parish.

Alabama borders Georgia (east), Tennessee (north), Mississippi (west), and Florida (south). Settlers who crossed the Georgia or Carolina border into the territory often left records in both their origin county and the new territory. Search Georgia county records (especially Washington, Burke, and Wilkes counties) for origins of early Alabama settlers.

The Creek War of 1813-1814 and earlier Creek/Cherokee conflicts generated U.S. military records at NARA that may be the only contemporaneous documentation of some settler families in the interior of present-day Alabama.
entry.guide_markdown:
# Locality Guide: Alabama Region (Pre-Statehood, circa 1780–1819)

## Jurisdiction overview

- **Formed:** Alabama achieved statehood on December 14, 1819. In 1800 the region did not exist as a named U.S. jurisdiction; it was the eastern portion of the Mississippi Territory (organized 1798). From 1817 to 1819 it was the Alabama Territory.
- **Administrative center:** Territorial capital was St. Stephens (present-day Washington County, Alabama); Mobile was the dominant town in the south.
- **Parent jurisdiction:** Mississippi Territory (1798–1817), itself carved from land ceded by Georgia and from territory taken from Spain. Before 1798, the interior was nominally claimed by Britain (1763–1780) and Spain (1780 onward); the Mobile coastal area was under Spanish administration until U.S. forces seized it in 1813.
- **Population during period:** Population data for the pre-statehood territory was not returned by tool queries. The 1810 federal census, which covered the Mississippi Territory, recorded approximately 9,000 free inhabitants in the eastern (present-day Alabama) portion. Growth accelerated sharply after the Creek War ended in 1814.
- **Economy:** Subsistence agriculture and small-scale cotton cultivation in the interior; trading post economy at Mobile; fur trade and river commerce along the Tombigbee and Alabama rivers.
- **Ethnic composition:** Creek and Cherokee nations occupied most of the interior until cessions accelerating after 1805. European-American settlers came predominantly from Georgia, the Carolinas, Virginia, and Tennessee. The Mobile area had a long-established French Creole and Spanish Creole community. Enslaved African Americans were present from the earliest European settlements and grew rapidly in numbers after 1810.
- **Religious denominations:** Roman Catholic (dominant in Mobile, established 1703); Baptist and Methodist circuit riders served the interior settlements; Presbyterian missions operated among some Creek communities.
- **Key historical events:** Spanish seizure of Mobile from Britain (1780); U.S. organization of the Mississippi Territory (1798); Burr Conspiracy land schemes (1805–1807); West Florida Rebellion and U.S. annexation of the Mobile District (1813); Creek War (1813–1814), which opened the interior to mass Anglo-American settlement; organization of the Alabama Territory (1817); statehood (1819).

## Boundary changes

This is a complex multi-layer jurisdictional history:

- **Before 1763:** French colonial territory (Province of Louisiana). Records generated under French administration.
- **1763–1780:** British West Florida. Records generated under British colonial administration.
- **1780–1813:** Spanish West Florida / Mobile District. The Mobile area remained under Spanish administration. Records generated under Spanish colonial authority.
- **1798–1817:** Mississippi Territory organized by the U.S. Congress. Initially a narrow strip; expanded in 1804 and 1812 to encompass all of present-day Alabama and Mississippi. The territory's eastern half (present-day Alabama) was under U.S. territorial authority, but Spain still physically held Mobile until 1813.
- **1813:** U.S. forces seized Mobile from Spain. The Mobile District was incorporated into the Mississippi Territory.
- **1817–1819:** Alabama Territory, organized when the western half of the Mississippi Territory became the state of Mississippi.
- **1819:** Alabama statehood.

The practical implication: a researcher working on events around 1800 in the Mobile area is working with Spanish colonial records, not American territorial records. A researcher working on the interior around 1800 is working with Mississippi Territory records. These are fundamentally different record systems held in different archives.

## Available record types

### Vital records (civil registration)

- **Start date:** There was no civil registration of births or deaths in the Alabama region during the pre-statehood period. Alabama did not mandate statewide vital registration until 1908.
- **Marriage records:** County-level marriage bonds and licenses began when individual counties were formed within the territory. Washington County (the first Alabama county, formed 1800) began marriage records from approximately 1809. FamilySearch has an indexed collection, **Alabama, County Marriages, 1809–1950** (collection 1598408, 612,345 records, with images), covering marriages beginning at the very end of the territorial period.
- **Gaps:** There is no civil record of births or deaths for the period surveyed. Events before individual county formation (Washington County, 1800; Madison County, 1808; Baldwin County, 1809) have no civil record at all.
- **Pre-registration alternatives:** Church records are the only vital-events source for births, deaths, and some marriages. See Church Records below.

### Church records

- **Denominations present:** Roman Catholic (Mobile, established by the French in 1703 and maintained through Spanish administration); Baptist and Methodist (interior settlements, circuit-rider ministry, organized congregations from approximately 1808–1815).
- **Record types:** Catholic registers at Mobile (Cathedral of the Immaculate Conception, established 1703) include baptisms, marriages, and burials and constitute the most continuous vital-events record for any community in present-day Alabama before 1819. Interior Protestant records are fragmentary and scattered.
- **Where held:** Mobile Catholic records are held at the Archdiocese of Mobile Archives and have been partially microfilmed. FamilySearch has an indexed collection, **Alabama, Church Records, 1803–1950** (collection 1986396, 156,789 records, images available), which begins in 1803 and covers the final years of the territorial period and early statehood. The specific coverage within that collection at the county or congregation level was not returned by tool queries.
- **Language:** Mobile Catholic records through the early territorial period were kept in French and Spanish. Interior Protestant records (where they survive) are in English.
- **Access:** The FamilySearch church records collection (1986396) is indexed and browsable online. Earlier Mobile Catholic registers may require contact with the Archdiocese of Mobile Archives or the Mobile Municipal Archives.

### Census records

- **Federal/national census:** The 1800 federal census covered the Mississippi Territory as a whole. The 1810 federal census covered the Mississippi Territory including present-day Alabama. The 1820 census was the first to cover Alabama as a state. The 1800 schedule for the Mississippi Territory is largely extant; the 1810 schedule for the eastern (Alabama) portion is partially extant.
- **Territorial censuses:** The Mississippi Territory conducted enumerations in 1801, 1805, 1808, and 1810 covering settlers in present-day Alabama. Per the FamilySearch Wiki ([Alabama Genealogy — Territorial Records](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Alabama_Genealogy#Territorial_Records)), these are held at the Alabama Department of Archives and History (ADAH) in Montgomery.
- **Compiled index:** FamilySearch has **Alabama, Compiled Census and Census Substitutes Index, 1810–1890** (collection 2016756, 287,634 records, name-indexed, no images). This index covers the very end of the territorial period (1810) and early statehood. It is a name index only — no images are attached.
- **Spanish colonial census:** The Spanish conducted census returns (padrones) of the Mobile District population periodically between 1780 and 1813. Per the FamilySearch Wiki ([Alabama Genealogy — Colonial Records](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Alabama_Genealogy#Colonial_Records)), these are held at the Archivo General de Indias in Seville, with copies at the Library of Congress.
- **Access:** The ADAH territorial census holdings are physical; contact ADAH directly (Montgomery, AL). The FamilySearch compiled census index (2016756) is searchable online. Spanish padrones require contact with the Library of Congress or the Mobile Municipal Archives for the copies.

### Probate and court records

- **Types:** Wills, estate administrations, guardianships, inventories. These were territorial and county-level records once counties were formed.
- **Date range:** Washington County (formed 1800) has the earliest probate records in present-day Alabama. FamilySearch has **Alabama, Probate Records, 1809–1985** (collection 1537764, 438,210 records, with images), beginning in 1809.
- **Territorial court records:** The Mississippi Territory had a general court and district courts. Records of the territorial courts for the eastern (Alabama) district are held at ADAH and NARA (Atlanta regional facility). These include civil suits, criminal cases, and land dispute adjudications that may name early settlers not documented elsewhere.
- **Where held:** County-level probate records for Washington, Baldwin, and Madison counties from the territorial period are at the respective county courthouses and partially at ADAH. The FamilySearch probate collection (1537764) covers from 1809 with images.
- **Access:** Indexed and browsable online through FamilySearch for records from 1809 onward. Earlier territorial court records are physical only at ADAH and NARA Atlanta.

### Land records

- **Survey system:** U.S. rectangular survey system (township and range) applied to the Alabama region from approximately 1803 onward, administered by the General Land Office (now Bureau of Land Management). Prior colonial grants used metes-and-bounds descriptions.
- **Land-distribution jurisdiction:** Three distinct systems operated in overlapping time periods:
  1. **Spanish and British colonial grants** (pre-1798 for the interior; pre-1813 for the Mobile area): Original grants filed with colonial authorities in Seville (Spanish) or London (British). Copies and confirmations of these grants were adjudicated by U.S. land commissioners after American takeover and are partially at NARA and ADAH.
  2. **Mississippi Territory land grants** (1798–1817): The U.S. Land Office at St. Stephens (established 1803) administered public land sales and grant confirmations in the eastern territory. Records are at NARA (Atlanta) and ADAH.
  3. **U.S. federal land patents** (post-1817 for Alabama Territory; ongoing after 1819): The Bureau of Land Management General Land Office (BLM GLO) website (glorecords.blm.gov) provides a searchable database of federal land patents issued for Alabama, including patents from the territorial period.
- **Types:** Deeds, grants, patents, land entry case files, survey plats, creek and cherokee cession maps, and bounty land warrants for veterans.
- **Where held:** BLM GLO website for federal patents (searchable online). ADAH for territorial land office records. NARA Atlanta for U.S. Land Office records. County courthouses for deed books once counties were recording.
- **Access:** BLM GLO is free and searchable online. ADAH and NARA holdings are physical, accessible in person or by correspondence.

### Military records

- **Relevant conflicts:** Creek War (1813–1814); War of 1812 (which intersected with the Creek War); earlier militia skirmishes during the territorial period.
- **Record types:** Service records and pension files for participants in the Creek War and War of 1812 are held at NARA (Washington, D.C.) and are partially digitized and indexed at Fold3 and Ancestry. Bounty land warrants were issued to War of 1812 veterans.
- **Militia rolls:** Mississippi Territory militia rolls for the eastern (Alabama) district survive partially at ADAH. These name heads of household who were mustered for service and constitute an important census substitute for the period.
- **Where held:** NARA (Washington, D.C.) for federal service records and pensions. ADAH for territorial militia rolls. Fold3 (subscription) for digitized pension files.
- **Access:** Many War of 1812 and Creek War service records and pension files are indexed and browsable at Fold3 and Ancestry. ADAH militia rolls are physical only.

### Cemetery records

- **Coverage:** Formal cemeteries in the pre-statehood period were primarily associated with churches, particularly the Mobile Catholic parish (established 1703) and early Protestant congregations in the interior.
- **Online coverage:** FindAGrave (findagrave.com) indexes many Alabama cemeteries including some with graves from the territorial period, though coverage of pre-1820 burials is very sparse.
- **Physical records:** Sexton records for the pre-statehood period, where they survive, are held at the originating church or at ADAH.
- **Access:** FindAGrave is free. Physical sexton records require contact with individual churches or ADAH.

### Newspaper records

- **Local papers:** The *Mobile Centinel* (founded 1811) was among the first newspapers in present-day Alabama. The *Halcyon and Tombeckbe Public Advertiser* (St. Stephens, 1818) was among the first inland Alabama papers.
- **Content value:** Territorial-era newspapers carried land sale notices, legal notices, and some personal announcements. They are an underused source for the period.
- **Where held:** The Alabama Department of Archives and History holds microfilm of early Alabama newspapers. Some are available through Newspapers.com (subscription) and the Library of Congress Chronicling America project (chroniclingamerica.loc.gov, free).
- **Access:** Chronicling America is searchable online and free. ADAH microfilm requires in-person access or reproduction requests.

### Immigration and emigration records

- **Relevant ports:** Mobile (Gulf Coast port); New Orleans (the dominant port for Gulf Coast immigration). The interior was reached overland via the Natchez Trace or Georgia roads.
- **Record types:** U.S. passenger arrival records (customs lists) at Mobile and New Orleans from 1820 onward are at NARA. Pre-1820 arrival records for the territorial period are sparse and largely not in standard NARA passenger list series.
- **Naturalization records:** Pre-1906 naturalizations in the Mississippi Territory and early Alabama were filed in territorial and county courts. Territorial court naturalizations are at NARA Atlanta and ADAH.
- **Note:** The most significant migration into the Alabama region circa 1800–1819 was overland from Georgia and the Carolinas, not by sea. These migrants would have left records in their origin counties (Georgia, South Carolina, North Carolina) rather than in arrival manifests. Research the origin state's records first.

### Tax records

- **Types:** Territorial and county property tax lists were assessed annually once county government was established. Washington County (formed 1800) has the earliest extant tax lists in present-day Alabama.
- **Where held:** Territorial and county tax records are held at ADAH and individual county courthouses.
- **Substitute value:** Tax lists from the territorial period (approximately 1800–1819) serve as the primary census substitute for years between enumerations and for persons who do not appear in the territorial censuses. They name heads of household, list taxable property (including enslaved persons), and can establish annual residence.
- **Access:** ADAH holdings are physical, accessible in person or by reproduction request. No FamilySearch indexed collection for Alabama tax records in this period was found.

### Other record types

- **Creek and Cherokee cession records:** Land cession treaties between the U.S. and the Creek and Cherokee nations (1805, 1814, and later) contain schedules of individual Native American property holders and claimants that name both Native Americans and mixed-heritage families. These are at NARA and are partially published.
- **Spanish colonial church records (Mobile):** Per the FamilySearch Wiki ([Alabama Genealogy — Colonial Records](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Alabama_Genealogy#Colonial_Records)), the Mobile District Spanish colonial records include census returns (padrones), church registers, and land grants at the Archivo General de Indias in Seville, with copies at the Library of Congress. These are the most genealogically rich records for the Mobile area before 1813 and are largely in Spanish and French.
- **Town and county histories:** Published local histories of early Alabama counties (many produced in the 1880s–1920s) often transcribe or abstract early land, court, and church records now lost. These are available at ADAH, the Alabama Genealogical Society, and major research libraries.
- **Territorial legislative and executive records:** The Mississippi Territory legislative journals and executive papers name residents in petitions, appointments, and land claims. These are at NARA and ADAH.

## Repository guide

### Online repositories

| Repository | Collections for this place | Access |
|---|---|---|
| FamilySearch | Alabama, County Marriages, 1809–1950 (1,224,690 persons, images); Alabama, Probate Records, 1809–1985 (438,210 records, images); Alabama, Church Records, 1803–1950 (156,789 records, images); Alabama, Compiled Census and Census Substitutes Index, 1810–1890 (287,634 records, index only, no images) | Free |
| BLM General Land Office (glorecords.blm.gov) | Federal land patents for Alabama including territorial-era patents | Free |
| Fold3 | War of 1812 and Creek War service records and pension files; some digitized NARA records | Subscription |
| Ancestry | War of 1812 records; some early Alabama county records | Subscription |
| Chronicling America (Library of Congress) | Early Alabama newspapers (Mobile Centinel and others) | Free |
| FindAGrave | Cemetery transcriptions (sparse pre-1820) | Free |

**Coverage of this survey:** FamilySearch `volume_search` returned zero digitized browsable volumes for Alabama with date ranges overlapping 1780–1830, even when searched across multiple record-type groups. This is a true digitization gap for the pre-statehood window: no FamilySearch-hosted browsable image volumes for this period and place were found. The four FamilySearch indexed collections begin in 1803–1810 and are the only FamilySearch online holdings overlapping the period. This is consistent with the general state of pre-statehood Alabama digitization: the richest holdings remain in physical repositories.

### Physical repositories

| Repository | Holdings | Access method |
|---|---|---|
| Alabama Dept. of Archives and History (ADAH), Montgomery | Territorial census lists (1801, 1805, 1808, 1810); territorial court and land office records; county tax lists from c.1800; militia rolls; early county records; territorial newspapers on microfilm | In-person; some reproduction requests by mail/email |
| NARA Atlanta regional facility | Mississippi Territory court records; U.S. Land Office records (St. Stephens); early naturalization records | In-person; reproduction requests |
| NARA Washington, D.C. | War of 1812 and Creek War service records and pension files; territorial legislative records | In-person; many records available via Fold3 |
| Archdiocese of Mobile Archives | Mobile Catholic baptism, marriage, and burial registers from 1703 onward | Contact archives directly |
| Mobile Municipal Archives | Microfilm of French and Spanish colonial records for the Mobile area; Mobile Centinel microfilm | In-person |
| Library of Congress | Microfilm copies of Spanish colonial records (Archivo General de Indias) relating to Mobile District | In-person |
| Archivo General de Indias, Seville, Spain | Original Spanish colonial records for the Mobile District (census, land grants, church registers) | In-person or through Library of Congress copies |
| Archives Nationales d'Outre-Mer, Aix-en-Provence, France | French colonial records for Louisiana/Alabama 1702–1763 | In-person; microfilm at Mobile Municipal Archives |

## Records NOT online

The following record types exist for the pre-statehood Alabama region but are not available in any online database in searchable or browsable form:

- Mississippi Territory territorial censuses (1801, 1805, 1808) — ADAH, physical only
- Territorial tax lists (approximately 1800–1817) — ADAH and county courthouses, physical only
- Mississippi Territory court records for the eastern (Alabama) district — NARA Atlanta, physical only
- Mississippi Territory land office records (St. Stephens, 1803–1817) — NARA Atlanta and ADAH, physical only
- Spanish colonial padrones (census returns) for the Mobile District (1780–1813) — Archivo General de Indias / Library of Congress copies, physical only
- French colonial records (1702–1763) — Archives Nationales d'Outre-Mer / Mobile Municipal Archives microfilm, physical only
- Alabama Territory militia rolls — ADAH, physical only
- Territorial legislative journals and executive papers — NARA and ADAH, physical only
- Creek and Cherokee cession schedules (some) — NARA, partially published in print

## Known record losses

- No specific courthouse fires or mass record destructions for the pre-statehood Alabama territorial period were identified in tool results. However, given the rudimentary record-keeping infrastructure of a frontier territory, many records were likely never created formally or have not survived in any organized collection.
- Mobile's Catholic registers have significant gaps in the late 18th-century Spanish period; some volumes were damaged or lost during multiple colonial transitions.
- ADAH has noted that not all territorial records were systematically transferred when the Mississippi Territory was divided; some records that should be at ADAH may be at Mississippi's Department of Archives and History in Jackson.

## Research tips

- **Start with jurisdiction, not place name.** In 1800, "Alabama" did not exist. File your search under Mississippi Territory (for the interior) or Spanish West Florida / Mobile District (for the Mobile area). Tools and databases that search under "Alabama" will miss territorial-era records filed under the earlier jurisdiction names. See FamilySearch Wiki: [Alabama Genealogy — Territorial Records](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Alabama_Genealogy#Territorial_Records).
- **Separate the Mobile area from the interior.** Before 1813, Mobile was Spanish territory; the interior was U.S. Mississippi Territory. A researcher whose ancestor appears in the interior in 1800 and in Mobile in 1812 is dealing with two completely different record systems and two different archives.
- **Check origin-state records first.** Most Anglo-American settlers in the territory around 1800 came from Georgia, South Carolina, North Carolina, Virginia, or Tennessee within the previous one to two decades. Early records (births, earlier land, family connections) are far more likely in the origin state than in the territory. Search the origin state before exhausting Alabama sources.
- **Tax lists are your census substitutes.** Between the 1810 and 1820 federal censuses, and for years not covered by the territorial enumerations, tax lists at ADAH are often the only annual record placing a specific head of household in the territory.
- **The BLM GLO site is the fastest entry point for land.** For settlers who entered public land after approximately 1803, the Bureau of Land Management GLO website (glorecords.blm.gov) is free, searchable by name, and returns patent images. This is the first stop for any land research in the territorial period.
- **War of 1812 / Creek War pension files are genealogically rich.** Pension application files at NARA (many indexed at Fold3 and Ancestry) often contain family affidavits, marriage evidence, and children's names — frequently the only documentation of an early Alabama family's vital events.
- **Do not overlook Mississippi's archives.** The Mississippi Department of Archives and History (MDAH) in Jackson holds records of the Mississippi Territory that were retained on the western side of the split when Mississippi became a state in 1817. Some records relevant to present-day Alabama families may be there rather than at ADAH.
- **Spanish colonial church records at Mobile go back to 1703.** If you have Mobile-area ancestry, the Catholic registers are the most continuous genealogical record source in the entire state and predate any American-era source by over a century. The Archdiocese of Mobile Archives is the first contact point.
- **Naming customs:** Southern Anglo-American families of this period commonly used maternal surnames as given names and frequently named children after grandparents. This can help identify family connections when direct vital records are absent. The FamilySearch Wiki did not return an Alabama-specific naming customs page; no additional specifics beyond general Southern conventions can be confirmed from tool results.
